source: Body Language: How to Read Others' Thoughts by Their Gestures (Pease, 1981)

assets.topic: Scrub the Origins: From Silent Film and Darwin to the Science of the Non-Verbalist
assets.visual_frame_description: A time-scrubber playhead glides across a silent film set where Chaplin gestures to the camera, then lands on Darwin's 1872 volume opening onto a modern research lab; a bar chart tilts showing 7 per cent verbal, 38 per cent vocal, 55 per cent non-verbal, while a woman's look to kill leaves a man frozen in place.
assets.player_mission: Your mission is to scrub through the birth of body language study: how a new breed of social scientist called the non-verbalist watches people's cues and signals, why the field only took off in the 1960s and reached the public via Julius Fast in 1970, how Chaplin and the silent actors pioneered gesture communication, and how Darwin's 1872 book spawned the modern field. Then weigh the numbers: the million recorded cues, Mehrabian's 7-38-55 split, and Birdwhistell's finding that over 65 per cent of face-to-face communication is non-verbal.
key_concepts: Pease introduces the non-verbalist as a new kind of social scientist who delights in watching the non-verbal cues and signals of human beings wherever people interact, just as the birdwatcher delights in watching birds.

The non-verbal aspects of communication have been actively studied on any scale only since the 1960s, and the public became aware of their existence only since Julius Fast published a book about body language in 1970.

Charlie Chaplin and many other silent movie actors were the pioneers of non-verbal communication skills because gestures and other body signals were the only means of communication available on the screen.

Each silent movie actor was classed as good or bad by the extent to which he could use gestures and other body signals to communicate effectively, while those with good verbal skills prevailed once talking films became popular.

The most influential pre-twentieth-century work on body language was Charles Darwin's The Expression of the Emotions in Man and Animals, published in 1872, which spawned the modern studies of facial expressions and body language.
Since Darwin's time researchers have noted and recorded almost one million nonverbal cues and signals.
Albert Mehrabian found that the total impact of a message is about 7 per cent verbal, 38 per cent vocal, and 55 per cent non-verbal.
Professor Birdwhistell estimated that the average person actually speaks words for a total of about ten or eleven minutes a day and that the average sentence takes only about 2.5 seconds.
Birdwhistell found that the verbal component of a face-to-face conversation is less than 35 per cent and that over 65 per cent of communication is done non-verbally.

Most researchers agree that the verbal channel is used primarily for conveying information, while the non-verbal channel is used for negotiating interpersonal attitudes and in some cases as a substitute for verbal messages.
A woman can give a man a look to kill and convey a very clear message to him without opening her mouth.

Birdwhistell maintains that words and movements occur together with such predictability that a well-trained person should be able to tell what movement a man is making by listening to his voice, and he learned to tell what language a person was speaking by watching his gestures.

assets.topic: Dialogue on the Signals: Inborn, Genetic, Learned and the Perceptive Mind
assets.visual_frame_description: A seminar table where one side argues inborn and the other argues learned while an evidence projector shows Eibl-Eibesfeldt's deaf-blind child smiling, Ekman's five culture masks, and a coat being put on right arm first by a man and left arm first by a woman; a hunch bubble floats over a listener whose arms are crossed and chin is down.
assets.player_mission: Your mission is to stage a dialogue on how signals get made: debate whether gestures are inborn, genetic, learned or cultural, using the evidence from deaf and blind children, five divergent cultures, and our ape relatives, and then walk the universal basics, from smiling and nodding to the shoulder shrug, and the claim that the human animal rarely notices that his body tells one story while his voice tells another. Then defend women's intuition: why perceptiveness is a technical reading of cues, why a hunch is a mismatch of channels, and why mothers become sharp negotiators.
key_concepts: Many people find difficulty in accepting that humans are still biologically animals, yet Homo sapiens is a species of primate, a hairless ape that has learned to walk on two limbs and has a clever, advanced brain.
Like any other species, humans are dominated by biological rules that control their actions, reactions, body language and gestures.
The fascinating thing about the human animal is that he is rarely aware of his postures, movements and gestures that can tell one story while his voice may be telling another.
Whenever we call someone perceptive or intuitive we are referring to his or her ability to read another person's non-verbal cues and to compare these cues with verbal signals.
When we say we have a hunch or gut feeling that someone has told us a lie, we really mean that their body language and their spoken words do not agree.

A perceptive speaker gets a hunch that his delivery is not going across when the audience sits back in their seats with chins down and arms crossed on their chest, and he knows he needs a different approach, while an unperceptive speaker blunders on regardless.

Women are generally more perceptive than men, which has given rise to what is commonly referred to as women's intuition, including an innate ability to pick up and decipher non-verbal signals and an accurate eye for small details.

Because few husbands can lie to their wives and get away with it, while most women can pull the wool over a man's eyes without his realising it, female intuition is particularly evident in women who have brought up young children.

For the first few years a mother relies solely on the non-verbal channel to communicate with the child, and this is believed to be the reason why women often become more perceptive negotiators than men.

Evidence about whether non-verbal signals are inborn, genetic, learned or acquired was collected from blind and deaf people who could not have learned through the auditory or visual channels, from many different cultures, and from our nearest anthropological relatives, the apes and monkeys.
The German scientist Eibl-Eibesfeldt found that the smiling expressions of children born deaf and blind occur independently of learning or copying, which means these must be inborn gestures.

Ekman, Friesen and Sorenson studied the facial expressions of people from five widely different cultures and found each culture used the same basic facial gestures to show emotion, leading them to conclude that these gestures must be inborn.

assets.topic: Audit the Universal and the Local: Gestures Across Cultures, From the OK Ring to the V Sign
assets.visual_frame_description: An audit ledger on a world map: a checklist of universal gestures stamps past, while three exhibit cards, the ring, the thumb-up and the V sign, are stamped with differing labels as they cross borders, and a caption reads When in Rome, do as the Romans do above a clashing flag row.
assets.player_mission: Your mission is to audit how a gesture's meaning survives travel: check off the universal basics like smiling, frowning, head nodding and the three-part shoulder shrug, then take the ring gesture, the thumb-up and the V sign through their cultural ledger, ticking off what OK means in France, Japan and the Mediterranean, why the thumb-up puts an Australian hitch-hiker in trouble in Greece, and how Churchill's palm-out victory sign becomes an obscenity when the palm faces in. Close the books with the safest rule for travellers and the exact cultural scope of the discussion.
key_concepts: Most of the basic communication gestures are the same all over the world: when people are happy they smile, and when they are sad or angry they frown or scowl.
Nodding the head is almost universally used to indicate yes or affirmation, appears to be a form of head lowering, and is probably an inborn gesture because it is also used by deaf and blind people.

Shaking the head from side to side to indicate no or negation is also universal and may well be a gesture learned in infancy, when a baby turns his head from side to side to reject his mother's breast and later shakes his head to stop a parent's spoon feeding.
Baring the teeth is derived from the act of attacking and is still used by modern man in the form of a sneer and other hostile gestures, even though he will not attack with his teeth.
Smiling was originally a threat gesture, but today it is done in conjunction with non-threatening gestures to show pleasure.

The shoulder shrug is a universal gesture used to show that a person does not know or understand what you are talking about, and it is a multiple gesture with three main parts: exposed palms, hunched shoulders and raised brow.

Just as verbal language differs from culture to culture, so the non-verbal language may also differ, and a gesture that is common in one culture may be meaningless in another or even have a completely opposite meaning.

The ring or OK gesture was popularised in the USA during the early nineteenth century by newspapers that were starting a craze of using initials to shorten common phrases, and the ring itself seems to represent the letter O in the OK signal.

Theories about the initials OK include the misspelled all correct or oll korrect, the opposite of knock-out or K.O., and Old Kinderhook, the birthplace of a nineteenth century American president who used the initials as a campaign slogan.
In France the OK ring gesture means zero or nothing, in Japan it can mean money, and in some Mediterranean countries it is an orifice signal often used to infer that a man is homosexual.

In Britain, Australia and New Zealand the thumb-up gesture means the hitch-hiker's thumbing a lift, an OK signal, and, when jerked sharply upwards, an insult meaning up yours or sit on this, while in Greece its main meaning is get stuffed.

Churchill popularised the V for victory sign during World War II with the palm facing out, whereas the palm faces towards the speaker in the obscene insult version, which still means victory in most parts of Europe and the number two in many parts of Europe.

assets.topic: Matrix Match: Clusters, Congruence, Context and the Status Equation
assets.visual_frame_description: A wall matrix with four columns labeled CLUSTER, CONGRUENCE, CONTEXT and STATUS; cards fly into place, a head-scratch man with dandruff and flea icons, a folded-arms politician behind a lectern, Freud's patient slipping her wedding ring, a shivering man at a bus terminal, a dead fish handshake, and a chart plotting vocabulary against gesticulation while an age slider runs from five years old to fifty.
assets.player_mission: Your mission is to build a four-cell matrix for reading gestures correctly: drop each evidence card into its cell, the scratch of the head with its multiple meanings into CLUSTER, the critical evaluation figure with the finger up the cheek and chin down into SENTENCE, the incongruent politician and Freud's wedding ring patient into CONGRUENCE, the cold man at the bus terminal and the arthritis sufferer's dead fish handshake into CONTEXT, and the vocabulary-versus-gesticulation finding into STATUS. Then place the ageing card showing how the five-year-old's hand slap becomes the adult's nose touch.
key_concepts: One of the most serious mistakes a novice in body language can make is to interpret a solitary gesture in isolation of other gestures or other circumstances.

Scratching the head can mean dandruff, fleas, sweating, uncertainty, forgetfulness or lying, depending on the other gestures that occur at the same time, so we must always look at gesture clusters for a correct reading.

Like any other language, body language consists of words, sentences and punctuation, with each gesture like a single word that may have several different meanings, and it is only when the word is put into a sentence with other words that its meaning is fully understood.

Gestures come in sentences and invariably tell the truth about a person's feelings or attitudes, and the perceptive person is one who can read the non-verbal sentences and accurately match them against the person's verbal sentences.

The critical evaluation gesture cluster in Figure 5 shows the hand-to-face gesture with the index finger pointing up the cheek, another finger covering the mouth and the thumb supporting the chin, plus tightly crossed legs, an arm crossing the body, and head and chin down, saying something like I don't like what you are saying and I disagree with you.

If a listener's words and gestures match or are consistent they are congruent, but if he claims to be enjoying what you say while his gestures show disagreement, he would be lying because his words and gestures would be incongruent.

Research shows that non-verbal signals carry about five times as much impact as the verbal channel and that, when the two are incongruent, people rely on the non-verbal message and the verbal content may be disregarded.
A high ranking politician may stand behind a lectern with his arms tightly folded across his chest and chin down while telling his audience how receptive and open he is to the ideas of young people.

Sigmund Freud once noted that while a patient was verbally expressing happiness with her marriage, she was unconsciously slipping her wedding ring on and off her finger, and he was not surprised when marriage problems began to surface.
Observation of gesture clusters and congruence of the verbal and non-verbal channels are the keys to accurate interpretation of body language.

All gestures should be considered in the context in which they occur: arms and legs tightly crossed with chin down at a bus terminal on a chilly winter's day most likely means the person is cold, but the same gestures across a table during a sale can be correctly interpreted as negative or defensive.

Linguistics research shows a direct relationship between the amount of status, power or prestige a person commands and his range of vocabulary, and non-verbal research reveals that status, power or prestige is also directly related to the number of gestures or body movements he uses, so the higher a person is on the socio-economic scale, the less gesticulation and body movement he uses.

assets.topic: Boss Level: Faking It, Lying and Learning to Read the Body
assets.visual_frame_description: A boss arena that is a police interrogation room with a suspect under lights in full view, while a slow motion camera freezes a microgesture mid-frame; on one wall the faker's open palms flash honesty while his eyebrow lifts, and on the other an airport concourse fills with travellers showing eagerness, anger, sorrow and happiness while a television silently plays captioned scenes.
assets.player_mission: Your mission is to defeat the final boss, the question of whether body language can be faked: hold the faker's open palms up to the light and catch the microgestures, contract his pupils, lift his eyebrow and twitch the corner of his mouth, then walk the fail-safe tilt mechanism, the Miss World charm school, the politician's charisma and Freud's failings. Then stage the lying gauntlet: the subconscious nervous energy, the refined gestures of politicians, lawyers and actors, the split-second microgestures seen on slow motion cameras, the police interrogation room, and the best way to lie over the telephone. Finish with the training ground: fifteen minutes a day, the airport spectrum, and turning the television sound down.
key_concepts: The general answer to whether you can fake your own body language is no, because of the lack of congruence that is likely to occur in the use of the main gestures, the body's microsignals and the spoken words.

Open palms are associated with honesty, but when the faker holds his palms out and smiles at you as he tells a lie, his microgestures give him away as his pupils contract, one eyebrow lifts or the corner of his mouth twitches, so the receiver tends not to believe what he hears.
The human mind seems to possess a fail-safe mechanism that registers tilt when it receives a series of incongruent non-verbal messages.

In a Miss World or Miss Universe contest each contestant uses studiously learned body movements to give the impression of warmth and sincerity, yet even the experts can only fake body language for a short period of time and eventually the body emits signals independent of conscious actions.
Many politicians are experts in faking body language in order to get the voters to believe what they are saying, and the politician who can successfully do this is said to have charisma.

The face is used more often than any other part of the body to cover up lies, as we use smiles, nods and winks in an attempt to cover up, but our body signals tell the truth and there is a lack of congruence between our body gestures and facial signals.

The difficulty with lying is that the subconscious mind acts automatically and independently of our verbal lie, so our body language gives us away, and people who rarely tell lies are easily caught regardless of how convincing they may sound.

During the lie the subconscious mind sends out nervous energy that appears as a gesture that can contradict what the person said, and people whose jobs involve lying, such as politicians, lawyers, actors and television announcers, have refined their body gestures to the point where it is difficult to see the lie.

If you tell a deliberate lie to an acquaintance and make a conscious effort to suppress all body gestures while your body is in full view, numerous microgestures will still be transmitted, including facial muscular twitching, expansion and contraction of pupils, sweating at the brow, flushing of the cheeks and increased rate of eye blinking.

Research using slow motion cameras shows that these microgestures can occur within a split second, and only people such as professional interviewers, sales people and those we call perceptive can consciously see them during a conversation or negotiation.

Police interrogation involves placing the suspect on a chair in the open or under lights with his body in full view of the interrogators because his lies are much easier to see under those circumstances, while telling lies is easier behind a desk, a fence or a closed door, and the best way to lie is over the telephone.

To learn body language, set aside at least fifteen minutes a day to study and read the gestures of other people, as well as acquiring a conscious awareness of your own gestures, and use television by turning down the sound and checking your reading every five minutes until you can watch an entire program without sound, just as deaf people do.

assets.topic: Scrub the Origins: Proxemics, Air Bubbles and How Man Claims Territory
assets.visual_frame_description: A time-scrubber playhead glides across a map of staked-out territories, from armed borders and city streets to a home with fences, then lands on Edward T. Hall's lecture podium where a sphere labelled proxemics expands; beside it a lion on the African plain marks a fifty-kilometre radius with a spray while a captive lion paces a tiny cage, and a man carries a glowing air bubble through a crowd.
assets.player_mission: Your mission is to scrub through the birth of spatial territory studies: how man, like the animals, birds and fish, stakes out and guards territory, how Edward T. Hall coined the word 'proxemics' in the early 1960s, and how a territory is an area or space claimed as an extension of the body, from country boundaries down to a defined air space around the body. Then weigh the evidence on the portable air bubble: how lions raised in remote Africa claim fifty kilometres while captive lions claim only metres, how a person's bubble size depends on the population density where he grew up, and how the bubble of Western suburban middle class people breaks down into four distinct zone distances.
key_concepts: Thousands of books and articles have been written about the staking out and guarding of territories by animals, birds, fish and primates, but only in recent years has it been discovered that man also has territories.

When man's territorial behaviour is learned and its implications understood, enormous insights into one's own behaviour and that of others can be gained and the face-to-face reactions of others can be predicted.
American anthropologist Edward T. Hall was one of the pioneers in the study of man's spatial needs and in the early 1960s he coined the word 'proxemics', from 'proximity' or nearness.

Every country is a territory staked out by clearly defined boundaries and sometimes protected by armed guards, and within each country are smaller territories in the form of states, counties, cities, suburbs and streets.
The inhabitants of each territory share an intangible allegiance to it and have been known to turn to savagery and killing in order to protect it.

A territory is also an area or space that a person claims as his own, as if it were an extension of his body, including the area around his possessions such as his fenced home, his motor vehicle, his bedroom or personal chair and, as Dr Hall discovered, a defined air space around his body.

Most animals have a certain air space around their bodies that they claim as their personal space, and how far the space extends is mainly dependent on how crowded were the conditions in which the animal was raised.

A lion raised in the remote regions of Africa may have a territorial air space with a radius of fifty kilometres or more, while a lion raised in captivity with other lions may have a personal space of only several metres as the direct result of crowded conditions.
Like the other animals, man has his own personal portable 'air bubble' that he carries around with him, and its size is dependent on the density of the population in the place where he grew up.
The personal zone distance is culturally determined: cultures such as the Japanese are accustomed to crowding, whereas other cultures prefer the 'wide open spaces' and like to keep their distance.

The radius of the air bubble around suburban middle class white people living in Australia, New Zealand, England, North America and Canada is generally the same, and it can be broken down into four distinct zone distances.

assets.topic: Dialogue on Zones: The Four Distances, the Intimate Zone and the Distance/Intimacy Rule
assets.visual_frame_description: A seminar table with four concentric glowing rings on the floor labelled INTIMATE, PERSONAL, SOCIAL and PUBLIC, each ring populated by the right kind of people, from lovers to the plumber and the postman; a heart monitor and adrenalin gauge spike as a stranger steps inside the innermost ring, a kissing couple press their torsos together while a New Year's Eve pair keep 15 centimetres of pelvis apart, and a managing director in the office keeps his fishing buddy behind the social distance line.
assets.player_mission: Your mission is to stage a dialogue on the four zone distances: walk the intimate zone from 15 to 45 centimetres with its close intimate sub-zone, the personal zone at cocktail parties and friendly gatherings, the social zone reserved for strangers and tradesmen, and the public zone beyond 3.6 metres. Then defend the golden rule of 'keep your distance': debate the physiological fight or flight changes triggered when a stranger enters the intimate zone, the new employee kept at social distance until better known, the kissing test of lovers versus New Year's Eve strangers, and the managing director who keeps his weekend fishing buddy at social distance in the office to maintain the unwritten social strata rules.
key_concepts: The intimate zone, between 15 and 45 centimetres or 6 to 18 inches, is by far the most important of the zone distances because it is this zone that a person guards as if it were his own property.
Only those who are emotionally close to a person are permitted to enter the intimate zone, including lovers, parents, spouse, children, close friends and relatives.
There is a sub-zone that extends up to 15 centimetres (6 inches) from the body that can be entered only during physical contact, and this is the close intimate zone.
The personal zone, between 46 centimetres and 1.22 metres or 18 to 48 inches, is the distance that we stand from others at cocktail parties, office parties, social functions and friendly gatherings.

The social zone, between 1.22 and 3.6 metres or 4 to 12 feet, is the distance at which we stand from strangers, the plumber or carpenter doing repairs, the postman, the local shopkeeper, the new employee at work and people whom we do not know very well.
The public zone is the distance over 3.6 metres or 12 feet, and whenever we address a large group of people this is the comfortable distance at which we choose to stand.

The intrusion of a stranger into our intimate zone causes physiological changes to take place: the heart pumps faster, adrenalin pours into the bloodstream and blood is pumped to the brain and the muscles as physical preparations for a possible fight or flight situation are made.

Putting your arm in a friendly way on or around someone you have just met may result in that person's feeling negative towards you, even though he or she may smile and appear to enjoy it so as not to offend you.

If you want people to feel comfortable in your company, the golden rule is 'keep your distance', because the more intimate our relationship is with other people, the closer we are permitted to move within their zones.

A new employee may initially feel that the other staff members are cold towards him, but they are only keeping him at the social zone distance until they know him better, after which the territorial distance between them decreases.

Lovers who kiss press their torsos hard against each other and move within each other's close intimate zones, whereas the kiss from a stranger on New Year's Eve or from your best friend's spouse keeps the pelvic area at least 15 centimetres away from yours.

One of the exceptions to the distance/intimacy rule occurs where the spatial distance is based on the person's social standing: the managing director of a company may be the weekend fishing buddy of one of his subordinates, yet at the office he keeps his fishing buddy at the social distance to maintain the unwritten social strata rules.

assets.topic: Audit the Crowd: Unwritten Rules, Non-Persons, High-Density Stress and Spacing Rituals
assets.visual_frame_description: An audit ledger inside a crowded elevator: a checklist of six unwritten rules stamps off one by one while blank poker faces stare at floor numbers above their heads; beside it a pack of James Island deer collapse beside a graph of overactive adrenal glands and a crime-rate map darkens over dense city areas; a cinema row and a towel rack show a newcomer claiming the widest gap in the centre while a toilet block diagram counts end stalls at 90 per cent.
assets.player_mission: Your mission is to audit what happens when the intimate zone is unavoidably invaded: check off the six unwritten rules that Western people rigidly follow in packed lifts, cinemas and public transport, from silence and no eye contact to the poker face, the engrossed newspaper and the compelled watching of floor numbers. Then audit the misjudgment of the 'miserable' rush hour commuter, why solo cinema-goers wait for the lights to go out, why the crowd around us becomes non-persons, why an angry mob turns uglier as density increases and the police break it up, and the James Island deer study showing death by overactive adrenal glands from overcrowding. Close the books with the spacing rituals of cinema seats, squash towel hooks and the 90 per cent rule of the end toilets.
key_concepts: Crowding at concerts, cinemas, in elevators, trains or buses results in unavoidable intrusion into other people's intimate zones, and reactions to this invasion are interesting to observe.
In a crowded situation such as a packed lift or public transport, you are not permitted to speak to anyone, including a person you know, and you must avoid eye contact with others at all times.
In crowded situations you are to maintain a 'poker face' with no emotion permitted to be displayed, and if you have a book or newspaper you must appear to be deeply engrossed in it.
The bigger the crowd, the less the body movement you are permitted to make, and in elevators you are compelled to watch the floor numbers above your head.

Labels such as 'miserable', 'unhappy' and 'despondent' applied to rush hour commuters are mis-judgments on the part of the observer, who is really seeing a group of people adhering to the rules that apply to the unavoidable invasion of their intimate zones in a crowded public place.
Those who go to a crowded cinema alone often do not take their seats until the cinema lights are extinguished and the movie actually begins.

In a crowded elevator, cinema or bus, people around us become non-persons who do not exist, as far as we are concerned, so we do not respond as if we were being attacked should someone inadvertently encroach upon our intimate territory.

An angry mob or group of protesters fighting for a mutual purpose does not react in the same way as individuals when their territory is invaded: as the density of the crowd increases each individual has less personal space and takes a hostile stand, which is why, as the size of the mob increases, it becomes angrier and uglier.
Police will try to break up a crowd so that each person can regain his own personal space and become calmer.

In a recent study of the deer population on James Island in Chesapeake Bay, many deer were dying in large numbers despite plenty of food, no predators and no infection, and further investigation showed they had died from overactive adrenal glands resulting from the stress caused by the deprivation of each deer's personal territory as the population increased.

The adrenal glands play an important part in the regulation of growth, reproduction and the level of the body's defences, and overpopulation on James Island caused a physiological reaction to the stress, not other factors such as starvation, infection or aggression from others.

In view of the James Island study it is easy to see why areas that have the highest density of human population also have the highest crime and violence rates, and only in recent years have governments and town planners given any credence to the effect that high-density housing projects have in depriving individuals of their personal territory.

assets.topic: Matrix Match: Police Interrogation, the Danish Couple and Country versus City Spatial Zones
assets.visual_frame_description: A wall matrix with four columns labelled PRACTICE, CULTURE, ADJUSTMENT and DENSITY: an interrogation room card slides in showing a criminal on an armless chair with an interrogator leaning into his intimate zone, a Danish couple at a Sydney party faces an Australian couple stepping backwards with confusion icons, two conference silhouettes slowly waltz around a room with the Japanese leading, and three handshake figures show wrist-to-torso distances of 46 centimetres, 100 centimetres and a full arm's wave across a 6-metre field.
assets.player_mission: Your mission is to build a four-cell matrix of zone clashes: drop the police interrogator's armless fixed chair and territorial harassment technique into PRACTICE, the Danish couple at the Sydney Jaycees whose 25-centimetre comfort distance invaded the Australians' 46-centimetre zone into CULTURE, the dancing American and Japanese conference delegates into ADJUSTMENT, and the city dweller's 46-centimetre handshake bubble versus the country person's 100-centimetre bubble and the farmer's distant wave into DENSITY. Then place the card showing why Asians are called 'pushy' and Europeans 'cold', and the sales lesson that a handshake with an isolated farmer is a territorial intrusion while a distant wave wins the deal.
key_concepts: Police interrogators use territorial invasion techniques to break down the resistance of criminals being questioned, seating the criminal on an armless, fixed chair in an open area of the room and encroaching into his intimate and close intimate zones when asking questions, remaining there until he answers.

It often takes only a short while for this territorial harassment to break down the criminal's resistance, and management people can use the same approach to extract information from subordinates who may be withholding it, but a sales person would be foolish to use this type of approach when dealing with customers.

A young couple who recently migrated from Denmark to live in Sydney were invited to join the local branch of the Jaycees, and some weeks after their admission several female members complained that the Danish man was making advances towards them.
Many Europeans have an intimate distance of only 20 to 30 centimetres (9 or 10 inches), and in some cultures it is even less.

The Danish couple felt quite at ease and relaxed when standing at a distance of 25 centimetres from the Australians, being totally unaware of their intrusion into the 46-centimetre intimate zone, and they also used eye gaze more frequently than the Australians, which gave rise to further misjudgments against them.

Moving into the intimate territory of someone of the opposite sex is a method that people use to show interest in that person and is commonly called an 'advance': if the advance is rejected the other person steps backwards to maintain the zone distance, but if it is accepted the other person holds his or her ground and allows the intruder to remain within the intimate zone.
The Danes thought the Australians were cold and unfriendly because they kept moving away to maintain the distance at which they felt comfortable.

When a Japanese attendee spoke with an American at a conference in the USA, the two slowly began to move around the room, the American moving backwards away from the Japanese and the Japanese gradually moving towards the American, and video recordings replayed at high speed give the impression that both men are dancing around the conference room with the Japanese leading.

The Japanese, with his smaller 25-centimetre intimate zone, continually stepped forward to adjust to his spatial need, but by doing so he invaded the American's intimate space, causing the American to step backwards to make his own spatial adjustment.

When negotiating business, Europeans or Americans refer to the Asians as 'pushy' and 'familiar', while Asians refer to the Europeans or Americans as 'cold', 'stand-offish' and 'cool', because the lack of awareness of the distance variation of the intimate zones in different cultures can easily lead to misconceptions and inaccurate assumptions about one culture by another.

Those who were brought up in sparsely populated rural areas require more personal space than those raised in densely populated capital cities: city dwellers have their private 46-centimetre 'bubble', which is also the measured distance between wrist and torso when they reach to shake hands so the hand meets the other person's on neutral territory.

People brought up in a country town may have a territorial 'bubble' of up to 100 centimetres or more, people raised in remote or sparsely populated areas may have a personal space requirement as wide as 6 metres and prefer not to shake hands but to stand at a distance and wave, and country people lean forward with feet planted to meet your handshake while a city dweller steps forward to greet you.

assets.topic: Boss Level: Territory and Ownership, the Stolen Chair and the Magnified Zone of the Motor Car
assets.visual_frame_description: A boss arena that is a suburban home: doors, gates and fences frame the rooms while a woman guards her kitchen, a businessman spreads pens and an ashtray around his conference chair, and father's armchair is marked with a pipe and magazine; a library card runs a stopwatch from seventy-seven minutes for a book to two hours for a jacket, an innocent sales person lands in the buyer's chair and the buyer's face turns red, and outside a car glows with a ten-times-magnified bubble reaching 9 to 10 metres front and back while an angry driver leans on his horn at a lane-cutter.
assets.player_mission: Your mission is to defeat the final boss, the question of what we fight to protect beyond air space: hold the home, office and motor car up as private territories with walls, gates, fences and doors, then trace how each sub-territory is marked, from the woman's kitchen and laundry, the businessman's conference seat spread with ashtrays, pens and books, father's chair and Desmond Morris's library findings of seventy-seven minutes for a book and two hours for a jacket. Then run the gauntlet of the stolen 'his' chair that puts a buyer on the defensive and the question 'Which chair is yours?', and finish with the motor car that magnifies personal space up to ten times, the driver who attacks when cut in front yet apologises in a lift, and the car as a protective cocoon hazard. Close with the summary rule: others invite or reject you by the respect you pay their personal space.
key_concepts: Property owned by a person or a place regularly used by him constitutes a private territory and, like personal air space, he will fight to protect it, with such things as a person's home, office and motor car representing a territory that has clearly marked boundaries in the form of walls, gates, fences and doors.

Each territory may have several sub-territories: in a home a woman's private territory may be her kitchen and laundry and she objects to anyone invading that space when she is using it, a businessman has his favourite place at the conference table, diners have their favourite seat in the canteen and father has his favourite chair at home.

Private areas are usually marked either by leaving personal possessions on or around the area or by frequent use of it, as when the businessman marks his territory at the conference table with an ashtray, pens, books and clothing spread around his 46-centimetre intimate zone border and the canteen diner may even carve his initials into 'his' place at the table.

Dr Desmond Morris noted that studies carried out into seating positions in libraries show that leaving a book or personal object on a library desk reserved that place for an average of seventy-seven minutes, while leaving a jacket over a chair reserved it for two hours.
At home a family member might mark his or her favourite chair by leaving a personal object, such as a pipe or magazine, on or near it to show his or her claim and ownership of the space.

If the head of the house asks a sales person to be seated and the sales person quite innocently sits in 'his' chair, the prospective buyer can become inadvertently agitated about this invasion of his territory and thus be put on the defensive.
A simple question such as 'Which chair is yours?' can avoid the negative results of making such a territorial error.

Psychologists have noted that people driving a motor car react in a manner that is often completely unlike their normal social behaviour as regards their territories, and it seems that a motor vehicle sometimes has a magnifying effect on the size of a person's personal space.
In some cases a person's territory is magnified by up to ten times the normal size, so the driver feels that he has a claim to an area of 9 to 10 metres in front of and behind his motor car.

When another driver cuts in front of him, even if no danger is involved, the driver may go through a physiological change, becoming angry and even attacking the other driver, whereas the same man stepping into a lift when another person steps in front of him is normally apologetic and allows the other man to go first.

For some people, the car becomes a protective cocoon in which they can hide from the outside world, and as they drive slowly beside the kerb, almost in the gutter, they can be as big a hazard on the road as the driver with the expanded personal space.

In summary, others will invite or reject you depending on the respect that you have for their personal space, which is why the happy-go-lucky person who slaps everyone he meets on the back or continually touches people during a conversation is secretly disliked by everyone, and because a number of factors can affect the spatial distance a person takes it is wise to consider every criterion before making a judgment.

assets.topic: Scrub the Open Palm: From Oaths and Beggars to the Honesty Display
assets.visual_frame_description: A time-scrubber playhead glides over an oath-taking court scene with the Bible in the left hand and the right palm raised, lands on a street beggar with palm up and a hand holding a box down, then cross-fades into a living room where a husband folds his arms with his palms hidden in his pockets while a sales counter shows a customer hesitating with one palm exposed.
assets.player_mission: Your mission is to scrub through the history of the open palm: how it has been tied to truth, honesty, allegiance and submission since ancient oaths, how the palm over the heart and the raised palm of the courtroom witness survive today, and how the two basic palm positions, the beggar's upward palm and the restraining downward palm, mark every day encounters. Then track the honesty display: the dog exposing its throat, the open palms of Let me be completely open with you, the child's hidden palms when lying, the husband's palms in his pockets after a night out, and why sales people are taught to watch for exposed palms when a customer refuses to buy. Close the scrub on the con man's art and the curious fact that most people find it difficult to lie with their palms exposed.
key_concepts: Throughout history, the open palm has been associated with truth, honesty, allegiance and submission.

Many oaths are taken with the palm of the hand over the heart, and the palm is held in the air when somebody is giving evidence in a court of law, with the Bible held in the left hand and the right palm held up for the members of the court to view.

In day-to-day encounters people use two basic palm positions: the first has the palm facing upwards and is characteristic of the beggar asking for money or food, and the second has the palm facing down as if it is holding down or restraining.
Just as a dog will expose its throat to show submission or surrender to the victor, so the human animal uses his or her palms to display the same attitude or emotion.
When people wish to be totally open or honest they will hold one or both palms out to the other person and say something like, 'Let me be completely open with you'.

When someone begins to open up or be truthful, he will expose all or part of his palms to another person, and like most body language this is a completely unconscious gesture that gives you a feeling or hunch that the other person is telling the truth.
When a child is lying or concealing something, his palms are hidden behind his back.

A husband who wants to conceal his whereabouts after a night out with the boys will often hide his palms in his pockets or in an arm fold position when he tries to explain where he was, and the hidden palms may give his wife a hunch that he is holding back the truth.
Sales people are often taught to look for the customer's exposed palms when he gives reasons why he cannot buy the product, because only valid reasons are given with exposed palms.

If you tell an outright lie with your palms exposed, you may still appear insincere to your listeners because many of the other gestures that should also be visible when displaying honesty will be absent and the negative gestures used when lying will be inconsistent with the open palms.

Con men and professional liars are people who have developed the special art of making their nonverbal signals complement their verbal lies, and the more effectively the professional con man can use the non-verbal gestures of honesty when telling a lie, the better he is at his vocation.

Most people find it difficult to lie with their palms exposed, and the use of palm signals can in fact help to suppress some of the false information others may give, while also encouraging them to be open with you.

assets.topic: Dialogue on Palm Power: The Up Palm, the Down Palm and the Pointed Finger
assets.visual_frame_description: A stage set with a single box: the same speaker, same words and same tone speaks three times while only the palm changes, once up like a beggar, once down like a restraining hand, and once as a fist with a pointed finger that thuds like a club against the words; off to one side an equal-status colleague turns away from the palm-down order but steps forward at the palm-up request.
assets.player_mission: Your mission is to stage a dialogue about the three palm command gestures, the palm-up, the palm-down and the palm-closed-finger-pointed, using the moving-box test in which tone of voice, words and facial expression stay the same and only the palm changes. Argue the case for the submissive, non-threatening upward palm, the immediate authority of the downward palm, the equal-status co-worker who rejects the order but would carry out the wish if asked palm-up, and the subordinate who must accept the downward palm. Then face the closed fist, whose pointed finger becomes a symbolic club that figuratively beats the listener into submission, and settle on the advice for the habitual finger-pointer: practise the palm-up and palm-down positions to create a more relaxed attitude and a more positive effect on others.
key_concepts: Palm power is one of the least noticed but most powerful non-verbal signals, and when used correctly it invests its user with a degree of authority and the power of silent command over others.
There are three main palm command gestures: the palm-up position, the palm-down position and the palm-closed-finger-pointed position.

The three palm positions can be compared with a test in which you ask someone to pick up a box and carry it to another location in the same room, using the same tone of voice, the same words and facial expressions, and changing only the position of the palm.
The palm facing up is used as a submissive, non-threatening gesture, reminiscent of the pleading gesture of a street beggar.

The person asked to move the box with the palm-up gesture will not feel that the request is given with pressure and, in a normal superior/subordinate situation, will not feel threatened by the request.
When the palm is turned to face downwards, you will have immediate authority and the person to whom you have directed the request feels that he has been given an order.
If the person to whom you gave a palm-down request was a co-worker of equal status, he could reject your request and would be more likely to carry out your wish if you had used the palm-up position.
If the person to whom you give the request is your subordinate, the palm-down gesture is acceptable, as you have the authority to use it.
In the palm-closed position the pointed finger becomes a symbolic club with which the speaker figuratively beats his listener into submission.
The pointed finger is one of the most irritating gestures that a person can use while speaking, particularly when it beats time to the speaker's words.
If you are an habitual finger-pointer, try practising the palm-up and palm-down positions and you will find that you create a more relaxed attitude and have a more positive effect on other people.

assets.topic: Audit the Handshake: From the Caveman's Raised Palms to the Three Attitudes
assets.visual_frame_description: An audit ledger spreads over a prehistoric plain where two cavemen raise open palms in the air, then flips through exhibit cards of a courtroom palm raised high and two modern hands pumping five to seven times; three attitude labels, dominance, submission and equality, stamp down on a handshake while a card of a father and son shows a vice-like vertical grip.
assets.player_mission: Your mission is to audit the handshake as a relic of the caveman era, checking off how the arms-in-the-air palms-exposed greeting of weaponless cavemen became the palm raised in the air, the palm over the heart and finally the interlocking and shaking of palms pumped five to seven times on greeting and departure. Then audit the three basic attitudes transmitted through the handshake, dominance, submission and equality, and weigh the evidence: the dominant palm-down turn and the study of fifty-four successful senior management people, the submissive palm-up offer of control, the mitigating circumstances of the arthritis sufferer and the surgeon, artist or musician protecting his hands, and the vice-like vertical grip of two dominant people that a father teaches his son as shaking hands like a man.
key_concepts: Shaking hands is a relic of the caveman era: whenever cavemen met, they would hold their arms in the air with their palms exposed to show that no weapons were being held or concealed.
The palms-in-air gesture of the cavemen became modified over the centuries, and such gestures as the palm raised in the air, the palm over the heart and numerous other variations developed.

The modern form of the ancient greeting ritual is the interlocking and shaking of the palms which, in most English-speaking countries, is performed both on initial greeting and on departure, with the hands normally pumped five to seven times.

One of three basic attitudes is transmitted through the handshake: dominance, 'This person is trying to dominate me', submission, 'I can dominate this person', and equality, 'I like this person. We will get on well together'.
Dominance is transmitted by turning your hand so that your palm faces down in the handshake, and this tells the other person that you wish to take control in the encounter that follows.
Studies of fifty-four successful senior management people have revealed that not only did forty-two initiate the handshake, but they also used dominant handshake control.
Just as the dog shows submission by rolling on its back and exposing its throat to the victor, so the human uses the palm-up gesture to show submission to others.

The reverse of the dominant handshake is to offer your hand with your palm facing upwards, which is particularly effective when you want to give the other person control or allow him to feel that he is in command of the situation.
A person who has arthritis in the hands will be forced to give you a limp handshake because of his condition, and this makes it easy to turn his palm into the submissive position.
People who use their hands in their profession, such as surgeons, artists and musicians, may also give a limp handshake purely to protect their hands.

When two dominant people shake hands, a symbolic struggle takes place as each person tries to turn the other's palm into the submissive position, resulting in a vice-like handshake with both palms remaining vertical as each transmits a feeling of respect and rapport.
The vice-like vertical palm grip is the handshake that a father teaches his son when he shows him how to 'shake hands like a man'.

assets.topic: Matrix Match: The Catalog of Handshake Styles, From the Glove to the Dead Fish
assets.visual_frame_description: A wall gallery of nine handshake frames side by side, each a different grip frozen in time with a label card underneath, the palm-down thrust, the glove, the dead fish, the knuckle grinder, the stiff-arm thrust, the finger-tip grab, the pull-in, and the double-handed wrist hold, elbow grasp, upper-arm grip and shoulder hold, with intimate-zone rings drawn around each receiver and a warning stamp of social suicide on the last frame.
assets.player_mission: Your mission is to build a gallery matrix of handshake styles, dropping each exhibit card into its cell: the palm-down thrust as the most aggressive style that forces the receiver submissive, the glove handshake or politician's handshake that breeds suspicion in a stranger, the universally unpopular dead fish handshake linked to weak character, the knuckle grinder with no counter but abuse or a punch, the stiff-arm thrust that guards the intimate zone and suits country folk with their larger territory, the finger-tip grab that hides the initiator's lack of confidence, the pull-into-territory with its two meanings, and the double-handed handshake whose left hand carries the extra feeling, from wrist hold to elbow grasp to upper-arm grip to shoulder hold, each one stepping deeper into the receiver's intimate zones and risking social suicide when used without a close bond.
key_concepts: The palm-down thrust is certainly the most aggressive handshake style as it gives the receiver little chance of establishing an equal relationship.

The palm-down thrust is typical of the aggressive, dominant male who always initiates it, and the stiff arm with palm facing directly downwards forces the receiver into the submissive position because he has to respond with his palm facing up.

The glove handshake is sometimes called the politician's handshake, as the initiator tries to give the receiver the impression that he is trustworthy and honest, but when this technique is used on a person he has just met it has the reverse effect and the receiver feels suspicious and cautious about the initiator's intentions.
The glove handshake should only be used with people to whom the initiator is well-known.

Few greeting gestures are as uninviting as the dead fish handshake, particularly when the hand is cold or clammy, and the soft, placid feel of the dead fish makes it universally unpopular, with most people relating it to weak character because of the ease with which the palm can be turned up.

Surprisingly, many people who use the dead fish handshake are unaware that they do so, and it is wise to ask your friends to comment on your own handshake delivery before deciding which style you will use in future.

The knuckle grinder is the trademark of the aggressive 'tough guy' type, and unfortunately there are no effective ways to counter it, apart from verbal abuse or physical action such as a punch on the nose.
Like the palm-down thrust, the stiff-arm thrust tends to be used by aggressive types and its main purpose is to keep you at a distance and out of the initiator's intimate zone.

The stiff-arm thrust is also used by people brought up in country areas who have a larger intimate zone to protect their personal territory, and with country folk there is a tendency to lean forward or even balance on one foot when delivering it.

The finger-tip grab is like the stiff-arm thrust that has missed the mark, as the user mistakenly grabs the other person's fingers, and even though the initiator may appear to have a keen and enthusiastic attitude toward the receiver, in fact he lacks confidence in himself.

Pulling the receiver into the initiator's territory can mean one of two things: either the initiator is an insecure type who feels safe only within his own personal space, or the initiator is from a culture that has a small intimate zone and is behaving normally.
The intention of the double-handed handshake is to show sincerity, trust or depth of feeling towards the receiver.

assets.topic: Boss Level: Disarming the Dominant Handshake and Mastering the Initiation Game
assets.visual_frame_description: A boss arena that is a corridor with two people squaring off for a handshake: a step-by-step floor diagram shows the left foot forward, the right leg sweeping left into the other person's personal space and the left leg closing to complete the manoeuvre, while on the wall a door marked unannounced call shows a buyer pulling back, and a politician shakes a voter's hand with both hands as a stamp reading social suicide falls over the frame.
assets.player_mission: Your mission is to defeat the final boss, the dominant hand shaker: study the left-foot step that moves you into his personal space and straightens the handshake, note why most right-footed people are at a great disadvantage, and practise the manoeuvre until a dominant handshake is neutralised. Then run the initiation gauntlet: ask yourself whether you are welcome and whether the person is glad to meet you, heed the sales trainees' warning about calling unannounced, and nod instead of shaking when the other party is an arthritic or a hands-dependent professional. Finish with the counters: the step-to-the-right technique, the grasp-on-top shake that puts your palm down in the superior position, and the double-handed handshake as social suicide when the extra feeling is not mutual, with the elbow grasp and shoulder hold marching up the receiver's arm and into his close intimate zone.
key_concepts: There is a simple technique for disarming the dominant hand shaker that, in addition to giving you back the control, can enable you to intimidate the other person by invading his personal space.

To disarm a dominant handshake you need to practise stepping forward with your left foot as you reach to shake hands, then bring your right leg forward, moving left in front of the person and into his personal space, and finally bring your left leg across to your right leg to complete the manoeuvre before shaking the person's hand.

The left-foot disarmament tactic allows you to straighten the handshake position or to turn the other person's hand into the submissive position, and it also allows you to take control by invading the other person's intimate zone.

Most people are right-footed and are therefore at a great disadvantage when they receive a dominant handshake, as they have little flexibility or room to move within the confines of the handshake and it allows the other person to take the control.
Practise stepping into a handshake with your left foot and you will find that it is quite simple to neutralise a dominant handshake and take the control.
Considering that a handshake is a sign of welcome, it is important to ask yourself several questions before you initiate one: Am I welcome? Is this person glad to meet me?

Sales trainees are taught that, if they initiate the handshake with a buyer on whom they call unannounced and uninvited, it can produce a negative result as the buyer may not want to welcome them and is forced to do something that he may not want to do.

Such people as arthritics and those whose hands are their profession may become defensive if they are forced to shake hands, so sales trainees are told that it is better to wait for the other person to initiate the handshake and, if it is not forthcoming, to nod as a sign of greeting.

A simple manoeuvre to counter the palm-down thrust is to grasp the person's hand on top and then shake it, making you the dominant party with your palm facing down in the superior position, though because this can be embarrassing to the aggressor it should be used with caution and discretion.
You can counter the palm-down thrust with the step-to-the-right technique, but sometimes this is difficult to use as the initiator's arm is often tense and stiff to prevent such tactics.

In the double-handed handshake the left hand is used to communicate the extra feeling the initiator wishes to transmit, and its extent is related to the distance that the left hand is moved up the receiver's right arm: the elbow grasp transmits more feeling than the wrist hold, and the shoulder hold transmits more than the upper-arm grip.

The shoulder hold and the upper-arm grip enter the receiver's close intimate zone and may involve actual body contact, so they should be used only between people who experience a close emotional bond at the time of the handshake, and unless the extra feeling is mutual the receiver will become suspicious and mistrust the initiator's intentions.

assets.topic: Scrub the Palm Rub: Reading Positive Expectation From the Hands
assets.visual_frame_description: A time-scrubber playhead glides across a party scene where a woman sits back smiling and rubbing her palms together, then lands on a dice thrower, a waiter's hand at the end of a table and a sales manager's office; a speed dial swings from a fast, bright palm rub to a slow, dark one as a real estate agent talks, while a frozen bus terminal fades in behind a caption reading his hands are simply cold.
assets.player_mission: Your mission is to scrub through the palm rub and the thumb and finger rub, the money gestures of the hands: the friend who sat back, smiled and rubbed her palms together before the skiing holiday, the dice thrower's expectancy, the master of ceremonies' welcome, the excited sales person's big order and the waiter's silent demand for a tip. Then weigh the speed signal: the quick palm rub of the real estate agent who benefits you versus the slow, crafty rub of the one who benefits himself, the sales training rule about fast hand action, the buyer who rubs his palms as he asks to see the goods, the cold man at the bus terminal, and the thumb-to-finger rub that professionals should avoid at all costs.
key_concepts: Rubbing the palms together is a way in which people non-verbally communicate positive expectation, as when a personal friend sat back in her chair, smiled broadly, rubbed her palms together and exclaimed 'I can hardly wait to go!' about a forthcoming skiing holiday.
The dice thrower rubs the dice between his palms as a sign of his positive expectancy of winning.
The master of ceremonies rubs his palms together and says to his audience, 'We have long looked forward to hearing our next speaker.'
The excited sales person struts into the sales manager's office, rubs his palms together and says excitedly, 'We've just got a big order, boss!'
The waiter who comes to your table at the end of the evening rubbing his palms together and asking 'Anything else, sir?' is non-verbally telling you that he is expecting a tip.
The speed at which a person rubs his palms together signals whom he thinks will receive the positive results that are expected.
A real estate agent who rubs his palms together quickly and says 'I've got just the right place for you!' signals that he expects the results to be to your benefit.

If the real estate agent rubbed his palms together very slowly as he told you he had the ideal property, he would appear to be crafty or devious and would give you the feeling that the expected results would be to his advantage rather than yours.

Sales people are taught that if they use the palm rub gesture when describing products or services to prospective buyers, they should be certain to use a fast hand action to avoid putting the buyer on the defensive.

When the buyer rubs his palms together and says to the sales person 'Let's see what you have to offer!', it is a signal that the buyer is expecting to be shown something good and is likely to make a purchase.

A person standing at a bus terminal in freezing winter conditions who rubs his palms together briskly may not necessarily be doing this because he is expecting a bus, because his hands are simply cold.

Rubbing the thumb against the fingertips or against the index finger is commonly used as a money expectancy gesture, as when the sales person rubs his fingertips and thumb together and says 'I can save you 40 per cent' or the man rubs his index finger and thumb together and says 'Lend me ten dollars', a gesture that should obviously be avoided at all times by a professional person when dealing with his clients.

assets.topic: Dialogue on the Clench and the Steeple: Frustration Versus Confidence
assets.visual_frame_description: A debating stage with two lecterns: on one side a smiling man with white-knuckled, welded-together fists in front of his face while a height gauge rises behind him, and on the other a confident speaker forming a raised steeple and a listener forming a lowered steeple, while a courtroom clock shows Nierenberg and Calero stamping their verdict and a salesman watches a customer's steeple appear over a seesaw of positive and negative gesture cards.
assets.player_mission: Your mission is to stage a dialogue between two rival hand positions: the hands clenched together, which looks like confidence yet is a frustration gesture, with Nierenberg and Calero's verdict, its three positions from face to crotch and the height-to-mood correlation, and the steepled hands, which Birdwhistell named and which signal confidence, with the raised steeple of the talker, the lowered steeple of the listener, the women's preference for the lowered version, and the smugness of the head-tilted raised steeple. Then test the salesman's dilemma: the steeple after positive gestures versus the steeple after negative gestures, and the rule that actions must be taken to unlock the hostile fingers.
key_concepts: At first the hands-clenched-together position seems to be a confidence gesture, because some people who use it are often smiling and sound happy.

When a sales person describing the sale he had just lost took the hands-clenched position, his fingers began to turn white and looked as though they were welding together, showing a frustrated or hostile attitude.
Research by Nierenberg and Calero on the hands-clenched position brought them to the conclusion that this was a frustration gesture, signalling that the person was holding back a negative attitude.
The hands-clenched gesture has three main positions: hands clenched in front of the face, hands resting on the desk or on the lap when seated, and hands placed in front of the crotch when standing.

There appears to be a correlation between the height at which the hands are held and the strength of the person's negative mood, so the person would be more difficult to handle when the hands are held high in front of the face than when they rest on the desk.

Like all negative gestures, the hands-clenched position needs some action to be taken to unlock the person's fingers to expose the palms and the front of the body, or the hostile attitude will remain.
'Steepling', as Birdwhistell called it, can be an exception to the rule that gestures come in clusters, because it is often used in isolation of other gestures.
People who are confident, superior types or who use minimal or restricted body gestures often use the steeple gesture, and by doing so they signal their confident attitude.

The steeple gesture is frequently used in superior/subordinate interaction and indicates a confident or 'know-it-all' attitude, being particularly common among accountants, lawyers and managers giving instructions or advice to subordinates.

The steeple has two versions: the raised steeple, the position normally taken when the steepler is giving his opinions or ideas and is doing the talking, and the lowered steeple, which is normally used when the steepler is listening rather than speaking.
Nierenberg and Calero noted that women tend to use the lowered steeple position more often than the raised steeple position.
When the raised steeple position is taken with the head tilted back, the person assumes an air of smugness or arrogance.

assets.domain: Body Language | Hand and Arm Gestures
assets.topic: Audit the Authority Grip: Palm-in-Palm Versus the Hand-Gripping-Wrist
assets.visual_frame_description: An audit ledger shaped like a walking figure with head up and chin out: a row of authority badges, crown, police badge, headmaster's mortarboard and military stars, stamp past the palm-in-palm position behind the back; a thermometer climbs as a hand climbs the opposite upper arm, and two Australian police officers stand side by side, one unarmed and rocking on his heels, the other with hands on hips.
assets.player_mission: Your mission is to audit the hands behind the back: check off the British Royal Family's head-up, chin-out, palm-in-palm walk, its spread among the Royalty of many countries, and its users in authority from the policeman on the beat to the headmaster and senior military personnel, then weigh the exposure of stomach, heart and throat as an unconscious act of fearlessness and the calm it produces outside the dentist's surgery. Open the second ledger on the Australian police: the firearm-free officers who rock on the balls of their feet versus the armed officers who switch to the hands-on-hips aggressive gesture. Close the books with the hand-gripping-wrist frustration tell, the further-up-the-back anger scale, 'Get a good grip on yourself', the nervous salesman in the reception area, and the calming fix of switching to palm-in-palm.
key_concepts: Several prominent male members of the British Royal Family are noted for their habit of walking with their head up, chin out and one palm gripping the other hand behind the back.

The palm-in-palm-behind-the-back gesture is common among Royalty of many countries and is also used by the policeman patrolling his beat, the headmaster walking through the school yard, senior military personnel and others in a position of authority.

The palm-in-palm gesture is a superiority/confidence gesture position that also allows the person to expose his vulnerable stomach, heart and throat regions to others in an unconscious act of fearlessness.

If you take the palm-in-palm position when you are in a high stress situation, such as being interviewed by newspaper reporters or simply waiting outside a dentist's surgery, you will feel quite relaxed, confident and even authoritative.
Observation of Australian police officers showed that the officers who do not wear firearms use the palm-in-palm gesture frequently and often rock back and forth on the balls of the feet.

The Australian police officers who do wear firearms seldom display the palm-in-palm gesture, using the hands-on-hips aggressive gesture instead, as if the firearm itself has sufficient authority for its wearer.

The palm-in-palm gesture should not be confused with the hand-gripping-wrist gesture, which is a signal of frustration and an attempt at self-control where one hand grips the other wrist or arm very tightly as if trying to prevent the other from striking out.
The further the hand is moved up the back, the more angry the person has become, so a man gripping his upper arm is showing a greater attempt at self-control than a man gripping just the wrist.
The hand-gripping-wrist gesture is the type of gesture that has given rise to expressions such as 'Get a good grip on yourself.'

Sales people who have called on a potential buyer and have been asked to wait in the buyer's reception area often use the self-control gesture in a poor attempt to disguise their nervousness, and an astute buyer is likely to sense this.
If a self-control gesture is changed to the palm-in-palm position, a calming and confident feeling results.

assets.domain: Body Language | Hand and Arm Gestures
assets.topic: Matrix Match: Thumb Displays and the Double Signals of Dominance
assets.visual_frame_description: A wall matrix of four columns labelled POSITIVE, SECONDARY, CONTRADICTION and DOUBLE SIGNAL: cards fly in showing a cool manager with thumbs hooked in his belt, a courting man, a lawyer tilting back his head with protruding thumbs, a woman with thumbs in her back pockets, and a man with folded arms and upward-pointing thumbs, while a shaking thumb-pointer targets a wife at the far end of a family table.
assets.player_mission: Your mission is to build a matrix of thumb displays: drop the palmistry card on strength of character and ego, the dominance, superiority and aggression card, and the card that makes thumb gestures secondary signals supporting a gesture cluster; then sort the positive displays of the 'cool' manager, the courting man and the wearer of prestige clothing, and the thumb thrusters rocking on the balls of their feet. Place the lawyer's 'In my humble opinion' contradiction into the incongruence cell and the humble substitute pose into the fix cell, and finally sort the secretive back-pocket thumbs of dominant women and the double signal of arms folded with thumbs pointing upwards, before the boss card of the shaking thumb pointed in ridicule at wives and disliked people.
key_concepts: In palmistry the thumbs denote strength of character and ego, and the non-verbal use of thumbs agrees with this.
Thumbs are used to display dominance, superiority or even aggression, and thumb gestures are secondary gestures, a supportive part of a gesture cluster.
Thumb displays are positive signals, often used in the typical pose of the 'cool' manager who uses them in the presence of subordinates.
A courting man uses thumb displays in the presence of a potential female partner, and they are common among people who wear high-status or prestige clothing.
People wearing new, attractive clothing use thumb displays more frequently than those who wear older, outdated clothing.

The thumbs which display superiority become most obvious when a person gives a contradictory verbal message, as when the lawyer turns to the jury and says 'In my humble opinion, ladies and gentlemen of the jury' while displaying dominant thumb gestures and tilting back his head to look down his nose, an effect that makes the jury feel that he is insincere, even pompous.

If the lawyer wished to appear humble, he should have approached the jury with one foot toward them, his coat open, an open palm display and stooping forward a little to show humility or subordination to the jury.
Thumbs most often protrude from people's pockets, sometimes from the back pockets in a secretive manner to try to hide the person's dominant attitude.
Dominant or aggressive women also use the thumb-in-pocket gesture, and the women's movement has allowed them to adopt many male gestures and positions.

Arms folded with thumbs pointing upwards is a double signal, being that of a defensive or negative attitude from the folded arms plus a superior attitude displayed by the thumbs, and the person using it usually gesticulates with his or her thumbs.

The thumb can also be used as a signal of ridicule or disrespect when it is used to point at another person, as when the husband leans across to his friend, points toward his wife with a closed fist thumb gesture and says 'Women are all the same, you know'.

The shaking thumb is used as a pointer to ridicule the unfortunate person at whom it is aimed, and thumb-pointing is irritating to most women, particularly when a man does it, while the shaking thumb is less common among women.

assets.domain: Body Language | Hand and Arm Gestures
assets.topic: Boss Level: Context, Clusters and the Outcome of Every Hand Gesture
assets.visual_frame_description: A boss arena shaped like a giant gesture dictionary whose pages blow away into a cluster of cards: a salesman faces a customer whose steeple appears after a bright trail of open palms and forward leans, then re-appears after a dark trail of arm folding and hand-to-face touches; a speed dial, a thermometer and a bus terminal backdrop spin in the corner while a verdict banner reads The movements preceding the gesture are the key to the outcome.
assets.player_mission: Your mission is to defeat the final boss, the question of what a hand gesture means once it leaves the dictionary: defend the rule that gestures come in clusters and must be read in context, then survive the steeple gauntlet, the positive signal that can follow a run of open palms, leaning forward and head up to cue the close of a sale, or follow arm folding, leg crossing, looking away and hand-to-face gestures to signal a confident refusal. Then handle the speed dial of the palm rub, the cold hands at the bus terminal, the height of the clenched hands, the unlocking of hostile fingers, the calming switch from wrist grip to palm-in-palm, and the secondary nature of thumb displays, before landing on the verdict that the movements preceding the gesture are the key to the outcome.
key_concepts: Gestures come in clusters like words in a sentence, and they must be interpreted in the context in which they are observed, a rule Pease states at the beginning of his book.
Although the steeple gesture is a positive signal, it can be used in either positive or negative circumstances and may be misinterpreted.

If the steeple follows a series of other positive gestures such as open palms, leaning forward and head up, appearing when the salesman shows the buyer the solution to his problem, the salesman has been given a cue to close the sale, ask for the order and expect to get it.

If the steeple gesture follows a series of negative gestures such as arm folding, leg crossing, looking away and numerous hand-to-face gestures, the buyer taking the steeple position may be confident that he will not buy or that he can get rid of the salesman.

In both these cases the steeple gesture means confidence, but one has positive results and the other negative consequences for the salesman, and the movements preceding the steeple gesture are the key to the outcome.

The speed at which a person rubs his palms together signals whom he thinks will receive the positive results, so a slow, crafty palm rub warns that the expected results will favour the other person while a fast palm rub signals the results will benefit you.

Because the person standing at a bus terminal in freezing winter conditions may rub his palms together briskly simply because his hands are cold, every palm rub must be judged in its context before it is read as positive expectation.

Because the hands-clenched position is a negative gesture, some action needs to be taken to unlock the person's fingers to expose the palms and the front of the body, or the hostile attitude will remain.

Thumb gestures are secondary gestures that act as a supportive part of a gesture cluster, so thumb displays must be read together with the gestures that surround them rather than as signals in their own right.

If a self-control gesture such as the hand-gripping-wrist is changed to the palm-in-palm position, a calming and confident feeling results, giving a stressed person a way to shift his own emotional state.
The steeple can be an exception to the cluster rule because it is often used in isolation of other gestures by confident, superior types who use minimal or restricted body gestures.

assets.domain: Body Language | Face and Hand Cues
assets.topic: Scrub the Origins: The Three Wise Monkeys and the Birth of the Deceit Gestures
assets.visual_frame_description: A three-wise-monkeys triptych morphs into a montage of people covering mouth, ears and eyes, ageing from a child's obvious hands to an adult's subtle touches; a clipboard checklist ticks off deceit can mean doubt, uncertainty, lying or exaggeration, while a split-screen role-play shows lying nurses gesturing more than truth-telling nurses.
assets.player_mission: Your mission is to scrub through the raw footage of deceit: how the hand-to-face actions of the three wise monkeys who hear, speak and see no evil form the basis of the human deceit gestures, why the young child covers his mouth, ears and eyes so openly, and how the gestures become refined and less obvious with age while still firing when a person lies, covers up or witnesses deceit.
