Then weigh the evidence: that a hand-to-face gesture does not always mean lying, that it must never be interpreted in isolation, and Desmond Morris's report that nurses instructed to lie to their patients showed a greater frequency of hand-to-face gestures than truth-tellers.
key_concepts: Recognition of the non-verbal deceit gestures can be one of the most important observation skills one can acquire.
The hand-to-face actions depicted by the three wise monkeys who hear, speak and see no evil form the basis of the human deceit gestures.
When we see, speak and hear untruths or deceit, we often attempt to cover our mouth, eyes or ears with our hands.
If the young child tells a lie, he will often cover his mouth with his hands in an attempt to stop the deceitful words from coming out.

If a child does not wish to listen to a reprimanding parent, he simply covers his ears with his hands, and when he sees something he doesn't wish to look at, he covers his eyes with his hands or arms.
As a person becomes older, the hand-to-face gestures become more refined and less obvious, but they still occur when a person is lying, covering up or witnessing deceit.
Deceit can also mean doubt, uncertainty, lying or exaggeration.
When someone uses a hand-to-face gesture, it does not always mean that he or she is lying, but it does indicate that the person may be deceiving you.
It is important that you do not interpret hand-to-face gestures in isolation, because further observation of other gesture clusters can confirm your suspicions.
Dr Desmond Morris noted that American researchers tested nurses who were instructed to lie to their patients about their health in a role-play situation.
The nurses who lied showed a greater frequency of hand-to-face gestures than those who told the truth to the patients.
The mouth guard is one of the few adult gestures that is as obvious as a child's, with the hand covering the mouth and the thumb pressed against the cheek.

assets.domain: Body Language | Face and Hand Cues
assets.topic: Dialogue on the Face Maskers: The Mouth Guard, Nose Touch, Eye Rub and Ear Rub
assets.visual_frame_description: A round-table debate with four seats: the mouth guard with thumb pressed to the cheek, the nose touched by light strokes, the eye rubbed by a man vigorously and by a woman gently below the eye, and the ear covered by a cupped hand; a cough bubble bursts from a fake cougher, Bogart leans in from a film frame, and a chain of gestures runs from lying through your teeth to a hand bending an ear forward.
assets.player_mission: Your mission is to stage a dialogue among the four maskers that hide deceit: the mouth guard whose hand covers the mouth while the brain subconsciously tries to suppress the deceitful words, the fake cough that disguises it and the Bogart gangster who used it, the speaker who signals his own lie and the listener who signals that he thinks you are lying. Then hear the nose touch argue that it is a disguised mouth guard, from the hand that pulls away at the last moment to the tingling nerve endings in the nose, and audit the eye rub, 'lying through your teeth', and the ear rub's 'hear no evil' variations from the finger drill to the earlobe pull.
key_concepts: The brain subconsciously instructs the hand covering the mouth to try and suppress the deceitful words that are being said, and sometimes the mouth guard gesture may only be several fingers over the mouth or even a closed fist, but its meaning remains the same.
Many people try to disguise the mouth guard gesture by giving a fake cough.
Humphrey Bogart often used the mouth guard gesture when playing a gangster discussing criminal activities or being interrogated by the police, to show non-verbally that he was being dishonest.
If the person who is speaking uses the mouth guard gesture, it indicates that he is telling a lie, while if he covers his mouth while you are speaking, it indicates that he feels you are lying.
When a public speaker sees his audience all using the mouth guard gesture whilst he is speaking, it is wise to stop the presentation and ask, 'Would someone care to comment on what I've just said?'

In essence, the nose touch gesture is a sophisticated, disguised version of the mouth guard gesture, consisting of several light rubs below the nose or one quick, almost imperceptible touch, and some women perform it with small discreet strokes to avoid smudging their make-up.

One explanation of the nose touch is that the subconscious instructs the hand to cover the mouth but, at the last moment, the hand pulls away from the face and a quick nose touch gesture is the result.
Another explanation of the nose touch is that lying causes the delicate nerve endings in the nose to tingle, and the rubbing action takes place to satisfy this feeling.
The itch in a person's nose is normally satisfied by a very deliberate rubbing or scratching action, as opposed to the light strokes of the nose touch gesture.

The eye rub is the brain's attempt to block out the deceit, doubt or lie that it sees or to avoid having to look at the face of the person to whom he is telling the lie, and men usually rub their eyes vigorously while women use a small, gentle rubbing motion just below the eye.
'Lying through your teeth' refers to a gesture cluster of clenched teeth and a false smile, combined with the eye rub gesture and an averted gaze.

The ear rub is an attempt by the listener to 'hear no evil' by putting the hand around or over the ear, and its variations include rubbing the back of the ear, the finger drill, pulling at the earlobe or bending the entire ear forward to cover the earhole.

assets.domain: Body Language | Face and Hand Cues
assets.topic: Audit the Deceit Kit: Neck Scratch, Collar Pull, Fingers in the Mouth and the Pain-in-the-Neck
assets.visual_frame_description: An evidence ledger with glass exhibits: a hand scratching the neck with a tally counter stuck at five, a collar pulled away from a sweaty neck, fingers, a cigarette and a pen held in the mouth, and a palm rubbing the back of the neck labeled pain-in-the-neck; a split figure slaps his forehead and then his neck while a caption asks whether you are not intimidated or literally a pain-in-the-neck.
assets.player_mission: Your mission is to audit the second drawer of the deceit kit, ticking off each exhibit: the neck scratch that scratches about five times as a signal of doubt or uncertainty, the collar pull that Morris traced to the tingling sensation lying causes in the facial and neck tissues and the trickle of sweat when the deceiver suspects he is caught, and the 'Would you repeat that, please?' probe that flushes the deceiver out. Then stamp the fingers-in-the-mouth as an unconscious return to the security of the mother's breast and a need for reassurance, and close the books on Calero's 'pain-in-the-neck' gesture, the forehead slap versus the neck slap of forgetfulness, and the habitual neck-rubber's negativity.
key_concepts: In the neck scratch gesture, the index finger of the writing hand scratches below the earlobe or the side of the neck, and the person scratches about five times, rarely less than five and seldom more than five.
The neck scratch gesture is a signal of doubt or uncertainty and is characteristic of the person who says, 'I'm not sure I agree.'

Desmond Morris noted that research into the gestures of those who tell lies revealed that the telling of a lie caused a tingling sensation in the delicate facial and neck tissues and a rub or scratch was required to satisfy it.

Some people use the collar pull gesture when they tell a lie and suspect that they have been caught out, as if the lie causes a slight trickle of sweat to form on the neck when the deceiver feels that you suspect he is lying.
The collar pull gesture is also used when a person is feeling angry or frustrated and needs to pull the collar away from his neck in an attempt to let the cool air circulate around it.
When you see someone use the collar pull gesture, a question like 'Would you repeat that, please?' or 'Could you clarify that point, please?' can cause the would-be deceiver to give the game away.

Morris's explanation of the fingers-in-the-mouth gesture is that the fingers are placed in the mouth when a person is under pressure, as an unconscious attempt to revert to the security of the child sucking on his mother's breast.
The young child substitutes his thumb for the breast, and as an adult he not only puts his fingers to his mouth but inserts such things as cigarettes, pipes, pens and the like into it.

Whereas most hand-to-mouth gestures involve lying or deception, the fingers-in-mouth gesture is an outward manifestation of an inner need for reassurance, so giving the person guarantees and assurances is appropriate when this gesture appears.

An exaggerated version of the collar pull gesture is the palm rubbing the back of the neck in what Calero called the 'pain-in-the-neck' gesture, which is also used as a signal of frustration or anger.
A person who uses the pain-in-the-neck gesture when lying usually avoids your gaze and looks down.

A subordinate who has forgotten to complete a task non-verbally signals his forgetfulness by slapping his head, either on the forehead or the back of the neck, as if he were symbolically hitting himself, and if he slaps his forehead he signals he is not intimidated while slapping the back of the neck tells you that you are literally a 'pain-in-the-neck' for pointing out his error.

assets.domain: Body Language | Face and Hand Cues
assets.topic: Matrix Match: Context, Clusters and the Art of Misinterpretation
assets.visual_frame_description: A wall matrix with columns labeled WHAT IS THE NEGATIVE, PRECEDING GESTURES, CONTEXT and CLUSTER: a chess player rubs his ear as he hesitates, an applicant rubs his eyes and touches his nose under interview lights, a videotape freezes on a mouth guard, a bored listener's head sinks fully into his hand, a finger drummer taps faster and faster, and an index finger points up the cheek while the thumb supports the chin.
assets.player_mission: Your mission is to build the interpretation matrix for hand-to-face gestures: drop each evidence card into its cell, the assumption that a negative thought has entered the mind into WHAT-IS-THE-NEGATIVE, the chess friend's ear rub and nose touch into PRECEDING GESTURES, the overseas applicant's eye-rubbing and nose-touching answers and the videotaped interviewee's sudden mouth guard into CONTEXT, and the head-supported boredom, finger drumming impatience and thumb-supported critical evaluation into the CLUSTER row. Then place the verdict card: only constant study and observation, with regard to context, leads to accurate assessment of someone's thoughts.
key_concepts: The ability to accurately interpret hand-to-face gestures in a given set of circumstances takes considerable time and observation to acquire.

We can confidently assume that, when a person uses one of the hand-to-face gestures just mentioned, a negative thought has entered his mind, whether it be doubt, deceit, uncertainty, exaggeration, apprehension or outright lying.

The real skill of interpretation is the ability to pick which of the negatives is the correct one, which can best be done by an analysis of the gestures preceding the hand-to-face gesture and interpreting it in context.
Pease's chess-playing friend often rubs his ear or touches his nose during the game, but only when he is unsure of his next move.

If, as Pease touches his chess piece, his opponent covers his mouth or rubs his nose or ear, it means that he is uncertain about the move, his next move or both, so the more moves Pease can make after a negative hand-to-face gesture, the greater his chances of winning.

A young man interviewed for a position in Pease's company kept his arms and legs crossed, used critical evaluation clusters, had very little palm exposure and met the interviewer's gaze less than one-third of the time.

Pease decided not to hire the overseas applicant based on what is commonly called 'gut feeling' after his answers were accompanied by a series of eye-rubbing and nose-touching gestures, and later discovered the man had given false information about his past.

During a videotape role play of an interview scene, the interviewee suddenly covered his mouth and rubbed his nose when asked a question, and he said afterwards that he had been thinking of the negative answer and the interviewer's possible reaction to it at that moment.

When the listener begins to use his hand to support his head, it is a signal that boredom has set in and his supporting hand is an attempt to hold his head up to stop himself from falling asleep, and extreme boredom is shown when the head is fully supported by the hand.

Drumming the fingers on the table and continual tapping of the feet on the floor signal impatience rather than boredom, and the speed of the finger tap or foot tap is related to the extent of the person's impatience.

Evaluation is shown by a closed hand resting on the cheek, often with the index finger pointing upwards, but should the person begin to lose interest the position will alter slightly so that the heel of the palm supports the head, and genuine interest is shown when the hand is on the cheek but not used as a head support.

When the index finger points vertically up the cheek and the thumb supports the chin, the listener is having negative or critical thoughts about the speaker, and because a gesture position affects a person's attitude, the longer he holds the gesture the longer the critical attitude will remain.

assets.domain: Body Language | Face and Hand Cues
assets.topic: Boss Level: From Evaluation to Decision — Reading the Chin Stroke and Closing the Sale
assets.visual_frame_description: A boss arena that is a boardroom sale: a presenter finishes his pitch while the audience's hands move from cheeks to chins; a buyer strokes his chin and then folds his arms and sits back under a red NO stamp, while a second buyer's chin stroke flows into a readiness gesture and a green PURCHASE stamp; a glasses frame and a pipe hover at a decision-maker's mouth, and a split-frame shows evaluation and boredom blending with the head resting on the hand.
assets.player_mission: Your mission is to defeat the final boss, the decision: hold the audience's evaluation gestures up to the light as you present your idea, then catch the moment the evaluation ceases and the hand moves to the chin for the chin-stroking gesture that signals the listener is making a decision. Then run the gauntlet of the sale: the buyer who must not be interrupted mid-stroke, the crossed arms and legs that spell 'No', the readiness gesture that ends in 'how would you prefer to pay?', the glasses frame and the pipe slipped into the mouth, the pen that stalls the decision, and the combination clusters where evaluation, boredom and decision-making blend at the same time.
key_concepts: The next time you present an idea to a group of people, most if not all the members of your audience will bring one hand up to their faces and begin to use evaluation gestures.
As you come to the conclusion of your presentation and ask for opinions or suggestions, the evaluation gestures will cease and one hand will move to the chin and begin a chin-stroking gesture.
The chin-stroking gesture is the signal that the listener is making a decision.

When you have asked the listeners for a decision and their gestures have changed from evaluation to decision-making, the following movements will indicate whether their decision is negative or positive.

A sales person would be foolish to interrupt or to speak when a buyer begins the chin-stroking gesture after he has been asked for a decision to purchase, and his best strategy is careful observation of the buyer's next gestures, which will indicate the decision he has reached.

If the chin-stroking gesture is followed by crossed arms and legs and the buyer sits back in his chair, the sales person has been non-verbally told 'No', and he would be wise to review the main points of the presentation immediately before the buyer verbalises his negative answer.

If the chin-stroking gesture is followed by the readiness gesture, the sales person only needs to ask how the buyer would prefer to pay for the product and the buyer will proceed to make his purchase.

Someone who wears glasses often follows evaluation clusters by removing them and putting one arm of the frame in his mouth instead of using the chin-stroking gesture when making a decision, and a pipe-smoker will put his pipe in his mouth.

When a person places an object such as a pen or a finger in his mouth after having been asked for a decision, it is a signal that he is unsure and reassurance is needed because the object in his mouth allows him to stall making an immediate decision.
As it is bad manners to speak with your mouth full, the buyer who places an object in his mouth feels justified in not giving an immediate decision.

Occasionally the boredom, evaluation and decision-making gestures come in combinations, each showing an element of the person's attitude, and when evaluation moves to the chin with the hand also stroking the chin, the person is evaluating the proposition while making decisions at the same time.
When the listener begins to lose interest in the speaker, the head begins to rest on the hand, as shown by evaluation with the head supported by the thumb while the listener becomes uninterested.

assets.topic: Scrub the Origins: From Childhood Hiding to the Folded-Arms Research Lab
assets.visual_frame_description: A time-scrubber playhead runs from a child hiding behind a table and mother's skirt to a six-year-old folding his arms, a teen relaxing the gesture with crossed legs, and a lecture room where one group sits with arms open and another with arms tightly folded while a bar chart tilts showing 38 per cent less retention for the folded-arms group.
assets.player_mission: Your mission is to scrub through the evolution of the arm barrier: how hiding behind solid objects as children, tables, chairs and mother's skirts, matured into the folded-arms posture by about age six, how the gesture was refined in our teens with crossed legs, and how folding one or both arms forms a barrier that blocks out the impending threat. Then weigh the evidence: the American lecture-room study in which the folded-arms group retained 38 per cent less and judged the lecturer more critically, why training centres should provide chairs with arms, and why 'it's comfortable' is really a match between gesture and a negative attitude.
key_concepts: Hiding behind a barrier is a normal human response that we learn at an early age to protect ourselves, and as children we hid behind solid objects such as tables, chairs, furniture and mother's skirts whenever we found ourselves in a threatening situation.

As we grew older, this hiding behaviour became more sophisticated, and by the age of about six, when hiding behind solid objects had become unacceptable behaviour, we learned to fold our arms tightly across our chests whenever a threatening situation arose.
During our teens we learned to make the crossed-arms gesture a little less obvious by relaxing our arms a little and combining the gesture with crossed legs.
By folding one or both arms across the chest, a barrier is formed that is, in essence, an attempt to block out the impending threat or undesirable circumstances.
When a person has a nervous, negative or defensive attitude, he will fold his arms firmly on his chest, a strong signal that he feels threatened.

In American research a group of students instructed to keep their arms tightly folded across their chests throughout a series of lectures learned and retained 38 per cent less than a group instructed to keep their arms unfolded.
The group that sat with folded arms during the lectures also had a more critical opinion of the lectures and of the lecturer.
When the listener folds his arms, not only does he have more negative thoughts about the speaker, but he is also paying less attention to what is being said.
Training centres should have chairs with arms so that the attendees can leave their arms uncrossed during lectures.

Many people claim they habitually take the arms folded position because it is comfortable, but any gesture will feel comfortable when you have the corresponding attitude, so the negative, defensive or nervous person genuinely finds the folded arms position good.

In non-verbal communication the meaning of the message is also in the receiver, not only the sender, and studies have shown that the reception of crossed-arms or stiff back and neck gestures is negative.

assets.topic: Dialogue on the Barrier: The Universal Defensive Gesture and the Speaker's Reply
assets.visual_frame_description: A two-person negotiation table where one side sits with arms tightly folded and the other slides a pen across and then leans forward with open palms, while an auditorium on the back wall shows 90 per cent of an audience folding their arms after a speaker's verbal attack.
assets.player_mission: Your mission is to stage a dialogue between the defensive listener and the challenged speaker: the standard arm-cross as a universal gesture seen among strangers in queues, cafeterias and elevators, the lecture-hall experiment in which 90 per cent of the audience folded their arms after Pease defamed respected colleagues, the experienced speaker's ice breaker, and the rule that the non-verbal medium does not lie while the verbal medium does. Then replay the unblocking moves: handing the person a pen or book, leaning forward to view a visual presentation, and the open palms-up invitation that exposes the hidden objection.
key_concepts: The standard arm-cross gesture is a universal gesture signifying the same defensive or negative attitude almost everywhere, commonly seen when a person is among strangers in public meetings, queues, cafeterias, elevators or anywhere that people feel uncertain or insecure.

In a lecture experiment Pease deliberately defamed several highly respected men well-known to the seminar audience, and about 90 per cent of the audience had taken the folded arms position immediately after the verbal attack began.
Most people will take an arms folded position when they disagree with what they are hearing.
Many public speakers have failed to communicate their message to the audience because they have not seen the folded arms gestures of their listeners.

Experienced speakers know that the folded arms gesture demonstrates the necessity of using a good ice breaker to move the audience into a more receptive posture that will alter the listeners' attitude towards the speaker.

When you see the arm-cross gesture during a face-to-face encounter, it is reasonable to assume that you may have said something with which the other person disagrees, even though the other person may be verbally agreeing with you.
The fact is that the non-verbal medium does not lie, whereas the verbal medium does.
As long as the arms-folded gesture remains, the negative attitude will remain, because the attitude causes the gestures to occur and prolonging the gesture forces the attitude to remain.

A simple but effective method of breaking the folded-arms position is to hand the person a pen, a book or something that forces him to unfold his arms to reach forward, which moves him into a more open posture and attitude.
Asking the person to lean forward to look at a visual presentation can also be an effective means of opening the folded-arms position.

Another useful method is to lean forward with your palms facing up and say, 'I can see you have a question, what would you like to know?' or, 'What do you think?' and then sit back to indicate that it is the other person's turn to speak.

By leaving your palms visible you non-verbally tell the other person that you would like an open, honest answer, and Pease as a salesman never proceeded with a presentation until he had uncovered a buyer's reason for suddenly folding his arms, which was more often than not a hidden objection.

assets.topic: Audit the Defensive Variations: Reinforced, Fist-Clenched and the Arm-Gripping Cluster
assets.visual_frame_description: An audit ledger of escalating arm barriers: three exhibit cards showing the plain arm-cross, the reinforced version with clenched fists and red face, and the arm-gripping pose with white knuckles, while a courtroom stamp marks the prosecutor fists-clenched and the defence arm-gripping, and a waiting-room scene shows a nervous patient gripping his upper arms.
assets.player_mission: Your mission is to audit the escalation ladder of the arm barrier: tick off the reinforced arm-cross in which clenched fists mark a hostile and defensive attitude, the clenched-teeth and red-face warning of an imminent attack and the submissive palms-up approach that defuses it, then the arm-gripping gesture with its white knuckles and cut circulation, seen in doctors' waiting-rooms and on first-time air travellers, and close the books with the courtroom contrast of the fists-clenched prosecutor against the arm-gripping defence.
key_concepts: If as well as the full arm-cross gesture the person has clenched fists, it indicates a hostile and defensive attitude.
The reinforced arm-cross cluster is often combined with clenched teeth and a red face, in which case a verbal or physical attack may be imminent.
A submissive palms-up approach is needed to discover what caused the hostile gestures if the reason is not already apparent.
The person using the fist-clenched gesture cluster has an attacking attitude, as opposed to the person who has taken a defending arm-cross position.
The arm-gripping gesture is characterised by the hands tightly gripping the upper arms to reinforce the position and to stop any attempt to unfold the arms and expose the body.
The arms in the arm-gripping gesture can often be gripped so tight that the fingers and knuckles turn white as the blood circulation is cut off.

The arm-gripping style is common to people sitting in doctors' and dentists' waiting-rooms, or first-time air travellers who are waiting for the plane to lift off, and it shows a negative restrained attitude.
In a lawyer's office the prosecutor may be seen using a fists-clenched arm-cross while the defence may have taken the arm-gripping position.
The full arm-cross gesture can escalate from a defensive attitude into an attacking one when the fists are clenched, signalling that the person may strike verbally or physically.
The tightly gripping hands of the arm-gripping gesture both reinforce the barrier and betray a stronger level of restraint than the standard folded arms.

assets.topic: Matrix Match: Status, Thumbs-Up and the Sales Close
assets.visual_frame_description: A wall matrix with four cells labelled STATUS, APPREHENSION, SUPERIOR-PEER and SALES CLOSE: cards fly into place showing a general manager with hands in the palm-in-palm position, new employees with folded arms, a young executive with both thumbs pointing up like the Fonz, and a buyer whose fist-clenched arms and poker face stop a salesperson at the close.
assets.player_mission: Your mission is to build the status and selling matrix: place the general manager who never folds his arms after his dominant handshake into the STATUS cell, the nervous new employees who take full or partial arm-folds into the APPREHENSION cell, and the young executive's thumbs-up arm-cross, the Fonz gesture of self-confidence and protection, into the SUPERIOR-PEER cell. Then work the selling grid: the thumbs-up combined with positive gestures as the green light to close, the fist-clenched poker-face as the red light to retreat to questions, the 'No' that becomes hard to change once verbalised, and the gun-carrying officer who only folds his arms with clenched fists on guard.
key_concepts: Status can influence arm-folding gestures, and a superior type can make his superiority felt in the presence of persons he has just met by not folding his arms.

At a company social function the general manager greets new employees with a dominant handshake and stands with his hands by his side, behind his back in the superior palm-in-palm position, or with one hand in his pocket, and he rarely folds his arms to show the slightest hint of nervousness.
After shaking hands with the boss, the new employees take full or partial arm-fold gestures because of their apprehension about being in the presence of the company's top man.
Both the general manager and the new employees feel comfortable with their respective gestures as each is signalling his status relative to the other.

When a general manager meets a young, up-and-coming executive who is also a superior type, the likely outcome is that after a dominant handshake the young executive takes an arm-fold gesture with both thumbs pointing vertically upwards.

The thumbs-up arm-cross is the defensive version of both arms being held horizontally in front of the body with both thumbs up to show that the user is 'cool', a gesture characterised by Henry Winkler, who played the Fonz in the television series Happy Days.
The thumbs-up gesture is our way of showing that we have a self-confident attitude and the folded arms give a feeling of protection.

If the buyer's thumbs-up gesture comes towards the end of the sales presentation and is combined with many other positive gestures, the sales person can move comfortably into closing the sale and asking for the order.

If at the close of the sale the buyer moves into the fist-clenched arm cross position and has a poker face, the sales person can be inviting disastrous consequences by attempting to ask for the order, and it is better to go back to the sales presentation and ask more questions to try to discover the buyer's objection.

In selling, if the buyer verbalises 'No', it can become difficult to change his decision, and the ability to read body language allows you to see the negative decision before it is verbalised and gives you time to take an alternative course of action.
People who carry weapons or wear armour rarely use defensive arm-fold gestures because their weapon or armour provides sufficient body protection.

Police officers who wear guns rarely fold their arms unless they are standing guard, and they normally use the fist-clenched position to show quite clearly that nobody is permitted to pass where they stand.

assets.topic: Boss Level: Partial and Disguised Barriers, Spotting the Hidden Nervousness
assets.visual_frame_description: A boss arena that is a crowded cocktail party: one figure crosses a dance floor to ask a lady to dance while adjusting his watch, a nervous woman holds a wine glass with two hands and a handbag in the crook of her arm, a politician touches his shirt cuff at the podium, and a freeze-frame spotlight catches the disguised barrier that the trained observer reads as a dead giveaway.
assets.player_mission: Your mission is to defeat the final boss, the subtlest arm barriers: catch the partial arm-cross that hides fear in meetings, the holding-hands-with-oneself gesture that Desmond Morris ties to the child's hand held by a parent, then the disguised arm-cross of politicians, sales people and television personalities who touch a handbag, bracelet, watch or shirt cuff instead of folding their arms, and finally the tell-tale two-handed wine glass, the dance-floor and trophy-walk of the young man in full view, and the famous figures who hide nervousness without knowing it.
key_concepts: The full arm-cross gesture is sometimes too obvious to use around others because it tells them that we are fearful, so occasionally we substitute a subtler version, the partial arm cross, in which one arm swings across the body to hold or touch the other arm to form the barrier.
The partial arm barrier is often seen at meetings where a person may be a stranger to the group or is lacking in self-confidence.
Another popular version of a partial arm barrier is holding hands with oneself, a gesture commonly used by people who stand before a crowd to receive an award or give a speech.

Desmond Morris says that the holding-hands-with-oneself gesture allows a person to relive the emotional security that he experienced as a child when his parent held his hand under fearful circumstances.

Disguised arm-cross gestures are highly sophisticated gestures used by people who are continually exposed to others, including politicians, sales people and television personalities, who do not want their audience to detect that they are unsure of themselves or nervous.

In the disguised arm-cross, one arm swings across in front of the body to grasp the other arm but, instead of the arms folding, one hand touches a handbag, bracelet, watch, shirt cuff or other object on or near the other arm, and once again the barrier is formed and the secure feeling is achieved.
When cufflinks were popular, men were often seen adjusting them as they crossed a room or dance floor where they were in full view of others.

As cufflinks lost their popularity, a man would adjust the band on his watch, check the contents of his wallet, clasp or rub his hands together, play with a button on his cuff or use any other gesture that would allow the arms to cross in front of the body.
To the trained observer these disguised gestures are a dead giveaway because they achieve no real purpose except as an attempt to disguise nervousness.

A good place to observe disguised barrier gestures is anywhere that people walk past a group of onlookers, such as a young man who crosses the dance floor to ask an attractive young lady to dance with him or someone crossing an open room to receive a trophy.
Women are less obvious than men in their use of disguised arm barrier gestures because they can grasp such things as handbags or purses when they become unsure of themselves.

One of the most common versions of the disguised arm barrier is holding a glass of beer or wine with two hands, and since you need only one hand to hold a glass of wine, the use of two hands allows the nervous person to form an almost undetectable arm barrier, a gesture used by almost everyone and often by well-known figures who are completely unaware they are doing it.

assets.topic: Scrub the Leg Barrier Basics: The Standard Leg Cross and the Meaning of Crossed Legs
assets.visual_frame_description: A showcase figure sits with one leg crossed neatly over the other, right over left, while ghost overlays show the heart and upper body defended by crossed arms and the genital area shielded by the crossed legs; a caption reads Women are taught this is how to sit like a lady, and a sales person steps back from a buyer whose arms and legs are tightly crossed.
assets.player_mission: Your mission is to scrub through the foundations of leg barriers: why crossed legs shield the genital area just as crossed arms defend the heart and upper body, why crossed arms signal a more negative attitude than crossed legs, and why women must be read with care because they were taught to sit like a lady. Then weigh the standard leg cross: its nervous, reserved or defensive meaning, when it is only a supportive gesture, how it reads during lectures and in cold weather, and why a sales person who asks for a decision from a buyer in the crossed arms and crossed legs pose is very foolish.
key_concepts: Like arm barrier gestures, crossed legs are a signal that a negative or defensive attitude may exist.
The purpose of crossing the arms on the chest was originally to defend the heart and upper body region, and crossing the legs is an attempt to shield the genital area.
Crossed arms indicate a more negative attitude than do crossed legs, and the arms gesture is more obvious.
Care should be taken when interpreting crossed leg gestures with women, because many have been taught that this is how to sit like a lady, yet the gesture can make them seem defensive.
There are two basic crossed leg-sitting conditions, the standard leg cross and the figure 4 leg lock.

In the standard leg cross position one leg is crossed neatly over the other, usually the right over the left, and it is the normal crossed-leg position used by European, British, Australian and New Zealand cultures.

The standard leg cross may be used to show a nervous, reserved or defensive attitude, but it is usually a supportive gesture that occurs with other negative gestures and should not be interpreted in isolation or out of context.
People often sit in the standard leg cross during lectures, on uncomfortable chairs for long periods, or in cold weather.
When the crossed legs gesture is combined with crossed arms (Figure 80), the person has withdrawn from the conversation.

A sales person would be very foolish even to attempt to ask for a decision from a buyer who has taken the crossed arms and crossed legs pose, and the sales person should ask probing questions to uncover his objection.
The crossed arms and crossed legs pose is popular among women in most countries, particularly to show their displeasure with a husband or boyfriend.

assets.topic: Dialogue on the Figure 4: The American Leg Lock, the Clamp and the Manager Meeting
assets.visual_frame_description: A debating arena where the American figure 4 leg lock faces the British leg cross: a man sits with his ankle on his knee in a competitive pose while one or both hands clamp the leg into place, and behind him an auditorium of managers shifts in unison from crossed arms to figure 4 as a salesman rages at the podium.
assets.player_mission: Your mission is to stage a dialogue on the American figure 4 leg lock: debate why it flags an argumentative or competitive attitude, why it is hard to read an American who habitually uses it but obvious when a British citizen sits this way, and why women in trousers and jeans also adopt the pose. Then walk the New Zealand meeting of 100 managers and 500 sales people, where managers shifted from the defensive pose to the figure 4 like an orchestra obeying its leader, watch the tough-minded few who clamp the leg with one or both hands, and rehearse the open appeal with palms up that gives the buyer the floor.
key_concepts: The American figure 4 leg lock position indicates that an argumentative or competitive attitude exists, and it is the sitting position used by many American males who have a competitive nature.

Because the figure 4 is so common among American males, it is difficult to interpret the attitude of an American during a conversation, but it is quite obvious when this gesture is used by a British citizen.

In a New Zealand meeting where the audience comprised about 100 managers and 500 sales people, the managers almost without exception took the defensive crossed pose when a salesman with a reputation as a stirrer took the stage, because they felt threatened by what they thought he was going to say.

While the stirrer raged about the poor quality of management, the sales people in the audience leaned forward showing interest and many used evaluation gestures, but the managers held their defensive positions.

When the salesman changed his address to discuss what the manager's role should be, the managers shifted almost as if they were players in an orchestra given a command by the orchestra leader into the competitive/argumentative figure 4 position (Figure 81).
Several managers who had also disagreed with the salesman were unable to sit in the figure 4 leg lock position for such reasons as obesity and arthritis.
In a selling situation it would be unwise to attempt to close the sale and ask for the order when the buyer takes the figure 4 position.

To handle a buyer in the figure 4 position, the sales person should use an open appeal, leaning forward with palms up and saying, 'I can see you have some ideas on this. I'd be interested in your opinion', and then sit back to signify that it is the buyer's turn to speak.
Women who wear trousers or jeans are also observed sitting in the figure 4 position on occasions.
The person who has a hard and fast attitude in an argument or debate will often lock the figure 4 into place with one or both hands, using them as a clamp.
The figure 4 leg clamp is a sign of the tough-minded, stubborn individual who may need a special approach to break through his resistance.

assets.topic: Audit the Standing Leg Gestures: Closed Stances, the Opening-Up Procedure and Defensive Versus Cold
assets.visual_frame_description: A party-concourse audit with two standing groups side by side: one closed with arms and legs crossed, coats buttoned and wide gaps between strangers, the other open with palms exposed, unbuttoned coats and toes pointing toward friends; a five-stage stairway descends from defensive crossed arms to a relaxed lean, while a frosty figure hugs his arms with straight, stiff legs beside a caption reading Defensive or Cold?
assets.player_mission: Your mission is to audit the standing leg cross: tick off the closed stance of strangers with their greater distances and buttoned coats, and the open stance of friends with exposed palms, unbuttoned coats and toes pointing into the group. Then run the field experiment where crossing your own arms and legs makes a whole group of strangers mirror you, check off the five stages of the standing opening-up procedure found in Australia, New Zealand, Canada and America, and close the books on the defensive-versus-cold debate, from the hands thrust into armpits to the body hug with straight, stiff legs.
key_concepts: At a meeting or function you will notice small groups of people standing with their arms and legs crossed, standing at a greater distance from each other than the customary one, and, if they are wearing coats or jackets, they are usually buttoned.

If you question people standing in the closed arms and legs stance, you will find that one or all of them are strangers to the others in the group, because this is how most people stand when they are among people whom they do not know well.

People in the open standing group have arms unfolded, palms exposed, coats unbuttoned, a relaxed appearance, and lean on one foot with the other pointing towards other members of the group, moving in and out of each other's intimate zones.
Close investigation reveals that the people in the open stance are friends or are known personally to each other.

People using the closed arms and legs stance may have relaxed facial expressions and conversation that sounds free and easy, but the folded arms and legs tell us that they are not relaxed or confident.

If you join a group of people who are standing in the open friendly stance but among whom you know no one, and stand with your arms and legs tightly crossed, one by one the other group members will cross their arms and legs and remain in that position until you leave them.
Studies of people in Australia, New Zealand, Canada and America reveal that the standing opening-up procedure is the same in each of these countries.

Stage one of the opening-up procedure is the defensive position with arms and legs crossed, stage two sees the legs uncrossed with the feet placed together in a neutral position, and in stage three the arm folded on top in the arm cross comes out and the palm is flashed when speaking but is not tucked back into the arm cross position.

In stage four of the opening-up procedure the arms unfold and one arm gesticulates or may be placed on the hip or in the pocket, and in stage five one person leans back on one leg and pushes the other forward to point at the person whom he finds the most interesting.
Alcohol can speed up the opening-up procedure or eliminate some of its stages.
When a person wants to warm his hands he normally thrusts them into the armpits rather than tucking them under the elbows, as is the case with a defensive arm-cross.

When a person feels cold he may fold his arms in a type of body hug, and when the legs are crossed they are usually straight, stiff and pressed hard against each other (Figure 86), as opposed to the more relaxed leg posture of the defensive stance or position.

assets.topic: Matrix Match: The Ankle Lock, Its Versions and What It Holds Back
assets.visual_frame_description: A wall matrix of the ankle lock: one cell shows the male version with clenched fists on the knees and hands gripping the chair arms, another the female version with knees held together, feet to one side and hands resting on the upper legs; a courtroom, an interview desk and a phone collector with ankles locked beneath his chair feed cards into the cells while an interviewer walks around the desk and the ankles finally unlock.
assets.player_mission: Your mission is to build a matrix around the ankle lock gesture: drop the male version with clenched fists on the knees or hands gripping the chair arms into one cell, and the female version with knees together, feet to one side and hands stacked on the upper legs into another. Then feed in the evidence cards from the lawyer's courtroom, the job interview where the interviewer must walk around the desk to unlock the ankles, the debt-collector who said his job was fun while his ankles stayed locked beneath the chair, and Nierenberg and Calero's finding that a locked ankle in negotiation can mean a valuable concession is being held back.
key_concepts: The ankle lock gesture suggests that a negative or defensive attitude exists, just as crossing or folding the arms or legs does.
The male version of the ankle lock is often combined with clenched fists resting on the knees or with the hands tightly gripping the arms of the chair.
In the female version of the ankle lock the knees are held together, the feet may be to one side, and the hands rest side by side or one on top of the other resting on the upper legs.

During more than a decade of interviewing and selling to people, Pease's observation revealed that when the interviewee locks his ankles he is mentally 'biting his lip', because the gesture is one of holding back a negative attitude, emotion, nervousness or fear.

A lawyer friend of Pease had often noticed that, just prior to a court hearing, the people who were involved in the case nearly always sat with their ankles tightly locked together, because they had been waiting to say something or had been trying to control their emotional state.
When interviewing prospective employees, Pease noted that most interviewees locked their ankles at some point during the interview, indicating that they were holding back an emotion or attitude.

Asking questions about the interviewee's feelings was often unsuccessful in unlocking his ankles and thus his mind, but when the interviewer walked around to the interviewee's side of the desk and sat beside him, removing the desk barrier, the interviewee's ankles would often unlock and the conversation took on an open, more personal atmosphere.

A young man whose unenviable job was calling customers who had not paid their accounts sounded relaxed and said the job was a lot of fun, yet his ankles were locked together beneath his chair, a verbal statement inconsistent with his non-verbal signals.

When pressed, the young man paused, unlocked his ankles, turned towards the interviewer with open palms and said, 'Well, actually, it drives me crazy', because he had been holding back his feelings about the rude customers so as not to transmit them to the other customers.
Sales people who do not enjoy using the telephone sit in the locked ankles position.

Nierenberg and Calero, leaders in the field of negotiating techniques, found that whenever one party locked his ankles during a negotiation it often meant that he was holding back a valuable concession, and by using questioning techniques they could often encourage him to unlock his ankles and reveal the concession.

Anyone who habitually sits in the ankle lock position because it feels comfortable should remember that any arm or leg position will feel comfortable when you have a defensive, negative or reserved attitude.

assets.topic: Boss Level: The Foot Lock, Female Fashion and Winning the Sale
assets.visual_frame_description: A boss arena around a sales desk: a shy young wife sits in a tight foot lock like a tortoise in its shell while an insurance salesman lectures past her to the husband; beside them a fashion timeline runs from the mini-skirt era's necessary ankle crosses to modern trousers, and a closing banner urges positive and open gestures to improve self-confidence and relationships.
assets.player_mission: Your mission is to defeat the final boss, the foot lock: catch the top of one foot locking around the other leg, recognize the woman who has become a mental recluse retreated like a tortoise into her shell, and learn why only a warm, friendly, low-key approach can open this clam. Then walk the caution tales: the insurance salesman who lost a sale to a young married couple while the wife sat in a tight foot lock he never noticed, the mini-skirt-era women who still cross their legs and ankles from habit and are misread with caution, and the fashion-trends warning that precedes any conclusion about a woman's leg position.
key_concepts: The foot lock gesture is almost exclusively used by women, with the top of one foot locking around the other leg to reinforce a defensive attitude.
When the foot lock gesture appears you can be sure that the woman has become a mental recluse or has retreated like a tortoise into her shell.
The foot lock position is common to shy or timid women, and a warm, friendly, low-key approach is needed if you eventually hope to open this clam.

A new salesman trying to sell insurance to a young married couple lost the sale and could not understand why, because he had followed the sales track perfectly but had failed to notice that the woman was sitting with a tight foot lock position throughout the interview.
Had the salesman understood the significance of the foot lock gesture, he could have involved the woman in the sales presentation, and might have achieved a better result.
Women who were teenagers during the mini-skirt era crossed their legs and ankles for obvious, necessary reasons, and through habit many of these women still sit in this position.
Because of the mini-skirt-era habit, these women may be misinterpreted by others, and people may react toward them with caution.
It is important to take female fashion trends into consideration, particularly how these may affect the woman's leg positions, before jumping to conclusions.
People who habitually take a crossed arms or legs position prefer to say that they are cold or comfortable rather than to admit that they could be nervous, shy or defensive.

Considering that a negative gesture can increase or prolong a negative attitude, and that other people interpret you as being defensive or negative, you would be well advised to practise using positive and open gestures to improve your self-confidence and relationships with others.

chapters.title: Chapter 8: Other Popular Gestures and Actions

assets.topic: Scrub the Shield: Chair Straddling and the Displacement Signals of Disapproval
assets.visual_frame_description: A medieval shield dissolves into the back of an office chair as a man straddles it in a meeting, while a second man stands behind him looking down; beside them a listener in a suit plucks imaginary lint from his sleeve and glances at the floor while a speech bubble above him reads I agree completely.
assets.player_mission: Your mission is to scrub through the protective behaviour of modern man: how the shield of the enemy became the chair back, why most chair straddlers are dominant individuals who take control when bored, and how to disarm the straddler by standing behind him, attacking non-verbally from above in a one-to-one swivel chair confrontation, or seating him on a fixed chair with arms. Then pick through the lint: why picking imaginary lint is a displacement gesture born of a withheld opinion, why the listener who looks at the floor while picking is silently disapproving, and how open palms and a direct question can surface the hidden objection.
key_concepts: Centuries ago men used shields to protect themselves from the spears and clubs of the enemy, and today civilised man uses whatever he has at his disposal to symbolise this same protective behaviour when he is under physical or verbal attack, including standing behind a gate, doorway, fence, desk, the open door of his motor vehicle or straddling a chair (Figure 91).
When a man straddles a chair, the back of the chair provides a shield to protect his body and can transform him into an aggressive, dominant warrior.

Most chair straddlers are dominant individuals who will try to take control of other people or groups when they become bored with the conversation, and the back of the chair serves as good protection from any attack by other members of the group.
The chair straddler is often discreet and can slip into the straddle position almost unnoticed.
The easiest way to disarm the straddler is to stand or sit behind him, making him feel vulnerable to attack and forcing him to change his position and become less aggressive.

In a one-to-one confrontation with a straddler on a swivel chair it is pointless to try to reason with him, so the best defence is non-verbal attack: conduct your conversation standing above and looking down upon the straddler and move within his personal territory, which is so disconcerting that he may even fall backwards off his chair.
If you have a straddler coming to visit you and his aggressive attitude annoys you, be sure to seat him on a fixed chair that has arms to stop him from taking his favourite position.

When a person disapproves of the opinions or attitudes of others but feels constrained in giving his point of view, the non-verbal gestures that occur are known as displacement gestures, that is, they result from a withheld opinion.

Picking imaginary pieces of lint from the clothing is a displacement gesture, and the lintpicker usually looks away from the other people towards the floor while performing this minor, irrelevant action.

When the listener continually picks imaginary pieces of lint off his clothing it is one of the most common signals of disapproval and a good indication that he does not like what is being said, even though he may be verbally agreeing with everything.

To reveal a hidden objection you can open your palms and say, Well, what do you think? or I can see you have some thoughts on this, then sit back with arms apart and palms visible and wait for the answer, and if he continues to pick the imaginary lint you may need an even more direct approach.

assets.topic: Dialogue on Head Gestures: Nods, Shakes, Tilts and the Three Basic Head Positions
assets.visual_frame_description: A round table where one speaker argues inborn and the other argues learned while a cradle rocks beside them and a deaf-blind child nods; above the table three heads float in a row, one level, one tilted with a question mark, and one down with folded arms, while a salesman at a lectern points at a tilted head in the audience.
assets.player_mission: Your mission is to stage a dialogue on the head movements that carry the conversation: debate whether the head nod is inborn (deaf, dumb and blind people use it) or whether the head shake is the first gesture a human learns at the mother's breast, then catch the disguised objection in the head shake that accompanies a verbal yes. Walk the three basic head positions, the neutral head-up, the interested head tilt first noted by Darwin, and the negative head-down, and finish with the professional speaker's trick of forcing audience participation to lift the heads up.
key_concepts: The two most widely used head movements are the head nod and the head shake, with the head nod being a positive gesture used in most cultures to signify yes or affirmation.

Research conducted with people who have been deaf, dumb and blind from birth shows that they also use the head nod to signify the affirmative, which has given rise to the theory that it may be an inborn gesture.

The headshake, usually meaning no, is also claimed by some to be an inborn action, but others theorise that it is the first gesture a human being learns, because the newborn baby who has had enough milk shakes his head from side to side to reject his mother's breast, and the young child uses the head shake to reject a parent's attempt to spoonfeed him.
One of the easiest ways to uncover a disguised objection when dealing with others is to watch if the person uses the headshake gesture while verbalising his agreement with you.

A person who verbalises yes, I can see your point of view, or I really enjoy working here, or we'll definitely do business after Christmas whilst shaking his head from side to side is signalling that a negative attitude exists, and you would be well advised to reject what he has said and question him further.

There are three basic head positions, the first being the head up position taken by the person who has a neutral attitude about what he is hearing, with the head usually remaining still and occasionally giving small nods.
Hand-to-cheek evaluation gestures are often used with the head up position.

When the head tilts to one side it shows that interest has developed, and Charles Darwin was one of the first to note that humans, as well as animals, tilt their heads to one side when they become interested in something.

If you are giving a sales presentation or delivering a speech, always make a point of looking for the head tilt among your audience, because when you see them tilt their heads and lean forward using hand-to-chin evaluation gestures, you are getting the point across.

Women use the head-tilted position to show interest in an attractive male, and when others are speaking to you all you need do is use the head-tilted position and head nods to make the listener feel warm towards you.

When the head is down it signals that the attitude is negative and even judgmental, critical evaluation clusters are normally made with the head down, and unless you can get the person's head up or tilted you may have a communication problem.

Professional speakers and trainers usually do something that involves audience participation before they begin their address, which is intended to get the audience's heads up and involved, and if the speaker's ploy is successful the audience's next head position will be the head tilted.

assets.topic: Audit the Dominance Clusters: Both Hands Behind Head and the Hands-on-Hips Pose
assets.visual_frame_description: An audit ledger with two columns: one ticking off accountants, lawyers, sales managers and bank managers beside a man leaning back with both hands behind his head, and the other showing a bird fluffing its feathers beside a man with hands on his hips; a wall chart reads 27 of 30 sales managers, and a caption warns The basic meaning is aggression.
assets.player_mission: Your mission is to audit the two great dominance clusters of this chapter: tick off the professionals who use both hands behind the head, the know-it-all and territorial messages it sends, the imaginary armchair origin and the insurance company research in which twenty-seven of thirty sales managers used it only with subordinates. Then balance the ledger on hands-on-hips: the child, the athlete and the boxer, the readiness and achiever labels that still spell aggression, the puffed-up bird analogy, and the male challenge across territory.
key_concepts: The both-hands-behind-head gesture is typical of such professionals as accountants, lawyers, sales managers and bank managers, or of people who are feeling confident, dominant or superior about something.

If we could read the mind of the person using the hands-behind-head gesture he would be saying something like I have all the answers, Maybe one day you'll be as smart as I am, or Everything's under control, and it is also a gesture used by the know-it-all individual, which many people find irritating.
Lawyers habitually use the hands-behind-head gesture with their peers as a non-verbal demonstration of how knowledgeable they are.

The hands-behind-head gesture can also be used as a territorial sign to show that the person has staked a claim to that particular area, and the man who combines it with a figure 4 leg lock position shows that he not only feels superior but is also likely to want to argue.
The origin of the hands-behind-head gesture is uncertain, but it is likely that the hands are used as an imaginary armchair in which the person lies back and relaxes.

Research into the hands-behind-head gesture showed that in one particular insurance company twenty-seven out of thirty sales managers used it regularly in the presence of their sales people or subordinates but seldom in the presence of their superiors, with whom the same managers used submissive and defensive gesture clusters.

If you want to discover the reason for the person's superior attitude, lean forward with palms up and say, I can see that you know about this. Would you care to comment? then sit back with palms still visible and wait for an answer, or force him to change his position by placing something just out of his reach and asking, Have you seen this?

If you want to show that you agree with the other person, all you need do is copy his gestures, and if the person using the hands-behind-head gesture is reprimanding you, you will non-verbally intimidate him by copying this gesture.

Two lawyers will use the hands-behind-head gesture in each other's presence to show equality and agreement, but the mischievous schoolboy would infuriate the school principal if he used it in his office.

The hands-on-hips pose is one of the most common gestures used by man to communicate an aggressive attitude, and it is the gesture seen with the young child arguing with his parent, the athlete waiting for his event to begin and the boxer in the dressing-room waiting for the bout to start.

Some observers have labelled the hands-on-hips pose readiness and others have called it the achiever stance related to the goal-directed individual ready to tackle his objectives, but the basic meaning is still an aggressive, forward-moving gesture.

Birds fluff their feathers to make themselves appear bigger when they are fighting or courting, and humans use the hands-on-hips gesture for the same purpose, to make themselves appear bigger, with males using it as a non-verbal challenge to other males who enter their territory and men often using it in the presence of women to show an aggressive, dominant male attitude.

assets.topic: Matrix Match: Readiness Clusters in Selling, Exit, Courtship and Confrontation
assets.visual_frame_description: A wall matrix with four columns: SALES shows a client chinstroking then sitting forward in his chair beside a crossed-arms client stamped unsold; EXIT shows a man leaning forward with both hands on his knees; COURTSHIP shows a gunslinger with thumbs tucked in his belt, one foot pointing toward a woman; and CONFRONTATION shows two men angled away in relaxed legs beside a red-flashing pair facing each other with feet planted.
assets.player_mission: Your mission is to build a four-cell matrix of readiness clusters: drop the selling cell in with seated readiness and the chinstroking gesture, backed by the insurance video replays in which the client bought whenever seated readiness followed chinstroking, and the exit cell with the starter's position that begs to end the conversation. Then match the courtship cell, thumbs tucked in the belt with expanded pupils and one foot pointing toward the female, and the confrontation cell, the two men sizing each other up with hands on hips and thumbs in belt, angled versus directly facing with planted feet.
key_concepts: One of the most valuable gestures that a negotiator can learn to recognise is seated readiness, because in the selling situation, if the potential buyer were to take this gesture at the end of the sales presentation and the interview had progressed successfully up to that point, the sales person could ask for the order and expect to get it.
Video replays of insurance sales people interviewing potential buyers revealed that whenever the seated readiness gesture followed the chinstroking gesture, the client bought the policy.
If, during the close of the sale, the client took the arms-crossed position immediately following the chin-stroking gesture, the sale was usually unsuccessful.

Most sales courses teach sales people always to ask for the order with little regard for the client's body position and gestures, and learning to recognise such gestures as readiness not only helps make more sales but helps to keep many more people in the selling profession.
The seated readiness gesture is also taken by the angry person who is ready for something else, to throw you out.

The readiness gestures that signal a desire to end a conversation or encounter are leaning forward with both hands on both knees (Figure 101) or leaning forward with both hands gripping the chair (Figure 102), and should either occur during a conversation it would be wise for you to take the lead and terminate it, which allows you to maintain a psychological advantage and keep the control.

Thumbs tucked into the belt or the tops of the pockets is the gesture display used to show a sexually aggressive attitude, and it is one of the most common gestures used in television Westerns to show viewers the virility of their favourite gunslinger (Figure 103).

In the thumbs-in-belt gesture the arms take the readiness position and the hands serve as central indicators, highlighting the genital region, and men use this gesture to stake their territory or to show other men that they are unafraid.

When the thumbs-in-belt gesture is used in the presence of females it can be interpreted as, I am virile, I can dominate you, and when it is combined with expanded pupils and one foot pointing toward a female it is easily decoded by most women.

The thumbs-in-belt cluster has always been predominantly male, but the fact that women wear jeans and trousers has allowed them to use the same cluster (Figure 104), although they usually only do it when wearing pants or trousers, and when wearing dresses the sexually aggressive female displays one thumb tucked into a belt or pocket.

When two men size each other up using the characteristic hands-on-hips and thumbs-in-belt gestures while both are turned at an angle away from each other and the lower halves of their bodies are relaxed, it would be reasonable to assume that they are unconsciously evaluating each other and that an attack is unlikely.

If two men using the hands-on-hips and thumbs-in-belt gestures were directly facing each other with their feet planted firmly on the ground, a fight would be likely to occur, and a completely relaxed atmosphere will not exist until their hands-on-hips gestures cease and open palm gestures are used.

assets.topic: Boss Level: Reading the Complete Aggressive-Readiness Cluster
assets.visual_frame_description: A boss arena styled as a fashion photography set where a model strikes the hands-on-hips pose with an open coat pushed back on to her hips while a trainer circles with measurement brackets; close-up callout circles freeze on clenched fists, feet evenly apart, and a critical-evaluation hand-to-face, and a wall plaque reads Fearlessness is exposed heart and throat.
assets.player_mission: Your mission is to defeat the final boss, the full aggressive-readiness cluster: read the circumstances and gestures immediately preceding the hands-on-hips pose, judge the coat, whether it is open and pushed back on to the hips in a directly aggressive display of fearlessness or buttoned in aggressive frustration, and scan for the reinforcements of feet evenly apart and clenched fists. Then master the variants, the one-hand-on-hip pose with the other hand showing another gesture, the critical evaluation gestures that ride on the pose, and the professional models who use these clusters to sell the modern, aggressive, forward-thinking woman.
key_concepts: To make a correct assessment of a person's attitude it is important to consider the circumstances and the gestures immediately preceding the hands-on-hips pose, and several other gestures can further support your conclusion.

Closed coat readiness shows aggressive frustration, whereas the coat open and pushed back on to the hips (Figure 98) is a directly aggressive pose because the person is openly exposing his heart and throat in a non-verbal display of fearlessness.
The aggressive hands-on-hips position can be further reinforced by placing the feet evenly apart on the ground or by adding clenched fists to the gesture cluster.
The aggressive-readiness clusters are used by professional models to give the impression that their clothing is for the modern, aggressive, forward-thinking woman.
Occasionally the hands-on-hips gesture may be done with only one hand on the hip and the other displaying another gesture (Figure 99).
Critical evaluation gestures are often seen with the hands-on-hips pose.

The two men in Figure 105 size each other up using the characteristic hands-on-hips and thumbs-in-belt gestures while their conversation may be casual or friendly, but a completely relaxed atmosphere will not exist until their hands-on-hips gestures cease and open palm gestures are used.

The straddler on a swivel chair who feels disconcerted by the non-verbal attack of a standing, looking-down opponent may even fall backwards off his chair in an attempt to avoid being forced to change position.

assets.topic: Scrub the Tell-Tale Eye: The Pupil Reflex and Its Ancient Track Record
assets.visual_frame_description: A time-scrubber playhead sweeps across a candle-lit romantic table where a lover's pupils balloon to four times their size, pans past a 'beady little eyes' snake-eye mask, a baby's huge dilating pupils, an ancient Chinese gem trader leaning over a buyer's eyes, a vial of belladonna, and a poker table where a dark-glassed opponent hides a four-ace hand while the expert folds in frustration.
assets.player_mission: Your mission is to scrub through the history of the eye's influence on behaviour: how everyday phrases like 'shifty eyes' and 'the Evil Eye' secretly refer to pupil size and gaze, Hess's claim in The Tell-Tale Eye that the pupils work independently, the four-fold pupil dilation of excitement versus the snake eyes of anger, the dimly lit dating rooms that cause dilation, babies and children pumping up their pupils to look appealing, and the old profession of pupil watching from belladonna drops and Chinese gem traders to the expert card players who lost games when dark glasses hid the aces.
key_concepts: Throughout history we have been preoccupied with the eye and its effect on human behaviour, as phrases like 'She looked daggers at him', 'He has shifty eyes' and 'He gave me the Evil Eye' unwittingly refer to the size of the person's pupils and to his or her gaze behaviour.

In his book The Tell-Tale Eye, Hess says that the eyes may well give the most revealing and accurate of all human communication signals because they are a focal point on the body and the pupils work independently.
In given light conditions, the pupils will dilate or contract as the person's attitude and mood change from positive to negative and vice versa.
When someone becomes excited, his pupils can dilate up to four times their normal size.
An angry, negative mood causes the pupils to contract to what are commonly known as 'beady little eyes' or 'snake eyes'.

If a woman loves a man, she will dilate her pupils at him and he will decode this signal correctly, without knowing he does so, which is why romantic encounters are often arranged in dimly lit places that cause the pupils to dilate.
Young lovers who look deeply into each other's eyes unknowingly look for pupil dilation, and each becomes excited by the dilation of the other's pupils.

Research has shown that when pornographic films showing men and women in sexual positions are shown to men, their pupils can dilate to almost three times the normal size, and the same films cause even greater dilation in women, which raises some doubt about the statement that women are less stimulated by pornography than men.
Young babies and children have larger pupils than adults and their pupils constantly dilate when adults are present in an attempt to look as appealing as possible and thus receive constant attention.

Tests conducted with expert card players show that fewer games were won by the experts when their opponents wore dark glasses, because an opponent dealt four aces could no longer give his hand away through rapid pupil dilation.

Pupil watching was used by the ancient Chinese gem traders who watched for the pupil dilation of their buyers when negotiating prices, and centuries ago prostitutes put drops of belladonna in their eyes to dilate their pupils and to make themselves appear more desirable.

The old cliché says 'Look a person in the eye when you talk to him', and when communicating or negotiating you should practise 'looking them in the pupil' and let the pupils tell you their real feelings.

assets.topic: Dialogue on the Gaze: Eye Contact, Trust, Liking and Cultural Rules
assets.visual_frame_description: A debate stage where one side argues the gaze clocks in at under one-third for the liar while the other side argues over two-thirds for the interested or the hostile, with pupil icons dilating and constricting; on a side screen Argyle's two figures point at each other and smile, a dark-glassed negotiator is crossed out, and a map lights up Southern Europe in one colour and Japan with a neck-gazing silhouette in another.
assets.player_mission: Your mission is to stage a dialogue on how long a gaze should last: argue the one-third versus two-thirds rule, where the dishonest or withholding person meets your eyes less than one-third of the time and a gaze of more than two-thirds signals either interest with dilated pupils or hostility with constricted pupils, bring in Argyle's finding that looking at someone makes them like you back, defend the 60 to 70 per cent rapport gaze, and then widen the table to culture: the nervous timid person who is rarely trusted, the banning of dark tinted glasses in negotiation, the high-frequency gaze of Southern Europeans, and the Japanese who gaze at the neck instead of the face.
key_concepts: It is only when you see 'eye to eye' with another person that a real basis for communication can be established.

The feeling that some people make us quite comfortable while others make us ill-at-ease or seem untrustworthy has to do primarily with the length of time that they look at us or hold our gaze as they speak.
When a person is being dishonest or holding back information, his eyes meet ours less than one-third of the time.

When a person's gaze meets yours for more than two-thirds of the time it can mean one of two things: first, he or she finds you very interesting or appealing, in which case the gaze will be associated with dilated pupils, and secondly, he or she is hostile towards you and may be issuing a non-verbal challenge, in which case the pupils will become constricted.
Argyle reported that he found that when person A likes person B, he will look at him a lot, which causes B to think that A likes him, so B will like A in return.
To build a good rapport with another person, your gaze should meet his about 60 to 70 per cent of the time, and this will also make him begin to like you.
It is not surprising that the nervous, timid person who meets your gaze less than one-third of the time is rarely trusted.
In negotiation, dark tinted glasses should be avoided at all times as they make others feel that you are staring at them.
Like most body language and gestures, the length of time that one person gazes at another is culturally determined.
Southern Europeans have a high frequency of gaze that may be offensive to others, and the Japanese gaze at the neck rather than at the face when conversing.
Always be sure to consider cultural circumstances before jumping to conclusions about another person's gaze.
It takes about thirty days of conscious practice before the eye techniques in this chapter can be effectively used to improve your communication skills.

assets.topic: Audit the Gaze Zones: Business, Social and Intimate Triangles
assets.visual_frame_description: An audit ledger with three face stamps: the business face wearing a triangle on the forehead labelled serious and in control, the social face with a triangle between eyes and mouth labelled friendly, and the intimate face with a triangle running from eyes to chest labelled interested, alongside a manager's desk where the three gazes are tested on a slouching employee whose reaction changes with each stamp.
assets.player_mission: Your mission is to audit the three gaze territories and tick each off against its occasion: check the business gaze with its imaginary triangle on the forehead that creates a serious atmosphere and keeps control of the interaction, the social gaze that drops below eye level to the triangle between the eyes and the mouth, and the intimate gaze that sweeps from the eyes down to the chest or breasts and, at a distance, to the crotch. Then apply the ledger to the manager reprimanding a lazy employee and confirm why only the business gaze carries the right weight.
key_concepts: When having discussions on a business level, imagine that there is a triangle on the other person's forehead, and by keeping your gaze directed at this area you create a serious atmosphere and the other person senses that you mean business.
Provided that your gaze does not drop below the level of the other person's eyes in a business discussion, you are able to maintain control of the interaction.
When the gaze drops below the other person's eye level, a social atmosphere develops.
Experiments into gazing reveal that during social encounters the gazer's eyes also look in a triangular area on the other person's face, in this case between the eyes and the mouth.
The intimate gaze is across the eyes and below the chin to other parts of the person's body, and in close encounters it is the triangular area between the eyes and the chest or breasts.
For distant gazing, the intimate gaze travels from the eyes to the crotch, and men and women use this gaze to show interest in each other, with those who are interested returning the gaze.

Not only is the length of the gaze significant; just as important is the geographical area of the person's face and body at which you direct your gaze, as this also affects the outcome of a negotiation.
These gaze signals are transmitted and received non-verbally and are accurately interpreted by the receiver.
If you were a manager going to reprimand a lazy employee and you used the social gaze, the employee would take less heed of your words, regardless of how loud or threatening you sounded.
The social gaze would take the sting out of your words, and the intimate gaze would either intimidate or embarrass the employee.
The business gaze is the appropriate one to use when reprimanding an employee, as it has a powerful effect on the receiver and tells him that you are serious.
The area of the other person's body upon which you direct your gaze can have a powerful effect on the outcome of any face-to-face encounter.

assets.topic: Matrix Match: Side-Glances, Eye Blocks and Reading the Courtship Signals
