assets.visual_frame_description: A wall matrix with four cells: INTEREST holds a raised-brow sideways glance and a smile, HOSTILITY holds a furrowed-brow sideways glance, COURTSHIP holds the come-on look with hearts and the hard-to-get player switching to the social gaze, and BLOCKOUT holds an eye-block face whose eyelids close for a second and a head tilted back in the 'looking down one's nose' pose.
assets.player_mission: Your mission is to build a matrix of the eyes' side messages: drop the sideways glance with raised eyebrows or a smile into INTEREST and the same glance with down-turned brows and drooping mouth corners into HOSTILITY, then chart the courtship side of the grid where the 'come-on' look combines the sideways glance with the intimate gaze, playing hard to get is merely dropping the intimate gaze for the social gaze, and the business gaze in courting earns a label of cold. Finish with the eye-block gesture, from the unconscious lid-closing of the bored or superior person to the head-back look known as 'looking down one's nose'.
key_concepts: The sideways glance is used to communicate either interest or hostility.
When the sideways glance is combined with slightly raised eyebrows or a smile, it communicates interest and is frequently used as a courtship signal.
When the sideways glance is combined with down-turned eyebrows, a furrowed brow or the corners of the mouth down-turned, it signals a suspicious, hostile or critical attitude.
What men describe as the 'come-on' look that women use relates to a sideways glance and an intimate gaze.
If a man or woman wants to play hard to get, he or she needs only avoid using the intimate gaze and instead use the social gaze.
To use the business gaze during courting would cause a man or woman to be labelled as cold or unfriendly.
When you use the intimate gaze on a potential sex partner, you give the game away.
Women are expert at sending and receiving the intimate gaze, but unfortunately most men are not.
Men are usually obvious when they use the intimate gaze and are generally unaware of having been given an intimate gaze, much to the frustration of the woman who has transmitted it.
The eye-block gesture occurs unconsciously and is an attempt by the person to block you from his sight because he has become bored or uninterested in you or feels that he is superior to you.

Compared to the normal rate of six to eight blinks per minute during conversation, the eyelids close and remain closed for a second or longer as the person momentarily wipes you from his mind, and the ultimate blockout is to fall asleep.

If a person feels superior to you, the eye-block gesture is combined with the head tilted backwards to give you a long look, commonly known as 'looking down one's nose', and seeing an eye block signals that the approach you are using may be causing a negative reaction and that a new tack is needed.

assets.topic: Boss Level: Take Command of the Other Person's Gaze
assets.visual_frame_description: A boss arena that is a presentation room where a listener's head is locked down on a chart, absorbing only 9 per cent, until the presenter lifts the pen from the visual aid and holds it between their eyes, magnetically raising the listener's head to meet his gaze while a palm stays visible and an intake meter climbs to maximum absorption.
assets.player_mission: Your mission is to defeat the final boss, the presenter's oldest enemy, the wandering gaze: survive the statistics that 87 per cent of the information relayed to the brain comes via the eyes and that a visual-aid-bound listener absorbs as little as 9 per cent of an unrelated message or only 25 to 30 per cent of a related one, then master the pen-lift manoeuvre that drags his head up from the visual aid to your eyes for maximum absorption, and finish the fight with your other palm kept visible as you speak.
key_concepts: Research shows that of the information relayed to a person's brain, 87 per cent comes via the eyes, 9 per cent via the ears, and 4 per cent via the other senses.
If a person is looking at your visual aid as you are speaking, he will absorb as little as 9 per cent of your message if the message is not directly related to what he sees.
If the message is related to the visual aid, he will absorb only 25 to 30 per cent of your message if he is looking at the visual aid.
To maintain maximum control of his gaze, use a pen or pointer to point to the visual aid and at the same time verbalise what he sees.

Lift the pen from the visual aid and hold it between his eyes and your own eyes, which has the magnetic effect of lifting his head so that he is looking at your eyes, and now he sees and hears what you are saying.
Holding the pen between his eyes and yours achieves maximum absorption of your message, so be sure that the palm of your other hand is visible when you are speaking.
The area of the other person's body upon which you direct your gaze can have a powerful effect on the outcome of any face-to-face encounter.
It takes about thirty days of conscious practice before the eye techniques described in this chapter can be effectively used to improve your communication skills.

assets.topic: Scrub the Ritual: From Graham's Built-in Radar to the Courtship Signals of the Human Animal
assets.visual_frame_description: A party scene where Graham's radar locks onto a woman across the room while an animated bird struts and puffs its feathers beside him; the exit doors swing open as he escorts her out, a traffic-light dot flashes green, and split captions show women whispering 'sexy, masculine' while men scowl 'aggressive, insincere'.
assets.player_mission: Your mission is to scrub through the courtship ritual from the start: how Graham's built-in radar psychs out the available women and escorts them out in record time, how zoologists find that animal courtship follows predetermined patterns with the strutting bird and the indifferent female, how courtship signals are sent and read back as a non-verbal green light for a more intimate approach, why success with the opposite sex depends on sending and recognising courtship signals, why women are aware of these gestures while men are blind to them, and how the same man is called 'sexy' by women and 'arrogant' by his male rivals.
key_concepts: Pease's friend Graham developed an art that most males would love to acquire, attending social functions where he could quickly 'psych out' the available women and sometimes in as little as ten minutes be seen heading towards the exit with the woman, escorting her to his car.

Research into animal courtship behaviour conducted by zoologists and behavioural scientists reveals that male and female animals use a series of intricate courtship gestures, some quite obvious and others extremely subtle, and that most are done subconsciously.

In the animal world, courtship behaviour in each species follows specific and predetermined patterns, as when the male bird struts around the female giving a vocal display, puffing up his feathers and performing many intricate body movements to gain her attention.
The bird courtship ritual, with the strutting male and the female who appears to display little or no interest, is similar to that performed by the human animal when courtship begins.

Graham's technique was to display male courtship gestures to the prospective females, and those who were interested would respond with the appropriate female courtship signals, giving Graham the non-verbal green light to proceed with a more intimate approach.
The success that people have in sexual encounters with members of the opposite sex is directly related to their ability to send courtship signals and to recognise those being sent back.
Women are aware of the courtship gestures, as they are aware of most other body gestures, but men are far less perceptive, often being totally blind to them.
Women described Graham as 'sexy', 'masculine' and 'someone who makes you feel feminine', their reactions to his constant array of courtship signals.

Men described Graham as 'aggressive', 'insincere' and 'arrogant', their reaction to the aggressive competition that Graham represented, and consequently he had very few male friends, since no male likes a rival for the attentions of his female.
More space is devoted to female courtship signals than to male signals because women have a greater range of courtship signals than men.

assets.topic: Dialogue on the Body's Answer: Inborn Cues and Scheflen's Quasicourtship
assets.visual_frame_description: A beach at dusk where a man and woman approach each other from a distance; as they meet each other's gaze a wireframe body straightens, the stomach pulls in and the chest protrudes, the bagging under the eyes smooths away, and then the old posture returns after they pass, with a footnote card reading Scheflen, 'Quasicourtship behaviour in psychotherapy'.
assets.player_mission: Your mission is to stage a dialogue about the body's automatic answer: debate whether courtship signals are studied and deliberate or completely unconscious and possibly inborn, walk through Dr Albert Scheflen's quasicourtship findings on high muscle tone, the protruding chest, the pulled-in stomach and the youthful erect posture, and watch the beach experiment where the changes switch on at the moment of eye contact and switch off after the couple passes each other, plus the pupil dilation and flushed cheeks of excited interest.
key_concepts: While some courtship signals are studied and deliberate, others are given completely unconsciously, and a popular theory is that they may be inborn.
Dr Albert Scheflen, in his article 'Quasicourtship behaviour in psychotherapy', noted that when a person enters the company of a member of the opposite sex, certain physiological changes take place.
Scheflen found that high muscle tone becomes evident in the body in preparation for a possible sexual encounter.
Scheflen found that 'bagging' around the face and eyes decreases, body sagging disappears, the chest protrudes and the stomach is automatically pulled in when courtship begins.
Pot-bellied slumping disappears, the body assumes an erect posture and the person appears to become more youthful in appearance during courtship interaction.
The ideal place to observe these courtship changes is on a beach, when a man and woman approach each other from a distance.

The physiological changes take place when the man and woman are close enough to meet each other's gaze and continue until after they have passed each other, at which time the original posture returns.
Excited interest also causes pupil dilation and a flushed appearance in the cheeks during courtship interaction.

assets.topic: Audit the Male Arsenal: Preening, Thumbs-in-Belt and the Intimate Gaze
assets.visual_frame_description: A checklist card for the male arsenal: a tie being straightened, an imaginary dust brush on a shoulder, thumbs hooked into a belt, a foot pointing at the female, hands on hips and an arrow tracing a seated crotch display; beside it a man stands in a river whacking the water with a big stick while a fish leaps into a woman's net.
assets.player_mission: Your mission is to audit the male courtship arsenal: check off the preening behaviour, the reach for the throat and the straightening of the tie, the smoothed collar and the imaginary dust brushed from the shoulder, the rearranged cufflinks and smoothed hair, the thumbs-in-belt genital highlight, the foot pointed at the female, the intimate gaze held a split second longer, the dilated pupils, the hands on hips and the seated crotch display, and weigh Pease's verdict that most men fish with a big stick while women carry the lures.
key_concepts: Like most animal species, the human male displays preening behaviour as the female approaches.
In addition to the automatic physiological reactions, the courting male will reach for his throat and straighten his tie as the female approaches.
If he is not wearing a tie, the male may smooth his collar or brush imaginary dust from his shoulder, and rearrange his cufflinks, shirt, coat and other clothing.
The male may also preen himself by smoothing his hair.
The most aggressive sexual display the male can make towards the female is the aggressive thumbs-in-belt gesture that highlights his genital region.
The courting male may turn his body towards the female and point his foot at her.
The courting male uses the intimate gaze and holds her gaze for a split second longer than normal.
If the courting male is really keen, his pupils will be dilated.
The courting male often stands with his hands on hips to accentuate his physical size and show his readiness to be involved with the female.
When seated or leaning against a wall, the courting male may spread his legs to give a crotch display.
Pease writes that when it comes to courtship rituals, most men are about as effective as someone standing in a river trying to catch fish by hitting them on the head with a big stick.
Pease notes that women have more lures and fishing skills to land their fish than any male could ever hope to acquire.

assets.topic: Matrix Match: The Female Courtship Signals I, From Head Toss to Wet Lips
assets.visual_frame_description: A signal-grid board where female courtship cards fly into place: the head toss with flying hair, a wrist exposed while smoking a cigarette, legs opened wide, rolling hips, a sideways glance under dropped eyelids, wet lips and a lipstick bullet, each card captioned with its meaning and provenance.
assets.player_mission: Your mission is to build a matrix of the female courtship signals, part one: place each signal card in its cell, the shared preening gestures of hair touching and clothing smoothing, the single thumb tucked in the belt, the head toss, the exposed wrists and visible palms, the open legs against the defensive crossed legs, the rolling hips, the sideways glance under dropped eyelids, and Desmond Morris's wet-lip selfmimicry with the ancient lipstick mimicry of reddened genitals.
key_concepts: Women use most of the same basic preening gestures as men, including touching the hair, smoothing the clothing, one or both hands on hips, foot and body pointing towards the male, extended intimate gaze and increasing eye contact.
Although the thumbs-in-belt is a male aggression gesture, women adopt it with feminine subtlety, displaying only one thumb tucked into a belt or protruding from a handbag or pocket.
The head toss is a female courtship gesture in which the head is flicked to toss the hair back over the shoulders or away from the face, and even women with short hair may use this gesture.

An interested female will gradually expose the smooth soft skin of her wrists to the potential male partner, because the wrist area has long been considered one of the highly erotic areas of the body, and she also makes her palms visible to the male while she is speaking.

Women who smoke cigarettes find this tantalising wrist and palm exposure quite simple to perform while smoking, and the exposed wrist and head toss gestures are often mimicked by homosexual males who want to take on a feminine appearance.

The open legs signal means the legs are opened wider than they would normally have been if the male had not arrived on the scene, whether the woman is sitting or standing, contrasting with the sexually defensive female who keeps her legs crossed and together at all times.

The hips have an accentuated roll when walking to highlight the pelvic region, and some of the more subtle female courtship gestures have been used for centuries in advertising to sell goods and services.

In the sideways glance the woman holds the man's gaze with partially dropped eyelids just long enough for him to notice, then she quickly looks away, creating the tantalising feeling of peeping and being peeped at that can light the fires of most normal men.

Dr Desmond Morris describes the mouth slightly open with wet lips as 'selfmimicry', as it is intended to symbolise the female genital region, with the lips made to appear wet either by saliva or cosmetics to give the appearance of sexual invitation.

When a woman becomes sexually aroused her lips, breasts and genitals become larger and redder as they fill with blood, and the use of lipstick is a technique thousands of years old intended to mimic the reddened genitals of the sexually aroused female.

assets.topic: Boss Level: The Complete Female Arsenal, From the Shoe Fondle to the Leg Twine
assets.visual_frame_description: A master-class split screen of the female arsenal: a hand fondling a wine glass stem, a glance over a raised shoulder in a cigar advertisement, three seated diagrams labelled knee point, shoe fondle and leg twine, and a low-voice silhouette of a woman slowly crossing and uncrossing her legs while stroking her thigh.
assets.player_mission: Your mission is to beat the final boss, the complete female arsenal: master the fondled cylindrical object as an unconscious indication of the mind, the sideways glance over the raised shoulder of the cigar advertisement, the three seated leg positions from the knee point to the shoe fondle to the leg twine that Scheflen links to high muscle tone, and the slow crossing and uncrossing of the legs with thigh stroking and the low voice that signals a desire to be touched.
key_concepts: Fondling cigarettes, the stem of a wine glass, a finger or any long, thin object is an unconscious indication of what may be in the mind.

The sideways glance over a raised shoulder is self-mimicry of the rounded female breasts, and Figure 119 makes use of dilated pupils, the head toss, exposed wrists, a sideways glance, wet lips, head up and fondling a cylindrical object, all intended to generate desire for a particular brand of cigar.
Men often sit with their legs apart in an aggressive crotch display, whereas women use leg crossing as protection for their delicate genital area.
Women use three basic leg positions to communicate a courting attitude.

With the knee point, one leg is tucked under the other and points to the person whom she finds interesting, a very relaxed position that takes the formality out of a conversation and gives the opportunity for a fleeting exposure of the thighs.
The shoe fondle also indicates a relaxed attitude and has the phallic effect of thrusting the foot in and out of the shoe, which can drive some men wild.
Most men agree that the leg twine is the most appealing sitting position a woman can take, and it is a gesture that women consciously use to attract attention.

Dr Scheflen states that in the leg twine one leg is pressed firmly against the other to give the appearance of high muscle tone, the condition that the body takes when a person is ready for sexual performance.
Other signals used by women include crossing and uncrossing the legs slowly in front of the man and gently stroking the thighs with her hand, indicating a desire to be touched.
The slow crossing and uncrossing of the legs and the gentle stroking of the thighs is often accompanied by speaking in a low voice.

chapters.title: Chapter 11: Cigars, Cigarettes, Pipes and Glasses

assets.topic: Scrub the Rituals: Smoking as Tension Release and the Staller's Toolkit
assets.visual_frame_description: A time-scrubber playhead glides over a split scene: on one side a patient jitters outside a dentist's surgery while a smoker draws on his cigarette, a nail-biter, a foot-tapper and a tie-player crowd the waiting room; on the other side a pipe smoker taps, packs and relights his pipe at a tense sales interview while a stopwatch runs, and a cigarette smoker twitches through a cascade of mini-gestures in fast-forward.
assets.player_mission: Your mission is to scrub through the opening of the chapter: why smoking is an outward manifestation of inner turmoil rather than nicotine addiction, how it works as a displacement activity for the tensions of social and business encounters, what the anxious non-smoker does instead, and why smoking gestures can be read because they are performed in a predictable, ritualistic manner. Then run the two ritual tapes side by side: the pipe smoker's cleaning, lighting, tapping, filling, packing and puffing routine with its sales research on delayed decisions, and the cigarette smoker's tapping, twisting, flicking and waving mini-gestures that betray above-normal tension and buy him stalling time.
key_concepts: Pease states that smoking is an outward manifestation of an inner turmoil or conflict and has little to do with nicotine addiction.
Smoking is described as one of the displacement activities that people in today's high-pressure society use to release the tensions that build up from social and business encounters.

Pease observes that most people experience inner tension while waiting outside the dentist's surgery to have a tooth removed, and while a smoker covers up his anxiety by smoking, non-smokers perform other rituals such as grooming, nail biting, finger and foot tapping, cufflink adjusting, head scratching, taking a ring off and putting it back on, and playing with a tie.
The reassurance gestures of the anxious non-smoker all tell us that the person needs reassurance.

Smoking gestures can play an important part in assessing a person's attitude because they are usually performed in a predictable, ritualistic manner that can give us important clues to the person's attitude.
Pipe smokers perform a cleaning, lighting, tapping, filling, packing and puffing ritual with their pipes, and this is a very useful way to help relieve tension when they are under pressure.

Sales research has shown that pipe smokers usually take longer to make a decision to buy than do cigarette smokers or non-smokers, and that the pipe ritual is performed most often during the tense moments of the sales interview.
Pipe smokers are people who like to stall decision-making and who can do so in an unobtrusive and socially acceptable way.
Pease advises that if you want a quick decision from a pipe smoker, you should hide his pipe before the interview.
Like pipe smoking, cigarette smoking is a displacement of inner tension and allows time to stall, but the cigarette smoker generally reaches his decision faster than the pipe smoker.
The pipe smoker is, in effect, a cigarette smoker who needs more time to stall in making decisions than his cigarettes allow.
The cigarette ritual involves tapping, twisting, flicking, waving and other mini-gestures indicating that the person is experiencing more tension than may be normal.

assets.topic: Dialogue on the Smoke: Up and Down Exhalation as a Window on Attitude
assets.visual_frame_description: A stage with two smoking figures facing each other in silhouette: one tilts his head back and fires smoke up at the ceiling with a superiority halo, the other blows a grey stream down from the corner of his mouth while secretive shadows creep in; a film strip flickers between a motorcycle gang leader's sharp head tilt and Bogart's inverted cigarette, then a poker player discards his four aces in a staged tantrum before a telltale upward puff.
assets.player_mission: Your mission is to stage a dialogue between the upward blower and the downward blower: argue the case that the direction of exhaled smoke reveals whether a person feels positive, superior and confident or negative, secretive and suspicious, and weigh the corner-of-mouth blow as an even darker signal, while conceding the caveat of the smoker who blows upwards just to avoid offending others. Then debate the speed of exhalation, the movie gang leader's ceiling-shot of superiority against Humphrey Bogart's downward puff as he plots a gaol break, and close on the poker table, where the four-aces bluffer throws his cards down in disgust and then sits back and blows the smoke upwards.
key_concepts: One particular signal indicates whether the person has a positive or negative attitude towards his circumstances, and that signal is the direction in which the smoke is exhaled, whether it is up or down.

A person who is feeling positive, superior or confident will blow the smoke in an upward direction most of the time, while a person in a negative, secretive or suspicious frame of mind will blow the smoke down most of the time.
Blowing the smoke down and from the corner of the mouth indicates an even more negative or secretive attitude.
The smoke-direction reading assumes that the smoker is not blowing the smoke upwards simply to avoid offending others, in which case he could have blown the smoke in either direction.

In motion pictures, the leader of a motorcycle gang or criminal syndicate is usually portrayed as a tough, aggressive person who, as he smokes, tilts his head back sharply and with controlled precision blows the smoke towards the ceiling to demonstrate his superiority to the rest of the gang.

Humphrey Bogart was often cast as a gangster or criminal who always held his cigarette inverted in his hand and blew the smoke down from the corner of his mouth as he planned a gaol break or other devious activity.
There appears to be a relationship between how positive or negative the person feels and the speed at which he or she exhales the smoke.
The faster the smoke is blown upwards the more superior or confident the person feels, and the faster it is blown down, the more negative he feels.
If a card player who is smoking is dealt a good hand, he is likely to blow the smoke upwards, whereas a poor hand may cause him to blow it downwards.

Some card players see a poker face when playing cards as a method of not displaying any body signals that may give them away, while other players like to be actors and use misleading body language to lull the other players into a false sense of security.

A poker player dealt four aces who wanted to bluff the other players could throw the cards face down on the table in disgust, curse, swear or fold his arms and put on a non-verbal display that would indicate that he had been dealt a poor hand, and then quietly sit back and blow the smoke upwards.

assets.topic: Audit the Close: Cigar Status, Nostril Smoke and the Termination Signals
assets.visual_frame_description: An audit ledger with stamps: a cigar floats in a golden circle beside executive silhouettes and a celebration scene with a baby, a wedding ring, a signed deal and a lottery ticket, next to a tally counter reading 320 of 400; a nose-blowing figure tilts his head back in superiority and then drops his head to snort like an angry bull; an ashtray receives a relentless series of taps and a cigarette is stubbed out long before its normal length while a clock hands over control of the conversation.
assets.player_mission: Your mission is to audit the remaining smoking signals and tick them off in the ledger: cigars as a display of superiority by cost and size, their place with executives, gang leaders and high-status people, and their use in celebrating victories, checked against Pease's own tally of 400 recorded cigar exhalations of which 320 were upward. Then verify the nostril-blown smoke of the confident individual who tilts his head back in a looking-down-his-nose position, against the head-down angry bull version, and finally stamp the two general signals, the continual tapping on the ashtray that shows inner conflict, and the cigarette extinguished early as the smoker's decision to terminate the conversation, which the alert observer can hijack to close on his own terms.
key_concepts: Cigars have always been used as a means of displaying superiority because of their cost and size.
The big-time business executive, the gang leader and people in high-status positions often smoke cigars.
Cigars are used to celebrate a victory or achievement such as the birth of a baby, a wedding, clinching a business deal or winning the lottery.

It is not surprising that most of the smoke exhaled by cigar smokers is upwards, and Pease records that of 400 recorded cigar smoke exhalations at a celebration dinner where cigars were distributed freely, 320 were in an upward direction.
Blowing smoke out through the nostrils is a sign of a superior, confident individual, and the smoke is blown downwards only because of the physical location of the nostrils.
The person who nose-blows his smoke often tilts his head back in a looking down his nose position.
If the person's head is down as he nose-blows the smoke, he is angry and is trying to look ferocious, like an angry bull.
The continual tapping of a cigar or cigarette end on the ashtray shows that an inner conflict is taking place and that you may need to reassure the smoker.
Most smokers smoke their cigarette down to a certain length before extinguishing it in the ashtray.
If the smoker lights a cigarette and suddenly extinguishes it earlier than he normally would, he has signalled his decision to terminate the conversation.
Watching for the early-extinguishing termination signal can allow you to take control or to close the conversation, making it appear that it was your idea to end it.

Observation of smoking gestures in selling shows that when a smoker is asked to buy, those who have reached a positive decision blow the smoke upwards, whereas those who have decided not to buy blow it downwards.

assets.topic: Matrix Match: Glasses as Props, From the Mouth Arm to the Folded Frame
assets.visual_frame_description: A wall matrix of four labelled cells; cards fly into place showing a man mouthing the arm of his glasses beside a baby at its mother's breast and a thumb-sucking child, a negotiator polishing his lenses while a pause meter ticks, a pair of glasses sliding back onto a nose as documents re-emerge, and folded frames disappearing into a pocket as the handshake begins.
assets.player_mission: Your mission is to build a four-cell matrix of the glasses wearer's gestures: drop the arm-of-the-frame-in-the-mouth card into REASSURANCE, citing Desmond Morris's finding that objects against the lips or in the mouth relive the baby's security at the mother's breast, and pair it with the stalling function that peaks at the close of a negotiation when a decision has been asked for. Then slot the lens-cleaning card into STALLING, where silence is the best tactic immediately after the request, read the follow-up gestures, the glasses put back on meaning the person wants to see the facts again, the folded frames put away signalling the wish to terminate, and map each cell to the negotiator's correct response.
key_concepts: Almost every artificial aid used by man gives its user an opportunity to perform many revealing gestures, and this is certainly the case with those who wear glasses.
One of the most common gestures with glasses is placing one arm of the frame in the mouth.

Desmond Morris says that the act of putting objects against the lips or in the mouth is a momentary attempt by the person to relive the security he experienced as a baby at his mother's breast, which means that glasses-in-mouth is essentially a reassurance gesture.
Smokers use their cigarettes for the same reassurance reason as the glasses-in-mouth gesture, and the child sucks his thumb.
Like pipe smoking, the glasses-in-mouth gesture can be used to stall or delay a decision.
In negotiating, it has been found that the glasses-in-mouth gesture appears most frequently at the close of the discussion when the person has been asked for a decision.
The act of continually taking the glasses off and cleaning the lenses is another method used by glasses wearers to gain time for a decision.
When the lens-cleaning gesture is seen immediately after a decision has been asked for, silence is the best tactic.
The gestures that follow the stall gesture signal the person's intention and allow an alert negotiator to respond accordingly.
If the person puts the glasses back on, this often means that he wants to see the facts again, whereas folding the glasses and putting them away signals an intention to terminate the conversation.
Watching for the glasses-folding termination signal allows the alert negotiator to take control and close the conversation on his own terms.

assets.topic: Boss Level: The Peering Over Glasses and the Etiquette of the Frames
assets.visual_frame_description: A boss arena lit like a 1930s movie set: a stern public-school master peers over his spectacles at a cowering pupil while the word JUDGED hovers between them, and the pupil's arms fold and legs cross frame by frame; beside it a diagram of the champion's move, glasses off for speaking with a green light, glasses on for listening with a red light, as the pupil learns when he may talk.
assets.player_mission: Your mission is to defeat the final boss, the critical peering-over-glasses look: trace it back to the actors of the 1920s and 1930s movies who used it to portray the judgmental master of an English public school, understand why the reading-glasses wearer finds looking over the tops more convenient than removing them, and feel the scrutiny of whoever is on the receiving end. Then beat the costly mistake: the listener's inevitable folded arms, crossed legs and negative attitude, and apply the counter-strategy of removing the glasses to speak and putting them back on to listen, which relaxes the other person, hands the wearer control of the conversation, and teaches the listener the off-and-on signal system of when to stay silent and when to talk.
key_concepts: Actors in the motion pictures made during the 1920s and 1930s used the peering-over-glasses gesture to portray a critical or judgmental person such as the master of an English public school.
Often the person may be wearing reading glasses and finds it more convenient to look over the tops, rather than removing them to look at the other person.
Whoever is on the receiving end of the peering look may feel as though he is being judged or scrutinised.
Looking over the glasses can be a very costly mistake, as the listener inevitably responds to this look with folded arms, crossed legs and a correspondingly negative attitude.
Glasses wearers should remove them when speaking and put them back on to listen.
Removing the glasses to speak and putting them back on to listen not only relaxes the other person but allows the glasses wearer to have control of the conversation.
The listener quickly learns that when the glasses are off he must not interrupt the wearer, and when they are put back on he had better start talking.
Almost every artificial aid used by man gives its user an opportunity to perform many revealing gestures, and glasses wearers are among the most revealing of all.
The continual tapping of a cigar or cigarette end on the ashtray shows that an inner conflict is taking place and that you may need to reassure the smoker.
If the smoker lights a cigarette and suddenly extinguishes it earlier than he normally would, he has signalled his decision to terminate the conversation.
Watching for the early-extinguishing termination signal can allow you to take control or to close the conversation, making it appear that it was your idea to end it.

assets.topic: Scrub the Territory: Leaning, Claiming and the Extension of the Body
assets.visual_frame_description: A freeze-frame photograph session where a proud owner leans against his new car with a foot on the bumper, the car glowing as an extension of his body; beside him a business executive sits with his feet on his desk while young lovers hold hands, and a doorway glows red as a man leans on it inside another's office.
assets.player_mission: Your mission is to scrub through the territorial gestures that stake a claim: why people lean against objects or other people to show a territorial claim, why leaning becomes dominance or intimidation when the object belongs to someone else, and how the man photographed beside his new car, boat or home puts his foot on it or his arm around it. Then track the extensions of the body: the lovers holding hands in public, the business executive with his feet on the desk or leaning against his office doorway, and the subtle intimidation of leaning on a doorway or sitting in another person's chair without permission.
key_concepts: People lean against other people or objects to show a territorial claim to that object or person.
Leaning can also be used as a method of dominance or intimidation when the object being leaned on belongs to someone else.

If you are going to take a photograph of a friend and his new car, boat, home or other personal belonging, you will inevitably find that he leans against his newly acquired property, putting his foot on it or his arm around it.
When a person touches the property, it becomes an extension of his body, and in this way he shows others that it belongs to him.
Young lovers continually hold hands or put their arms around one another in public and social situations to show others the claim that they have on each other.
The business executive puts his feet on his desk or desk drawers or leans against his office doorway to show his claim to that office and its furnishings.
An easy way to intimidate someone is to lean against, sit upon or use their possessions without their permission.
In addition to the obvious abuses of another's territory such as sitting at his desk or borrowing his car without asking, there are other very subtle intimidation techniques.
One very subtle intimidation technique is to lean against the doorway in another's office or to inadvertently sit in his chair.
The territorial claim is staked by touch: when the owner touches his property it becomes an extension of his body, so the car, desk or doorway silently announces who it belongs to.

assets.topic: Dialogue on Intimidation: Doorways, Chairs and the Salesman's Question
assets.visual_frame_description: A two-seat interview stage: on one side a habitual doorway leaner slouches against a doorframe with a hostile shimmer around him, while on the other a salesman asks a customer 'Which seat is yours?'; a ninety-second hourglass runs in the corner as an erect stance with open palms receives a warm glow.
assets.player_mission: Your mission is to stage a dialogue between the habitual doorway leaner and the sales professional about intimidation at first meeting: how the doorway leaner goes through life intimidating most people from the very first introduction, why he is well advised to practise an erect stance with palms visible, and how the salesman who asks 'Which seat is yours?' protects his sale from the offside customer. Then weigh the opening ninety seconds, where people form 90 per cent of their opinion of you, and the hard rule that you never get a second chance to make a first impression.
key_concepts: Some people, like the man shown in Figure 131, are habitual doorway leaners and go through life intimidating most people from the first introduction.
Habitual doorway leaners are well advised to practise an erect stance with palms visible to make a favourable impression on others.
People form 90 per cent of their opinion about you in the first ninety seconds of meeting you.
You never get a second chance to make a first impression.
A sales person calling on a customer at his home is well advised to ask him 'Which seat is yours?' before he sits down.
Sitting in the wrong chair intimidates the customer and puts him offside, which can have a detrimental effect on the chance of a successful sale.
The doorway is a favourite spot for the intimidator, because leaning against the doorway in another's office is one of the very subtle techniques of intimidation.
An erect stance with the palms visible is the recommended antidote for the habitual doorway leaner who wants to stop intimidating people from the moment of introduction.
Because people form 90 per cent of their opinion about you in the first ninety seconds, the doorway leaner's first-introduction intimidation is fixed within that opening window.
The customer put offside by the salesman sitting in his chair is an example of how an innocent territorial violation can damage the chance of a successful sale.

assets.topic: Audit the Ownership Gestures: Who Suddenly Uses Them and Why
assets.visual_frame_description: An audit ledger styled as an executive office: a clipboard ticks off 'newly appointed' employees who suddenly grow a leg-over-chair pose, a Figure 132 card stamps OWNERSHIP on an armchair, and a sliding scale shows the boss's feet rising from the bottom drawer to the desktop as a superior's shadow recedes from the door.
assets.player_mission: Your mission is to audit the ownership gestures of management: tick off the finding that management personnel are particularly guilty of continually using them and that newly appointed employees suddenly begin to use them despite seldom doing so before promotion. Then take the inventory of claims, from the leg-over-chair gesture that signifies ownership of the chair or space and signals that customary etiquettes may be relaxed, to the feet on the desk, the foot on the bottom drawer, and the foot placed hard against the desk leg, and check which version the boss dares to use when his superior enters the office.
key_concepts: Management personnel are particularly guilty of continually using the ownership gestures.
Employees who have been newly appointed to management positions suddenly begin to use the ownership gestures, despite the fact that they seldom used them prior to their promotion.
The leg-over-chair gesture not only signifies the man's ownership of that particular chair or space, but also signals that customary etiquettes may be relaxed.
It would be normal to assume that the position of the man in Figure 132 reflects an easygoing, relaxed and carefree attitude, because that is in fact what it is.
It is common to see two close friends seated in the leg-over-chair position, laughing and joking with each other.
If the boss's chair has no arms, which is unlikely because this is usually the visitor's chair, he may be seen with one or both feet on the desk.

If his superior enters the office, it is unlikely that the boss would use an obvious territorial or ownership gesture, but would resort to more subtle versions such as putting his foot on the bottom drawer of his desk.
If the desk has no drawers, the boss stakes his claim by placing his foot hard against the leg of the desk.

The sudden appearance of ownership gestures in the newly promoted is telling: these people used the gestures seldom before their promotion, but began to use them continually as soon as they reached management.
The relaxed etiquettes signalled by the leg-over-chair gesture explain why two close friends may laugh and joke in that position while a subordinate in the same chair would be a territorial insult.

assets.topic: Matrix Match: The Boss's Leg-Over-Chair Moment
assets.visual_frame_description: A four-cell matrix on an office wall: in one cell a dejected employee leans forward with hands on knees and face down, in the next a motionless boss suddenly swings a leg over the chair arm, in the third the boss wears a concerned mask while his thought bubble reads 'same old story', and in the fourth the boss breathes a sigh of relief as the employee leaves through the door.
assets.player_mission: Your mission is to build a four-cell matrix around the employee-in-the-boss's-office scene: drop the employee's dejection cluster, hands on his knees, face down and lowered tone, into one cell, the boss's motionless listening and sudden leg-over-chair flip into the next, and the boss's change to lack of concern or indifference, his concerned-look cover-up, his dismissal of the problem and his sigh of relief into the reading cells. Then follow the boss's retreat to the no-arms visitor's chair and the subtle feet-on-desk and foot-against-desk-leg staking that marks the claim when the superior is absent.
key_concepts: In the typical situation an employee with a personal problem goes into the boss's office to ask his advice on a possible solution.
As the employee explains, he leans forward in the chair, his hands on his knees, his face down and looking dejected and his tone of voice lowered.
The boss listens intently, sitting motionless, then suddenly leans back in his chair and puts one leg over the arm.
In these circumstances the boss's attitude has changed to lack of concern or indifference because of his carefree gesture.
When the boss puts one leg over the chair arm he may even feel that his time is being wasted with the 'same old story'.
While he remains in the leg-over-chair position, the boss will probably have a concerned look on his face throughout the discussion to cover up his lack of interest.
The boss may terminate the discussion by telling his employee that he need not worry and that the problem will simply go away.
When the employee leaves the office, the boss may breathe a sigh of relief and say to himself 'Thank heavens he's gone!' and take his leg off the chair.
The employee's cluster, hands on knees, face down, dejected look and lowered tone, is the read-out of genuine concern, against which the boss's sudden leg-over-chair flip reads as indifference.
Because the no-arms chair is usually the visitor's chair, the boss with a no-arms chair is the one seen with one or both feet on the desk in the ownership version of the claim.

assets.topic: Boss Level: Breaking the Indifferent Posture at the Negotiating Table
assets.visual_frame_description: A boss arena that is a negotiation table where a hostile counterpart sprawls with a leg over the chair arm and feet on the desk, radiating a red indifferent aura that grows with every second; a counter-card slides across the table holding an unreachable document, and a speech bubble delivers the 'split in his trousers' line that breaks the pose with a laugh.
assets.player_mission: Your mission is to defeat the final boss, the indifferent or hostile negotiator locked in the leg-over-chair or feet-on-desk position: hold your ground against the annoyance these gestures cause during negotiation, apply the vital rule that the person must change to a different position because the longer he stays, the longer his indifferent or hostile attitude lasts, then deploy the two counter-moves, handing him something he cannot reach so he must lean across, and the split-in-his-trousers joke for those who share your sense of humour.
key_concepts: These territorial gestures can be quite annoying if they occur during negotiation.

It is vital that the person should change to a different position because the longer he stays in the leg-over-chair or feet-on-desk position, the longer he will have an indifferent or hostile attitude.
An easy way to break the leg-over-chair or feet-on-desk position is to hand him something that he cannot reach and ask him to lean across and look at it.
If you and he have a similar sense of humour, tell him he has a split in his trousers.
The longer a negotiator stays in the leg-over-chair or feet-on-desk position, the longer his indifferent or hostile attitude persists, so the position itself must be changed.
Because the leg-over-chair position covers a lack of interest with a concerned look, breaking the posture with an unreachable object forces the person to re-engage.
The ownership gestures of management, once detected at the negotiating table, are a warning that the user's attitude has shifted to indifference or hostility.
The same carefree leg-over-chair gesture that shows two friends laughing and joking becomes a hostile signal when it appears across a negotiation table.
Handing the counterpart something he cannot reach changes the position and thereby shortens the indifferent or hostile attitude that the position prolongs.
The split-in-his-trousers remark works as a counter-move only when you and he have a similar sense of humour, and it too forces a change of position.

chapters.title: Chapter 13: Carbon Copies and Mirror Images

assets.topic: Scrub the Phenomenon: What Carbon Copying Is and What It Says
assets.visual_frame_description: A time-scrubber playhead glides over a social gathering where pairs of people stand in matching postures; it pauses on two men at a hotel bar who uncross their arms and pocket their hands in sync, then zooms out to married couples walking in identical stride, while a caption reads I think the same as you over one pair's mirrored stances.
assets.player_mission: Your mission is to scrub through the carbon copy phenomenon itself: how people at social functions adopt the identical gestures and posture of the person they are talking with, how this unconscious mimicry tells the other person I think the same as you, and how the copying continues for as long as the two people remain in agreement. Then trace the evidence, from the two men at the hotel bar who mirror every move, to the way married couples walk, stand, sit and move in identical ways, to Scheflen's finding that strangers studiously avoid holding mutual positions, and finish with why this is one of the most important non-verbal lessons we can learn.
key_concepts: At any social function or place where people meet and interact, a number of people will have adopted the identical gestures and posture of the person with whom they are talking, and this is called carbon copying.
Carbon copying is a means by which one person tells the other that he is in agreement with his ideas and attitudes.
By copying his postures and gestures a person non-verbally says to the other, 'As you can see, I think the same as you, so I will copy your posture and gestures.'

This unconscious mimicry is quite interesting to observe, as shown by the two men standing at the hotel bar in Figure 134, who had mirrored each other's gestures, making it reasonable to assume they were discussing a topic upon which they had the same thoughts and feelings.

If one of the two men at the bar uncrosses his arms and legs or stands on the other foot, the other will follow, and if one puts his hand in his pocket, the other will copy, and this mimicry will continue for as long as the two men are in agreement.
Carbon copying also occurs among good friends or people at the same status level, and it is common to see married couples walk, stand, sit and move in identical ways.
Scheflen found that people who are strangers studiously avoid holding mutual positions.
The significance of carbon copying can be one of the most important non-verbal lessons we can learn, for it is one way that others tell us that they agree with us or like us.
Carbon copying is also a way for us to tell others that we like them, by simply copying their gestures.
If an employer wishes to develop an immediate rapport and create a relaxed atmosphere with an employee, he need only copy the employee's posture to achieve this end.

assets.topic: Dialogue on Status and Rapport: Who Copies Whom Among Bosses, Employees and Couples
assets.visual_frame_description: A seminar table showing two matched pairs: an employer leaning into an employee's mirrored posture on one side, and an up-and-coming employee mirroring his boss's hands-behind-head gesture on the other; above them a doorway where the boss walks through first, a boardroom where he sits at the head of the table, and a couch where a wife's gesture is copied by a talking husband.
assets.player_mission: Your mission is to stage a dialogue on the social choreography of mirroring: debate the employer who copies an employee's posture to build rapport against the up-and-coming employee who copies his boss's gestures to show agreement, then trace how groups fall into step with their leaders, from the first man through a doorway to the boss at the head of the boardroom table, and finish in the living room, where married couples walk, stand, sit and move in identical ways and the salesperson must watch who initiates the gestures and who follows.
key_concepts: If an employer wishes to develop an immediate rapport and create a relaxed atmosphere with an employee, he need only copy the employee's posture to achieve this end.
An up-and-coming employee may be seen copying his boss's gestures in an attempt to show agreement.
Research shows that when the leader of a group uses certain gestures and positions, subordinates copy them.
Leaders also tend to be the first of a group to walk through a doorway, and they like to sit on the end of a couch or bench seat rather than in the centre.
When a group of executives walk into a room, the boss usually goes first.
When executives are seated in the board room, the boss usually sits at the head of the table, often farthest from the door.
If the boss sits with a hands-behind-head T-cross gesture (Figure 96), his subordinates will copy.
It is common to see married couples walk, stand, sit and move in identical ways because carbon copying occurs among good friends or people at the same status level.
People who sell to married couples in their home are well advised to watch the couple's gestures, to see who initiates the gestures and who follows.

If the husband is doing all the talking and the wife sits there saying nothing, but the husband copies his wife's gestures, you will inevitably find that she makes the decisions and writes the cheques, so it is a good idea to direct your presentation to her.

assets.topic: Audit the Deliberate Technique: Mirroring as a Sales Instrument
assets.visual_frame_description: An audit ledger opens on a sales ledger page: a clipboard with a checklist showing Copy positive gestures, Create receptive frame of mind, Establish strong enough rapport, and Proceed with presentation, while a figure 135 caption reads he can 'see' that you understand his point of view over a salesman and prospect in matching postures, and a bell rings marked SALE when the prospect copies back.
assets.player_mission: Your mission is to audit mirroring used as a deliberate tool of influence: check off how copying the positive gestures and postures of the other person can influence a face-to-face encounter, how it puts the other person in a receptive and relaxed frame of mind because he can 'see' that you understand his point of view, and then open Pease's own sales ledger, where he deliberately copied every movement of a 'cold' insurance prospect until rapport was established, and where a sale resulted whenever the prospect began copying his gestures.
key_concepts: Using the knowledge of carbon copying, it is possible to influence a face-to-face encounter by copying the positive gestures and postures of the other person.
Copying the other person's postures has the effect of putting the other person in a receptive and relaxed frame of mind, as he can 'see' that you understand his point of view (Figure 135).
When Pease was selling insurance he found copying a very effective technique for a 'cold' prospective customer.
Pease deliberately copied each movement the prospective customer made until he felt he had established a strong enough rapport to allow the presentation to proceed.
Invariably, if the prospect began copying his gestures, a sale would result.
An employer who copies an employee's posture can develop an immediate rapport and create a relaxed atmosphere, without saying a word about agreement.
Because copying the other person's gestures tells him you think the same as he does, it is a way for us to tell others that we like them.
The mimicry between two people will continue only for as long as the two are in agreement, so a copying prospect in the midst of a sales presentation is itself a signal of agreement.
People who sell to married couples in their home are well advised to watch the couple's gestures, to see who initiates the gestures and who follows, before aiming the presentation.
When the husband copies his wife's gestures while he does the talking, the wife makes the decisions and writes the cheques, so the presentation should be directed to her.

assets.topic: Matrix Match: When Mirroring Backfires, the Status Equation and Taking Control
assets.visual_frame_description: A wall matrix with four cells: one shows the clerk copying the manager's T-cross and figure 4 leg lock while a red X stamps JOB IN JEOPARDY, another shows accountants, lawyers and managers leaning back in dominance, a third shows a man taking the same posture and disconcerting a 'superior' type who shifts in his chair, and the fourth shows a boardroom where subordinates copy the boss's hands-behind-head gesture.
assets.player_mission: Your mission is to build a matrix of when copying works and when it backfires: drop the junior clerk who copies his manager's superiority T-cross and figure 4 leg lock into the backfire cell, note that even subordinate verbal communication cannot save him from the intimidated, insulted manager, then place the accountants, lawyers and management personnel who assume these postures in the presence of those they consider inferior, and finish in the control cell, where taking the same posture as a 'superior' type disconcerts him and forces him to change position, handing you the control.
key_concepts: Before copying the other person's gestures when negotiating, it is vital that your relationship with that person be taken into consideration.

When the junior clerk of a large corporation has asked for a pay rise and is called into the manager's office, the manager may ask him to sit down and then assume a superiority T-cross gesture (Figure 96) and a figure 4 leg lock (Figure 81) while he leans back in his chair to show his superior, dominant and competitive attitude.

If the clerk copied the manager's dominant posture while discussing his potential salary rise (Figure 136), even if his verbal communication were on the subordinate level, the manager would feel intimidated and even insulted by the clerk's non-verbal behaviour.
A clerk who copies his manager's dominant posture while asking for a salary rise could put his job in jeopardy.
Copying a superior's dominant posture is a highly effective method of disarming 'superior' types who try to take the control.
Accountants, lawyers and management personnel are known for assuming these dominant postures in the presence of people whom they consider inferior.

By taking the same posture as a person who assumes a superior, dominant and competitive attitude, you can effectively disconcert them and force them to change their position, allowing you to take the control.

Research shows that when the leader of a group uses certain gestures and positions, subordinates copy them, which is why the boss's hands-behind-head T-cross gesture (Figure 96) is copied in the board room.
Because strangers studiously avoid holding mutual positions, while friends and equals copy each other, copying is only appropriate when the relationship already supports rapport.
The mimicry between two people continues only as long as they are in agreement, so copying the wrong posture, such as a dominant one, tells the other person you are claiming his territory of control.

assets.topic: Boss Level: Reading the Mirror to Find the Decision Maker and Win the Encounter
assets.visual_frame_description: A boss arena shaped like a board room where the boss sits at the head of the table farthest from the door with a hands-behind-head T-cross gesture and subordinates copy him; a spotlight picks out a silent wife whose every gesture is mirrored by her talking husband, while a ledger stamp reads SHE WRITES THE CHEQUES, and a final challenger forces a leaning-back manager to shift in his chair and surrender the control.
assets.player_mission: Your mission is to defeat the final boss, a boardroom negotiation where everyone copies the leader: read who initiates the gestures and who follows, spot the boss as the first through the doorway and at the head of the table, catch the husband who copies his silent wife and know that she writes the cheques, use copying to put the other person in a receptive and relaxed frame of mind, and turn the manoeuvre on the 'superior' types who lean back with T-cross and figure 4 leg lock, forcing them to change position so you take the control.
key_concepts: The next time you attend a social function or a place where people meet and interact, take note of the number of people who have adopted the identical gestures and posture of the person with whom they are talking, for this carbon copying is a means by which one person tells the other that he is in agreement with his ideas and attitudes.
The significance of carbon copying can be one of the most important non-verbal lessons we can learn, for this is one way that others tell us that they agree with us or like us.
By simply copying another person's gestures we can tell them that we like them, which is why an employer need only copy an employee's posture to develop an immediate rapport and a relaxed atmosphere.
Scheflen found that people who are strangers studiously avoid holding mutual positions, while married couples commonly walk, stand, sit and move in identical ways.

Using the knowledge of carbon copying it is possible to influence a face-to-face encounter, because copying the other person's positive gestures and postures puts him in a receptive and relaxed frame of mind as he can 'see' that you understand his point of view.

In selling insurance to a 'cold' prospective customer, Pease deliberately copied each movement the prospect made until he felt he had established a strong enough rapport to allow the presentation to proceed, and invariably, if the prospect began copying his gestures, a sale would result.

People who sell to married couples in their home are well advised to watch the couple's gestures to see who initiates the gestures and who follows, because if the husband copies his wife's gestures, she makes the decisions and writes the cheques.

When a group of executives walk into a room the boss usually goes first, and when they are seated in the board room he sits at the head of the table, often farthest from the door, where his hands-behind-head T-cross gesture (Figure 96) is copied by his subordinates.

Accountants, lawyers and management personnel are known for assuming superior, dominant postures in the presence of people they consider inferior, and by taking the same posture you can effectively disconcert them and force them to change their position, allowing you to take the control.

Before copying the other person's gestures when negotiating it is vital that your relationship with that person be taken into consideration, because a junior clerk who copies his manager's dominant posture could find his job in jeopardy.
The mimicry between two people will continue for as long as they are in agreement, so both the mirroring you copy and the mirroring you receive are running signals of whether agreement is holding.

assets.topic: Scrub the History: Highness, Lowness and the Ancient Language of Height
assets.visual_frame_description: A time-scrubber playhead glides over a royal court where a woman curtseys and a man removes his hat before a seated monarch, then over a rally speaker on a soapbox, a judge on a raised bench, a penthouse skyline, and a soldier's salute morphing from a deep bow into the raised hand of the modern military salute.
assets.player_mission: Your mission is to scrub through the historical record of body lowering: how lowering the height of one's body in front of another person has been used to establish superior and subordinate relationships, why we call royalty 'Your Highness' and unpleasant people 'low', how the soapbox speaker, the elevated judge and the penthouse dweller each command more authority by their height, how cultures divide themselves into upper and lower classes, and how the curtsey, the inclined head and the modern salute all survive as relics of the act of making yourself smaller than the other person.
key_concepts: Historically, lowering the height of one's body in front of another person has been used as a means of establishing superior and subordinate relationships.
We refer to a member of Royalty as 'Your Highness', whereas individuals who commit unsavoury acts are called 'low'.
The protest rally speaker stands on a soapbox to be higher than everyone else, and the judge sits higher than the rest of the court.
Those who live in a penthouse command more authority than those who live at ground level, and some cultures divide their social classes into the 'upper class' and 'lower class'.
Despite what many people would like to believe, tall people command more authority than short people.
Most women curtsey when they meet Royalty and men incline their heads or remove their hats, making themselves appear smaller than the Royal person.
The modern salute is a relic of the act of body lowering.
The more humble or subordinate an individual feels towards another, the lower he stoops his body.
In business, the people who continually 'bow' to the management are labelled with such derogatory name tags as 'bootlickers' or 'crawlers'.
Unfortunately, little can be done to help people become taller or shorter, so Pease turns to exploring some useful applications of height.

assets.topic: Dialogue on the Height Principle: Authority, Eye-to-Eye Contact and Shrinking Yourself

Then weigh what the stooped body signals about humility and subordination, and what the slouched body signals when informality itself becomes the aggression.

The more humble or subordinate an individual feels towards another, the lower he stoops his body.

It is the complete informality on the other person's territory that communicates the dominant or aggressive attitude.

assets.topic: Audit the Speeding Stop: The Negatives of Staying in the Car and the Four-Step Stoop Technique
assets.visual_frame_description: An audit ledger by a parked patrol car: on the debit column a driver stays inside his car while a policeman crosses from his patrol car to the window, a barrier drawn between them; on the credit column the driver walks to the officer's car, stoops over smaller than the officer, shows open palms and a trembling voice, and the officer's ticket book closes unmarked with a 50 per cent stamp.
assets.player_mission: Your mission is to audit the roadside encounter step by step: tick off why the officer may regard you as an adversary, then run the ledger of the driver's usual behaviour, debiting the officer's forced exit from his territory, the excuses that read as an attack, and the barrier created by staying in the car, each increasing your chances of being booked. Then pass the alternative: leaving your car for his territory, stooping to be smaller than him, lowering your own status while raising his, and the open palms with trembling voice, and close the books on the claim that this technique can save you from being booked more than 50 per cent of the time.
key_concepts: In the circumstances where you have been speeding in your car and are stopped by the police, the officer may regard you as an adversary as he approaches your vehicle.
A driver's usual reaction when stopped is to remain in the car, wind the window down and make excuses for having exceeded the speed limit.
One nonverbal negative of staying in the car is that the officer is forced to leave his territory, the patrol car, and come across to your territory, your vehicle.
Another negative is that, assuming you have in fact broken the speed limit, your excuses may represent an attack to the officer.
By remaining in your car, you create a barrier between yourself and the policeman.

Considering that under these circumstances the police officer is obviously in a superior position to you, this type of behaviour only serves to make things go from bad to worse and your chances of being booked are increased.

The recommended approach when flagged down is to get immediately out of your car, your territory, and go over to the police officer's car, his territory, so that he is not inconvenienced by having to leave his territory.
You should stoop your body over so that you are smaller than the police officer is.

You should lower your own status by telling the officer how foolish and irresponsible you are and raise his status by thanking him for pointing out the error of your ways and telling him that you realise how difficult his job must be with fools like you around.
With your palms out and in a trembling voice, you should ask the officer not to give you a ticket.

This type of behaviour shows the police officer that you are not a threat to him and often causes him to take the role of an angry parent, in which case he gives you a stern warning and tells you to be on your way, without a speeding ticket.
When this technique is used as directed, it can save you from being booked more than 50 per cent of the time.

assets.topic: Matrix Match: The Counter Barrier, Territory and the Two Faces of Lowering
assets.visual_frame_description: A wall matrix of four storefront cards: an irate customer faced across a counter with a barrier line drawn, a storekeeper ducking around to the customer's side with open palms, a visitor slouched deep in an easy chair while the standing owner watches, and a map showing home territory marked superior while a caption reads A person will always be superior on his own territory.
assets.player_mission: Your mission is to build a four-cell matrix from the chapter's situations: place the irate customer and the store counter barrier into one cell, the storekeeper's escape from his own side of the counter with stooped body and visible palms into another, the slouch in the easy chair that inverts lowering into a dominance signal into a third, and the rule that a person is always superior on his own territory into the fourth. Then drop the territorial law into each scenario to explain why the officer, the storekeeper and the home owner each behave as they do.
key_concepts: The same technique that works with the police officer can be used to calm an irate customer who is returning some faulty goods to a retail store.
In the retail situation, the counter represents a barrier between the store owner and the customer.
Control of an irate customer would be difficult if the storekeeper remained on his own side of the counter, and this staking-out of territory would make the customer angrier.

The best approach would be for the storekeeper to come around to the customer's side of the counter with his body stooped over and palms visible and to use the same technique as was used with the police officer.
Interestingly, there are some circumstances under which lowering the body can be a dominance signal.
Lowering the body becomes a dominance signal where you slouch down and make yourself comfortable in an easy chair in another person's home while the owner is standing.
It is the complete informality on the other person's territory that communicates the dominant or aggressive attitude.
It is also important to remember that a person will always be superior on his own territory, especially in his own home.
Submissive gestures and behaviour are very effective methods for getting the person on side with you.
The more humble or subordinate an individual feels towards another, the lower he stoops his body.

assets.topic: Boss Level: Invert the Bow, Own the Territory and Win the Person Over
assets.visual_frame_description: A boss arena that is a living room: the visitor sinks low into the owner's easy chair, relaxed and sprawled, while the standing owner's authority visibly drains; a mirror then flips the scene to the same visitor stooping small before a police officer and a storekeeper, and a banner reads Submissive gestures get the person on side.
