This dominance effect occurs where you slouch down and make yourself comfortable in an easy chair in another person's home while the owner is standing.
It is the complete informality on the other person's territory that communicates the dominant or aggressive attitude.
A person will always be superior on his own territory, especially in his own home.
Submissive gestures and behaviour are very effective methods for getting the person on side with you.
It is possible to avoid intimidating others by consciously making yourself appear smaller in relation to them.

This type of behaviour shows the police officer that you are not a threat to him and often causes him to take the role of an angry parent, in which case he gives you a stern warning and tells you to be on your way, without a speeding ticket.
When the stooped-body technique is used as directed, it can save you from being booked more than 50 per cent of the time.
The best approach for a storekeeper facing an irate customer is to come around to the customer's side of the counter with his body stooped over and palms visible.
Historically, lowering the height of one's body in front of another person has been used as a means of establishing superior and subordinate relationships.
The more humble or subordinate an individual feels towards another, the lower he stoops his body.
Most women curtsey when they meet Royalty and men incline their heads or remove their hats, making themselves appear smaller than the Royal person.

assets.topic: Scrub the Origins: Where the Body Points, Where It Wants to Go
assets.visual_frame_description: A still-photograph frame freezes a smiling, nodding head over a torso that points away at an exit sign; a door threshold shows two men facing off while an arrow traces the listener's body line towards the corridor, and a negotiation table tilts as a seated man swivels his feet towards the nearest exit while a caption asks whether to re-engage or end on your terms.
assets.player_mission: Your mission is to scrub through the opening evidence of body pointing: why a person who seems to enjoy your company may still show a still photograph in which the head smiles and nods at you while the body and feet point away towards another person or an exit, how the torso and feet act as pointers to a person's preferred direction, the two men in the doorway and what it takes to make a conversation mutually interesting, and the negotiator who turns his body or swings his feet towards the nearest exit when he has decided to terminate. Then weigh the signal's payoff: either get the person involved or terminate the conversation on your terms and keep control, remembering that the angle at which people orient their bodies gives many non-verbal clues to their attitudes and relationships.
key_concepts: The direction in which a person points his or her torso or feet is a signal of where he or she would prefer to be going.

A still photograph of someone who would rather be elsewhere would probably reveal the head turned towards you with facial signals such as smiling and nodding, while the body and feet point away from you, either towards another person or towards an exit.

In Figure 139 the man on the left is trying to hold the other man's attention, but his listener wishes to continue in the direction to which his body is pointing, although his head is turned to acknowledge the other man's presence.
It is only when the man on the right turns his body towards the other that a mutually interesting conversation can take place.
Often in negotiations, when one person has decided to terminate the negotiation or wants to leave, he will turn his body or swing his feet to point towards the nearest exit.

If you see exit-pointing signals during a face-to-face encounter, you should do something to get the person involved and interested or else terminate the conversation on your terms, which allows you to maintain the control.
The angle at which people orient their bodies gives many non-verbal clues to their attitudes and relationships.
People in most English speaking countries stand with their bodies oriented to form an angle of 90 degrees during ordinary social intercourse.

assets.topic: Dialogue on Angles and Triangles: Open and Closed Formations
assets.visual_frame_description: A debate stage where a triangle icon argues with a zero-degree line icon: on one side two torsos angle at 90 degrees around an imaginary third point with a chair waiting at the apex, morphing into a square and then two triangles as figures join; on the other side two torsos close to 0 degrees while a third figure is granted only a head turn, his ghostly torso arrow pointing away from the pair.
assets.player_mission: Your mission is to stage a dialogue between the open formation and the closed formation: argue for the 90-degree triangle of ordinary social intercourse that invites a third person of similar status to the third point, and the square and circle-or-two-triangles that form as a fourth and fifth person are accepted, then defend the closed formation, where the torso angle drops from 90 degrees to 0, the distance shrinks, courtship begins with a body pointed at the partner and the partner's torso turning to 0 degrees, mirroring signals mutual interest, and hostility can turn the same formation into a non-verbal challenge. Settle the argument over inclusion and exclusion: the torso turn that invites a third person to stay versus the head-only turn that recognises his presence while showing he is not invited to remain.
key_concepts: Two men with their bodies angled towards an imaginary third point form a triangle, which serves as a non-verbal invitation for a third person to join the conversation by standing at the third point.
The two men in Figure 140 display similar status by holding similar gestures and posture, and the angle formed by their torsos indicates that an impersonal conversation is probably taking place.
The formation of the triangle invites a third person of similar status to join the conversation.
When a fourth person is accepted into the group a square will be formed, and for a fifth person, either a circle or two triangles.
When intimacy or privacy is required by two people, the angle formed by their torsos decreases from 90 degrees down to 0 degrees.

A man wishing to attract a female partner points his body towards her and closes the distance between them as he moves into her intimate zone, and to accept his approach she need only orient her torso angle to 0 degrees and allow him to enter her territory.
The distance between two people standing in the closed formation is usually less than that of the open formation.
In addition to the usual courtship displays, both parties may mirror each other's gestures if they are interested in each other.
Like some other courtship gestures, the closed formation can be used as a non-verbal challenge between people who are hostile to each other.

When a third person wishes to join two others who are standing in a closed formation, he may be invited to join the conversation only when the other two orient their torsos towards a mutual third point to form the triangle.

If the third person is not accepted, the others will hold the closed formation position and turn only their heads towards him as a sign of recognition of the third person's presence, but the direction of their torsos shows that he is not invited to remain.

A conversation among three people may begin in the open triangular formation but eventually two may take the closed formation position to exclude the third person, a clear signal to the third person that he should leave the group to avoid embarrassment.

assets.topic: Audit the Seated and the Feet: Knees, Foot Pointing and Inclusion
assets.visual_frame_description: An audit ledger over a lounge scene: a seated couple cross knees towards each other with mirrored posture while an excluded man on the right holds a chair, three men at a party each angle one foot at an attractive woman who stands feet-together and glances sideways, and a round table where a head swivels between a talkative questioner and a silent listener as a checklist ticks off each inclusion move.
assets.player_mission: Your mission is to audit the body pointing that happens below the desk and across the room: check off the seated knee cross as a sign of acceptance or interest and the mutual copying of movements that seals a seated closed formation, tick off the excluded man's only remedies, the chair moved in front of the couple and the attempt to form a triangle, then open the ledger of foot pointing, where feet point at people who are interesting or attractive, three men each point one foot at the woman they want, the woman holds the neutral feet-together position before pointing one foot at her favourite man, and a sideways glance lands on the man using the thumbs-in-belt gesture. Close the books with the interview technique that lets the silent partner feel involved by turning your head from questioner to listener and back again.
key_concepts: Crossing the knees towards another person is a sign of acceptance or interest in that person.

If the other person also becomes interested, he or she will cross knees towards the first person, and as the two people become more involved with each other they will begin to copy each other's movements and gestures, forming a closed formation that excludes all others.

The only way in which a man excluded from a seated closed formation could participate in the conversation would be to move a chair to a position in front of the couple and attempt to form a triangle, or take some other action to break the formation.
Not only do the feet serve as pointers, indicating the direction in which a person would like to go, but they are also used to point at people who are interesting or attractive.

At a social function where a group of three men talks with one very attractive woman, the men all having one foot pointing towards the woman is a simple non-verbal cue with which they are all telling the woman that they are interested in her.
Subconsciously, the woman sees the foot gestures and is likely to remain with the group for as long as she is receiving this attention.
In Figure 146 the woman stands with both feet together in the neutral position and she may eventually point one foot toward the man whom she finds the most attractive or interesting.
In Figure 146 you will also notice that the woman is giving a sideways glance to the man who is using the thumbs-in-belt gesture.

When interviewing two people and the talkative person A asks a question, look at him as you begin to answer, then turn your head towards the silent person B, then back to A, then to B again until you make your final statement, looking at A again as you finish your sentence.
The head-turning inclusion technique lets the silent person feel involved in the conversation and is particularly useful if you need to have that person on side with you.

assets.topic: Matrix Match: The Counselling Room, Chairs and Angle Formations
assets.visual_frame_description: A counselling office matrix with four labelled cells: in SET-UP, a boss steps around his desk to the employee's side while a fixed-leg armless chair and a swivel chair with arms stand ready; in the angle cells, a triangle over two relaxed torsos, a swivel chair swinging to point directly at a subordinate who rubs his eye and mouth and looks away under a business gaze, and a right-angle seat where an embarrassing question is asked without pressure.
assets.player_mission: Your mission is to build the counselling room matrix for the supervisor about to counsel a subordinate whose work performance has been unsatisfactory and erratic: place the co-operative position, the boss who moves from behind his desk to the employee's side while keeping unspoken control, the subordinate's fixed-leg, armless chair that forces revealing gestures, and the boss's own swivel chair with arms into the SET-UP cell, then sort the three angle formations into their cells, the open triangle that opens the session and shows agreement by copying, the direct body point with the business gaze and reduced gestures that presses for direct answers and can force the truth when the subordinate rubs his eye and mouth and looks away, and the right angle position that takes the pressure off for delicate questions, remembering that for a difficult nut you may revert to the direct body point technique to get to the facts.
key_concepts: The fact that the counselling session is in your office and that you are the boss allows you to move from behind your desk to the employee's side of the desk, the co-operative position, and still maintain unspoken control.
The subordinate should be seated on a chair with fixed legs and no arms, one that forces him to use body gestures and postures that will give you a better understanding of his attitudes.
You should be sitting on a swivel chair with arms, giving you more control and letting you eliminate some of your own giveaway gestures by allowing you to move around.
Like the standing triangular position, the open triangular formation lends an informal, relaxed attitude to the meeting and is a good position in which to open a counselling session.

You can show non-verbal agreement with the subordinate from the open triangular position by copying his movements and gestures, and as both torsos point to a third mutual point to form a triangle, this can show mutual agreement.
By turning your chair to point your body directly at your subordinate you are non-verbally telling him that you want direct answers to your questions.
Combining the direct body point position with the business gaze and reduced body and facial gestures makes the subject feel tremendous non-verbal pressure.
If, after you have asked him a question, he rubs his eye and mouth and looks away when he answers, swing your chair to point directly at him and say, 'Are you sure about that?'
The simple movement of swinging your chair to point directly at the subordinate exerts non-verbal pressure on him and can force him to tell the truth.

When you position your body at a right angle away from your subject, you take the pressure off the interview, and this is an excellent position from which to ask delicate or embarrassing questions, encouraging more open answers to your questions without any pressure coming from you.
If the nut you are trying to crack is a difficult one, you may need to revert to the direct body point technique to get to the facts.

assets.topic: Boss Level: Mastering the Point, From Rapport to Natural Movement
assets.visual_frame_description: A boss arena shaped like a coaching office: three pedestals hold the triangle for rapport, the direct body point for pressure and the right angle for independent thinking, a practice dolly zooms as stiff techniques soften into natural movement, and a final cutscene shows a friendly encounter with foot pointing, open arms, visible palms, leaning forward, head tilting and a smile radiating influence from one person to another.
assets.player_mission: Your mission is to defeat the final boss, mastery of body pointing in day-to-day encounters: hold the triangular position to build rapport, deploy the direct body point when you need non-verbal pressure, and adopt the right angle position so the other person can think and act independently, then survive the gauntlet of practice that turns these techniques into natural movements, the swivel chair skill that is worth acquiring if you deal with others for a living, and the exit-pointing signal that tells you when to re-engage or end the conversation on your terms. Finish the level by sending the positive cluster out into the world, where foot pointing, body pointing and gestures such as open arms, visible palms, leaning forward, head tilting and smiling make others enjoy your company and be influenced by your point of view.
key_concepts: If you want a person to have rapport with you, use the triangular position, and when you need to exert non-verbal pressure, use the direct body point.
The right angle position allows the other person to think and act independently, without non-verbal pressure from you.
Few people have ever considered the effect of body pointing in influencing the attitudes and the responses of others.
These techniques take much practice to master but they can become natural movements before long.
If you deal with others for a living, mastery of body point and swivel chair techniques are very useful skills to acquire.

In your day-to-day encounters with others, foot pointing, body pointing and positive gesture clusters such as open arms, visible palms, leaning forward, head tilting and smiling can make it easy for others not only to enjoy your company, but to be influenced by your point of view.

When you see a person turn his body or swing his feet to point towards the nearest exit during a face-to-face encounter, do something to get him involved and interested or else terminate the conversation on your terms, which allows you to maintain the control.

When answering a question from a talkative person while a silent person listens, look at the questioner as you begin to answer, then turn your head towards the silent person, then back and forth again until you make your final statement looking at the questioner, so the silent person feels involved and on side with you.

The open triangular formation lends an informal, relaxed attitude to a meeting and is a good position in which to open a session, whereas turning your chair to point your body directly at your subject and combining it with the business gaze and reduced gestures makes him feel tremendous non-verbal pressure.

chapters.title: Chapter 16: Desks, Tables and Seating Arrangements

assets.topic: Scrub the Territory: From Knapp's Environments to the Four Basic Seating Positions
assets.visual_frame_description: A cutaway office with a rectangular desk and person A at the head while four labelled positions B1, B2, B3 and B4 circle around it; a playhead sweeps from a crowded restaurant where a couple is forced to sit facing each other, to the desk corner glowing as the friendly slot with eye-contact beams crossing it, to a technical expert seated opposite the client while the sales person sits beside him.
assets.player_mission: Your mission is to scrub through the geography of the desk: how Mark Knapp warned that the environment and the direction of the seats distort seating behaviour, how crowded restaurants force intimate couples into a defensive opposite position, and how the standard rectangular office desk gives person B four basic positions in relation to person A. Then walk the corner position B1 as the friendly casual slot with unlimited eye contact and a partial barrier at the desk corner, and the co-operative position B2 as the mutually oriented slot where the trick is taking it without invading A's territory, including the three-party strategy of 'siding with the opposition'.
key_concepts: Mark Knapp, in his book Non-Verbal Communication in Human Interaction, noted that although there is a general formula for the interpretation of seating positions, the environment may have an effect on the position chosen.
Research conducted with white middle-class Americans showed that seating positions taken in the public bar of a hotel can vary from the seating positions taken in a high-class restaurant.
The direction in which the seats are facing and the distance between tables can have a distorting influence on seating behaviour.

Intimate couples prefer to sit side by side wherever possible, but in a crowded restaurant where the tables are close together this is not possible and the couples are forced to sit opposite each other in what is normally a defensive position.
Because of a wide range of moderating circumstances, the seating examples in the chapter relate primarily to arrangements in an office environment with a standard rectangular desk.
Person B can take four basic seating positions in relation to person A: the corner position, the co-operative position, the competitive-defensive position and the independent position.

The corner position is normally used by people who are engaged in friendly, casual conversation and allows for unlimited eye contact and the opportunity to use numerous gestures and to observe the gestures of the other person.
The corner of the desk provides a partial barrier should one person begin to feel threatened, and this position avoids territorial division on the top of the table.

The most successful strategic position from which a sales person can deliver a presentation to a new customer is the corner position, assuming A is the buyer, and simply moving the chair to this position can relieve a tense atmosphere and increase the chances of a favourable negotiation.

The co-operative position occurs when two people are mutually oriented, both thinking alike or working on a task together, and it is one of the most strategic positions for presenting a case and having it accepted.
The trick in taking the co-operative position is for B to be able to take it without A feeling as though his territory has been invaded.

When a sales person introduces a technical expert into a second interview, the expert is seated at position C opposite customer A and the sales person takes the co-operative or corner position, a strategy known as 'siding with the opposition' that lets him question the technician on behalf of the client.

assets.topic: Dialogue on the Battle Line: The Competitive Position, the Doctor's Desk and the Invaded Territory
assets.visual_frame_description: A dialogue scene split in two: left, a doctor's office where a gauge jumps from 10 per cent to 55 per cent as the desk is removed, right, a small rectangular restaurant table with the salt, pepper, sugar bowl and napkins being pushed across a dashed centre line by two opposing hands while a bead of sweat forms on the victim's brow.
assets.player_mission: Your mission is to stage a dialogue across the table: argue the competitive-defensive position as the solid barrier that makes parties take firm stands, and weigh Argyle's doctor's office experiment where removing the desk raised the at-ease patients from 10 per cent to 55 per cent. Then cross-examine the influencing business, the deliberate reprimand, the unconscious division of the table into two equal territories, and re-enact Pease's restaurant test in which the menu, ashtray, sugar bowl and salt and pepper shakers were pushed across the centre line until the victim squirmed, sweated and fled.
key_concepts: Sitting across the table from a person can create a defensive, competitive atmosphere and can lead to each party taking a firm stand on his point of view because the table becomes a solid barrier between both parties.

The competitive-defensive position is taken by people who are either competing with each other or when one is reprimanding the other, and it can also establish that a superior/subordinate role exists when it is used in A's office.
Argyle noted that an experiment conducted in a doctor's office showed that the presence or absence of a desk had a significant effect on whether a patient was at ease or not.
Only 10 per cent of the patients were perceived to be at ease when the doctor's desk was present and the doctor sat behind it, but this figure increased to 55 per cent when the desk was absent.
If B is seeking to persuade A, the competitive-defensive position reduces the chance of a successful negotiation unless B is deliberately sitting opposite as part of a pre-planned strategy.
It may be that A is a manager who must severely reprimand employee B, and the competitive position can strengthen the reprimand, or B may deliberately sit directly opposite A to make A feel superior.

Whatever line of business you are in, if it involves dealing with people you are in the influencing business, and your objective should always be to see the other person's point of view, to put him or her at ease and make him or her feel right about dealing with you.

The competitive position does not lead towards putting the other person at ease, and more co-operation will be gained from the corner and co-operative positions than will ever be achieved from the competitive position.
Conversations are shorter and more specific in the competitive position than from any other seating position.

Whenever people sit directly opposite each other across a table, they unconsciously divide it into two equal territories, with each claiming half as his own territory and rejecting the other's encroaching upon it, which is why two people seated competitively at a restaurant table mark their territorial boundaries with the salt, pepper, sugar bowl and napkins.

In Pease's restaurant test the menu, ashtray, sugar bowl and salt and pepper shakers were pushed one by one into the companion's territory, making him sit back, squirm around in his seat and break into a light film of sweat on his brow.

When Pease returned to the table after the salesman had excused himself, he found all the table items had been pushed back to the centre line, demonstrating the tremendous resistance that a person has to the invasion of his territory.

assets.topic: Audit the Signal Test: The Article on the Desk, the Independent Position and the Shape of the Table
assets.visual_frame_description: An audit board with three stamped cards above a rectangular desk: a book placed on the table while a figure leans forward, another hand taking the book across the line and a red-stamped push back card; below, three table shapes, a square with a friendly arrow to the side seat and a red arrow to the opposite seat, a round table with equal wedge territories, and a library bench where two people sit apart with an angry bubble between them.
assets.player_mission: Your mission is to audit the reader's reactions at the desk: place the book, quotation or sample on the table and tick off the three possible responses, the lean forward that says stay on your side, the take into the territory that invites the corner or co-operative position, and the push back that spells trouble, against the golden rule of never encroaching without permission. Then audit the independent position in library, park bench and restaurant, and work through the square table's beside-you co-operation and opposite-you resistance and the round table's relaxed informality of equal status.
key_concepts: When you have a visual presentation, such as a book, quotation or sample, to show to a person sitting behind a rectangular desk, you should first place the article on the table.
The other person will lean forward and look at the article, take it into his territory, or push it back into your territory.

If the other person leans forward to look at the article, you must deliver your presentation from where you sit, as this action non-verbally tells you that he does not want you on his side of the desk.
If he takes the article into his territory, this gives you the opportunity to ask permission to enter his territory and take either the corner or co-operative positions.

If, however, he pushes the article back, you are in trouble, and the golden rule is never to encroach on the other person's territory unless you have been given verbal or non-verbal permission to do so or you will put them offside.
The independent position is the position taken by people when they do not wish to interact with each other, and it occurs in such places as a library, park bench or restaurant.

The independent position signifies lack of interest and can even be interpreted as hostile by the other person if the territorial boundaries are invaded, so it should be avoided where open discussion between A and B is required.

Square tables create a competitive or defensive relationship between people of equal status and are ideal for having short, to-the-point conversations or to create a superior/subordinate relationship.
At a square table the most co-operation usually comes from the person seated beside you, and the one on the right tends to be more co-operative than the one on the left.
At a square table the most resistance usually comes from the person seated directly opposite.
A round table creates an atmosphere of relaxed informality and is ideal for promoting discussion among people who are of equal status, as each person can claim the same amount of table territory.
Removing the table and sitting in a circle also promotes the same relaxed, equal-status result as the round table.

assets.topic: Matrix of Power: King Arthur's Round Table, the Rectangular Boardroom and the Family Dining Room
assets.visual_frame_description: A wall matrix with four labelled cells: a round table with a crown at the top and power numbers fading with distance to the knight opposite, a rectangular boardroom table with A, B, C and D name badges and a red flash on the chair whose back faces the door, three family table shapes labelled OPEN, CLOSED and AUTHORITATIVE, and an executive office where a square desk faces a round coffee table with wrap-around seating.
assets.player_mission: Your mission is to build a power matrix from the table shapes: plot King Arthur's Round Table where the king held the most power, the knights on his right and left the next amount and the knight directly across in the competitive-defensive position, then map the rectangular table's influence order of A, B, C, D with the back-to-the-door reversal, and the name badge strategy for structuring power plays. Finish by sorting the family dining table into the round 'open' family, the square 'closed' family and the rectangular 'authoritative' family, and the executive's split use of square work desk and round persuasion table.
key_concepts: King Arthur used the Round Table as an attempt to give each of his knights an equal amount of authority and status.
King Arthur was unaware that if the status of one person is higher than the others in the group, it alters the power and authority of each other individual.

The king held the most power at the Round Table, so the knights seated on either side of him were non-verbally granted the next highest amount of power, the one on his right having a little more than the one on the left.
The amount of power at the Round Table diminished relative to the distance that each knight was seated away from the king.
The knight seated directly across the table from King Arthur was, in effect, in the competitive-defensive position and was likely to be the one who gave the most trouble.

Many of today's business executives use both square and round tables, with the square work desk used for business activity, brief conversations and reprimands, and the round coffee table with wrap-around seating used to create an informal relaxed atmosphere or to persuade.

On a rectangular table position A has always commanded the most influence, and in a meeting of people of equal status the person sitting at position A will have the most influence, assuming that he does not have his back to the door.
If A's back were facing the door at a rectangular table, the person seated at B would be the most influential and would be strong competition for A.
Assuming that A was in the best power position at a rectangular table, person B has the next most authority, then C, then D.

This seating information makes it possible to structure power plays at meetings by placing name badges on the seats where you want each person to sit so that you may have the maximum influence over them.

The choice of the shape of a family dining room table can give a clue to the power distribution in that family, assuming that the dining-room could have accommodated a table of any shape and that the table shape was selected after considerable thought.
'Open' families go for round tables, 'closed' families select square tables and 'authoritative' types select rectangular tables.

assets.topic: Boss Level: Getting the Decision Over Dinner, From the Cave Feast to the Restaurant
assets.visual_frame_description: A boss arena that is a cave mouth at dusk: hunters divide the spoils around an open fire while one caveman eats with his back against the cave wall, then the scene crossfades to a candle-lit restaurant booth where the prospect sits with his back to a solid wall, a large green plant obscures the room, dim lights glow and muffled music plays, while a gauge shows respiration, heart rate, brain wave frequencies and blood pressure calming down.
assets.player_mission: Your mission is to defeat the final boss, the dinner-table decision: trace man's feeding behaviour from the vegetarian tree-dweller to the co-operative hunter who divided the spoils at dusk in the communal cave, with the fire at the entrance and his back against the wall, and then re-enact that safety at the restaurant with the prospect's back to a solid wall or screen, dimmed lights, muffled music, a round table and the prospect's view of others obscured by a screen or large green plant. Finish by weighing the physiology of the open space behind the back and the relaxation techniques top restaurants use to extract money from their customers' wallets.
key_concepts: Anthropologists tell us that man's origin was that of a tree-dweller who was strictly vegetarian, his diet consisting of roots, leaves, berries, fruit and the like, until about a million years ago he came out of the trees onto the plains to become a hunter of prey.

Prior to becoming a land dweller man's eating habits were those of the monkeys, involving continual nibbling throughout the day, with each individual entirely responsible for his own survival and for obtaining his own food.

As a hunter man needed the co-operation of other individuals to capture large prey, so large co-operative hunting groups were formed that would leave at sunrise to hunt throughout the day and return at dusk with the day's spoils.
The spoils of the hunt were divided equally among the hunters, who would eat inside a communal cave where a fire was lit at the entrance to ward off dangerous animals and to provide warmth.
Each caveman sat with his back against the wall of the cave to avoid the possibility of being attacked from behind while he was engrossed in eating his meal.

The ancient process of food sharing at dusk around an open fire was the beginning of a social event that modern man re-enacts in the form of barbecues, cookouts and dinner parties, and modern man reacts and behaves at these events in much the same way as he did over a million years ago.
A positive decision in your favour is easier to obtain when your prospect is relaxed, free of tension and his or her defensive barriers have been lowered.
Research shows that respiration, heart rate, brain wave frequencies and blood pressure rapidly increase when a person sits with his back to an open space, particularly where others are moving about.

Tension is further increased if the person's back is towards an open door or a window at ground level, so whether dining at home or at a restaurant you should have your prospect seated with his back to a solid wall or screen.

The lights should be dimmed and muffled background music played, and many top restaurants have an open fireplace or facsimile near the entrance of the restaurant to recreate the fire that burned at the ancient cave feasts.
It would be best to use a round table and to have your prospect's view of other people obscured by a screen or large green plant if you are to have a captive audience.

It is far easier to obtain a favourable decision in a relaxed restaurant than in one with bright lighting, tables and chairs placed in open areas and the banging of plates, knives and forks, which is why top restaurants use these types of relaxation techniques to extract large amounts of money from their customers' wallets for ordinary food, and men have been using them for thousands of years to create a romantic atmosphere for the benefit of their women.

assets.topic: Scrub the Power of Chairs: Size, Height, Accessories and Location
assets.visual_frame_description: A chair showroom floor morphs into an office: a throne with a 250-centimetre back towers beside a low-backed visitor's chair, a swivel chair spins freely while a fixed chair stays bolted, and a visitor sinks into a low sofa with his eyes level with the executive's desk top while an ashtray sits an inch beyond his fingers.
assets.player_mission: Your mission is to scrub through the three factors that make a chair a weapon of status: the size of the chair and its accessories, the height of the chair from the floor, and the location of the chair relative to the other person. Weigh the high-backed chair from the throne of kings and popes down to the executive's leather swivel, check off why swivel chairs beat fixed chairs, and trace the power plays of the competitive position, the lowered sofa and the ashtray set just out of the visitor's reach.
key_concepts: Pease asks whether you have ever felt overwhelmed or helpless when you sat in the visitor's chair at a job interview, where the interviewer seemed big and overwhelming while you felt small and insignificant.

It is likely that the interviewer had cunningly arranged his office furnishings to raise his own status and power and, in so doing, to lower yours, and certain strategies using chairs and seating arrangements can create this atmosphere in an office.

The factors involved in raising status and power by using chairs are the size of the chair and its accessories, the height of the chair from the floor and the location of the chair relative to the other person.

The height of the back of a chair raises or lowers a person's status, the high-backed chair being a well-known example, and the higher the back of the chair, the greater the power and status of the person sitting in it.

Kings, queens, popes and other high-status people may have the back of their throne or official chair as high as 250 centimetres, or over 8 feet, to show their status relative to their subjects, while the senior executive has a high-backed leather chair and his visitor's chair has a low back.
Swivel chairs have more power and status than fixed chairs because they allow the user freedom of movement when he is placed under pressure.
Fixed chairs allow little or no movement, and this lack of movement is compensated by body gestures that can reveal a person's attitudes and feelings.
Chairs with arm rests, chairs that lean back and chairs that have wheels are better than chairs that have none of these features.
Status is gained if your chair is adjusted higher off the floor than the other person's chair.

Some advertising executives are known for sitting on high-backed chairs adjusted for maximum height while their visitors sit opposite, in the competitive position, on a sofa or chair so low that their eyes are level with the executive's desk.
A common ploy is to have the ashtray just out of the visitor's reach, which forces him to be inconvenienced when ashing his cigarette.

As mentioned in the chapter on seating arrangements, the most power is exerted on the visitor when his chair is placed in the competitive position, and a common power play is to place the visitor's chair as far away as possible from the executive's desk into the social or public territory zone, which further reduces the visitor's status.

assets.topic: Dialogue with John: Diagnosing a Manager's Hostile Office
assets.visual_frame_description: A manager's office rendered in wireframe: a glass partition lets a row of employees stare through at the visitor's chair, the desk front is solid and hides the occupant, the visitor's back faces an open door, and a thought bubble over the seated manager shows him with both hands clasped behind his head and one leg hooked over the chair arm.
assets.player_mission: Your mission is to stage a dialogue with John, the newly promoted insurance manager whose employees disliked dealing with him: walk through the six observations of his office layout, from the visitor's chair in the competitive position and the clear glass partition that let the whole office watch, to the solid-fronted desk that hid his gestures, the visitor's back turned to the open door, his own threatening both-hands-behind-head and leg-over-chair poses, and the mismatch between his high-backed swivel and the visitor's plain fixed chair.
key_concepts: Pease presents a case study of John, an employee in an insurance company who had been promoted to a manager's position and was given an office, and after a few months in the role John found that the other employees disliked dealing with him and his relationship with them was occasionally hostile, particularly when they were in his office.
John found it difficult to get the employees to follow his instructions and guidance, and he heard that they were talking about him behind his back.

Pease's observations of John's plight revealed that the communication breakdowns were at their worst when the employees were in his office, and for the purpose of the exercise management skills were ignored to concentrate on the non-verbal aspects of the problem.
The first observation of John's office layout was that the visitor's chair was placed in the competitive position in relation to John.
The walls of John's office were timber panels except for an outside window and a clear glass partition that looked into the general office area.

The clear glass partition reduced John's status and could increase the power of a subordinate sitting in the visitor's chair because the other employees were directly behind him and could see what was happening.
John's desk had a solid front that hid the lower part of his body and prevented the subordinates from observing many of John's gestures.
The visitor's chair in John's office was placed so that the visitor's back was to the open door.
John often sat in the both-hands-behind-head position and in the leg-over-chair position whenever a subordinate was in his office.
John had a swivel chair with a high back, arm rests and wheels, while the visitor's chair was a plain low-backed chair with fixed legs and no arm rests.
Considering that between 60 and 80 per cent of human communication is done non-verbally, it was obvious to Pease that these aspects of John's non-verbal communication spelt disaster.

assets.topic: Audit the Fix: Six Rearrangements That Saved John's Office
assets.visual_frame_description: An office floor plan with a before and after split: the before plan shows the desk half-claimed by the visitor while the after plan shows the desk in front of a mirror-tinted partition, a corner-positioned hot seat, and a round table with three matching swivel chairs, while a tick list of six changes stamps past.
assets.player_mission: Your mission is to audit the six rearrangements made to John's office and their result: the desk moved in front of the glass partition, the hot seat swung into the corner position, the partition sprayed with a mirror finish, the round coffee table with three identical swivel chairs, the desk top claimed entirely by John, and his new relaxed open gestures with frequent palm displays, ending with employees calling John an easygoing and relaxed supervisor.
key_concepts: The first rearrangement was to place John's desk in front of the glass partition, making his office appear bigger and allowing him to be visible to those who entered his office.
The hot seat was placed in the corner position, making communication more open and allowing the corner to act as a partial barrier when necessary.

The glass partition was sprayed with a mirror finish, allowing John to see out while not permitting others to see in, which raised John's status and created a more intimate atmosphere within his office.
A round coffee table with three identical swivel chairs was placed at the other end of the office to allow informal meetings to take place on an equal level.
In the original layout John's desk gave half the table territory to the visitor, while the revised layout gave John complete claim to the desk top.
John practised relaxed open arms and legs gestures combined with frequent palm gestures when speaking with subordinates in his office.
The result of the rearrangements was that supervisor/employee relationships improved and the employees began describing John as an easygoing and relaxed supervisor.
The original layout, shown in Figure 163, gave the visitor half of John's desk territory, and Pease notes that most executive offices are arranged like the one in this figure.
The revised layout, shown in Figure 164, was created by treating the desk placement, the hot seat, the mirror-finished partition and the round coffee table as deliberate non-verbal statements.
John's case demonstrates that fixing the non-verbal signals of an office can solve supervisor/employee relationship problems that management skills alone had failed to fix.
Because the corner of the desk acted as a partial barrier in the revised layout, John could open communication without removing all protection.

assets.topic: Matrix Match: The Status Raiser Ledger of Office Objects
assets.visual_frame_description: A wall matrix of seven labelled cards, each showing an office object: a low sofa, a padlocked telephone, a distant ashtray, an overseas cigarette tin, red Confidential folders, a wall of framed awards and a slim briefcase; one card flips over to show a bulky stuffed briefcase with the caption carried by those who do all the work.
assets.player_mission: Your mission is to build a matrix of seven status raisers and match each object to its power effect: the low sofa, the telephone with a lock, the expensive ashtray beyond reach, the overseas cigarette container, the red Strictly Confidential folders, the wall of photos and awards, and the slim combination-lock briefcase versus the bulky briefcase of the worker who does all the work, then balance the ledger against the negative signals most executive offices unwittingly send.
key_concepts: Certain objects strategically placed around the office can be subtly used non-verbally to increase the status and power of the occupant.
Low sofas for visitors to sit on are one example of an object that raises the status of the office occupant by lowering the visitor.
A telephone with a lock on it is a status raiser, signalling that the occupant's phone line is important or restricted enough to need locking.
An expensive ashtray placed out of the reach of the visitor causes him inconvenience when ashing his cigarette, and is therefore a subtle status play.
A cigarette container from overseas raises status by hinting at foreign travel and connections beyond the ordinary office worker.
Some red folders left on the desk marked Strictly Confidential raise the occupant's status by implying he handles secret material.
A wall covered with photos, awards or qualifications that the occupant has received is a status raiser that displays his achievements to every visitor.
A slim briefcase with a combination lock raises status, while large, bulky briefcases are carried by those who do all the work.
All that is needed to raise your status, increase your power and increase your effectiveness with others is a little thought given to non-verbal gymnastics in your office or home.
Unfortunately, most executive offices are arranged like the one in Figure 163, and rarely is consideration given to the negative non-verbal signals that are unwittingly communicated to others.

assets.topic: Boss Level: Owning Your Office Layout as a Power Statement
assets.visual_frame_description: A boss arena that is an executive office seen from above: a visitor's chair floats far from the desk in the public territory zone while a high-backed swivel throne dominates, a mirror-finished partition reflects the visitor's image, and a checklist card slides in reading study your own office layout and make the positive changes needed.
assets.player_mission: Your mission is to defeat the final boss, the skill of reading and arranging the whole office as a power statement: open with the interview scene that started the chapter, then master the three chair factors, the territorial zones into which the visitor's chair is pushed, the glass partition and mirror finish as status levers, and close by studying your own office layout and applying the status raisers, because every desk, chair and wall either gives you power or quietly gives it away.
key_concepts: Pease opens the chapter by asking whether you have been for a job interview and felt overwhelmed or helpless when you sat in the visitor's chair, where the interviewer seemed so big and overwhelming and you felt small and insignificant.
The interviewer in such a scene had likely cunningly arranged his office furnishings to raise his own status and power and, in so doing, to lower yours.
Having read the book, you should be able to arrange your office furniture in such a way as to have as much power, status or control over others as you wish.

The factors involved in raising status and power by using chairs are the size of the chair and its accessories, the height of the chair from the floor and the location of the chair relative to the other person.
A common power play is to place the visitor's chair as far away as possible from the executive's desk, into the social or public territory zone, which further reduces the visitor's status.
The clear glass partition looked into the general office area and reduced John's status because the other employees were directly behind the visitor and could see what was happening.
Spraying the glass partition with a mirror finish allowed John to see out but not permitted others to see in, which raised his status and created a more intimate atmosphere within his office.
The high-backed chair is a well-known status device, and the higher the back of the chair, the greater the power and status of the person sitting in it.
Considering that between 60 and 80 per cent of human communication is done non-verbally, the non-verbal messages of an office layout can spell either disaster or success.
Pease suggests that you study your own office layout and use the preceding information to make the positive changes needed to raise your status, power and effectiveness with others.

assets.topic: Scrub the Method: From a Million Years of Gesture to the Art of Conscious Observation
assets.visual_frame_description: A montage of the century: a million-year timeline of gestures flares into a 1970s classroom where a chalkboard reads 'Society is your testing ground'; a playhead scrubs over figure cards of a bearded, sunglassed man hidden behind a folder while a clock ticks ninety seconds, and an eye-and-ear icon watches the observer watching himself.
assets.player_mission: Your mission is to scrub through Pease's closing framework: how body language has been going on for over a million years yet only became a science in the last twenty years, how it went popular in the 1970s and will end the century as part of formal education, why society is the best research and testing ground, and why conscious observation of your own actions and those of others is the master skill. Then weigh the reader's own test: study each picture sequence before reading the notes, see how much perceptiveness has improved, and keep in mind the ninety-second rule that decides first base in the Figure 171 encounter.
key_concepts: Communication through body language has been going on for over a million years but has only been scientifically studied to any extent in the last twenty years or so.
Body language became popular during the 1970s, and Pease predicts that by the end of the century its impact and meaning in human communication will be part of formal education.
Pease encourages the reader to seek further knowledge through his or her own research and experience and through the examples given in the book.
Ultimately, society will be your best research and testing ground for body language.

Conscious observation of your own actions and those of others is the best way for each person to gain a better understanding of the communication methods of the earth's most complex and interesting beast, man himself.
The remainder of the book is devoted to social and business situations and shows how gestures and body signals occur in clusters and the circumstances that may affect your interpretation.

Before reading the notes on each picture sequence, you are told to study each picture and see how many gestures you can interpret through what you have read, and you will be amazed to find how much your perceptiveness has improved.

Considering that people form 90 per cent of their opinion of someone in the first ninety seconds, the man in Figure 171, whose face is largely hidden by his beard and sunglasses, is unlikely ever to get to first base with another person.
Gestures and body signals occur in clusters, and the circumstances in which they appear may affect your interpretation of them.
The introduction of this final section promises the reader a better understanding of the communication methods of man through the testing ground of society.

assets.topic: Dialogue on the Open Hand and the Hidden Eye: Openness Versus Deceit Clusters
assets.visual_frame_description: Two lecterns face off across a stage: on one side a man with open palms and spread fingers glows neutral and non-threatening, while on the other a man rubs his eye, looks at the floor with raised disbelief eyebrows and wears a tight-lipped smile; between them floats a torn ledger of signals, nose touch, lint-picking, leg-over-chair, each stamped with its meaning.
assets.player_mission: Your mission is to stage a dialogue between two clusters: the openness cluster of Figure 165 with its exposed palms, spread fingers, neutral head and parted arms and legs, and the deceit clusters of Figures 166, 171, 177 and 179, with the eye rub and raised disbelief eyebrows, the tight-lipped insincere smile, the folder barrier and buttoned coat, the nose touch while speaking, the leg-over-chair indifference, the lint-picking disapproval, the gripped chair arms and locked ankles of the man holding back, and the story that fails to go across despite a perfect openness display.
key_concepts: Figure 165 is a good example of an openness cluster: the palms are fully exposed in the submissive position and the fingers are spread wide to give more impact to the gesture.
In Figure 165 the head is in the neutral position and the arms and legs are apart, and the man is communicating a submissive, non-threatening attitude.
Figure 166 is a classic deceit cluster: as the man rubs his eye he looks away towards the floor and both eyebrows are raised to the disbelief position.
In Figure 166 the man's head is turned away and down, showing a negative attitude, and he has an insincere, tight-lipped smile.

In Figure 167 inconsistency of gestures is obvious: the man is smiling confidently as he crosses the room but one hand has crossed his body to play with his watch and form a partial arm barrier, which shows that he is unsure of himself and/or his circumstances.

In Figure 177 the man on the right is causing the problem because of his negative gesture cluster, using the nose touch gesture (deceit) as he speaks and crossing his right arm over his body to make a partial arm barrier (defensive).
In Figure 177 the man on the right's lack of concern about the other men's opinions is shown by the leg-over-chair gesture, and his body is pointed away from them.
In Figure 177 the man on the left disapproves of what the man on the right has to say, using the lint-picking gesture (disapproval) with his legs crossed (defensive) and pointed away (uninterested).
In Figure 177 the man in the middle would like to say something but is holding back his opinion, shown by his self-restraint gesture of gripping the arms of the chair and locked ankles.

In Figure 179 the man on the left is using an excellent gesture cluster to convey openness and honesty, with exposed palms, foot forward, head up, coat unbuttoned, arms and legs apart, leaning forward and smiling gestures, but unfortunately for him his story is not going across.

assets.topic: Audit the Status Ledger: Dominance, Superiority and Territorial Claims
assets.visual_frame_description: An audit ledger unrolls across a boardroom: columns for CHAIR, HANDS and TERRITORY receive stamps, a high-back wheeled chair with a telephone lock is checked off, and exhibit cards show a man with both hands on his head and feet on the desk, a straddler with clenched fingers and locked feet, an eye-blocking nose-looker, and a lapel-grasper flicking a thumb-point at his neighbour.
assets.player_mission: Your mission is to audit the ledger of status signals: check off the both-hands-on-head know-it-all, the feet-on-desk territorial claim, the locking telephone and the high-status leaning-back wheeled chair of Figure 169; then walk the Figure 173 boardroom, the straddled chair and direct body point of the controller, the clenched fingers and locked feet of the frustrated speaker, the hands-behind-head and figure 4 leg lock of the competitor, and the low-status fixed chair that leaves its occupant buying nothing; then close the books with the eye block and the look down the nose, the wine glass barrier, the thumbs-in-waistcoat and the lapel-grasping thumb-up in Figures 175 and 176.
key_concepts: In Figure 169 dominance, superiority and territoriality are evident: the both-hands-on-head gesture shows a superior know-it-all attitude and feet-on-desk shows a territorial claim to it.
In Figure 169 the man further highlights his status with a high-status, leaning-back chair with wheels and a telephone with a lock on it, and he is also sitting in the defensive/competitive position.

In Figure 173 the man on the left is straddling his chair in an attempt to take control of the discussion or to dominate the man on the right, and he is also using the direct body point at the man on the right.

In Figure 173 the man on the left has clenched fingers and his feet are locked together under his chair, showing a frustrated attitude, which means that he is probably having difficulty in getting his point across.

In Figure 173 the man in the centre feels superior to the other two because of the hands-behind-head gesture he has taken, and he also has the figure 4 leg lock position, meaning that he will compete or be argumentative.

In Figure 173 the man in the centre has a high-status chair that swivels, leans back and has wheels and arm rests, while the man on the right is seated on a low-status chair that has fixed legs and no accessories.
In Figure 173 the man on the right has his arms and legs tightly crossed (defensive) and his head down (hostile), indicating that he does not buy what he hears.

In Figure 175 the man on the left is using superiority gestures and appears to have an arrogant attitude, using the eye block signal as his brain attempts to block the other man from sight and tilting his head back to look down his nose at him.
In Figure 175 the man on the left's defensiveness is also evident as his knees are held tightly together and he is holding his wine glass with both hands to form a barrier.
In Figure 175 the man in the middle seems aloof as shown by his thumbs-in-waistcoat gesture (superiority), leaning back on his chair and using a crotch display, with his head in the neutral position.
In Figure 176 the man in the middle shows superiority and sarcasm using the lapel-grasping gesture with a thumb-up (superiority) plus a thumb-point gesture toward the man on his left (ridicule).

assets.topic: Matrix Match: Aggression, Readiness and Courtship on the Social Grid
assets.visual_frame_description: A four-cell grid on a party floor: cells labeled READINESS, TERRITORY, COURTSHIP and DEFENCE fill with cards, two men pointing bodies at each other, a woman blowing smoke upward toward a preening tie-adjuster, a mirrored couple forming bookends on a couch, and a timeline strip where three strangers unfold from crossed arms to a courtship display while the excluded man grips his hips.
assets.player_mission: Your mission is to drop every signal card into the social grid: the hands-on-hips man and the thumbs-in-belt man of Figure 172 with their body points aimed and turned away; the courtship cluster of Figure 174 with its forward foot, hand-on-hip and thumb-in-belt readiness, exposed wrist and upward-blown smoke against the unimpressed man blowing smoke down; the mirroring bookends of Figure 178 exposing their wrists on the couch; and the whole Figure 180 to 182 party sequence, from the first-meeting defensive fold to the complete courtship display with tighter belt grip, hair touching, exposed cleavage and the loser's hands-on-hips displeasure.
key_concepts: In Figure 172 both men are using aggressive and readiness gestures, the man on the left using the hands-on-hips gesture and the man on the right the thumbs-in-belt.

In Figure 172 the man on the left is less aggressive than the man on the right as he is leaning backwards and his body is pointing away from the man on the right, while the man on the right assumes an intimidating pose by pointing his body directly at the other man.

In Figure 174 the woman is displaying the classic courtship gestures: one foot forward pointing towards the man on the far left (interest), a combination of hand-on-hip and thumb-in-belt (sexual readiness), her left wrist exposed and her cigarette smoke blown upwards (confident, positive).
In Figure 174 the man on the far left is responding to her courtship gestures by adjusting his tie (preening) and pointing his foot at her, with his head up (interested).

In Figure 174 the man in the centre is obviously unimpressed with the other man, with his body pointing away, an aggressive sideways glance, palms out of sight and cigarette smoke blown down (negative), and he is leaning against the wall (territorial aggression).

In Figure 178 the man on the left and the woman have mirrored each other's gestures and are forming bookends on the couch, having positioned their hands so that they can expose their wrists and having crossed their legs toward one another.

In Figure 180 the three people all have their arms folded, two have their legs crossed (defensive) and all have their bodies oriented away from each other, all indicating that they have just met for the first time.

In Figure 181 the man on the left has uncrossed his legs and is pointing one foot at the woman (interest) and using the thumbs-in-belt gesture, which is intended either for the other man, in which case the attitude is aggression, or for the woman, making it a sexual signal.

In Figure 182 the man on the left has kept his thumbs-in-belt, foot-forward position and has turned his body slightly towards the woman, making it a complete courtship display, with his thumbs gripping the belt much tighter and his body become even more erect.

In Figure 182 the woman is responding to this courtship display with her own, uncrossing her arms, turning her body toward him and pointing one foot at him, with courtship gestures including hair touching, exposed wrists, chest forward with exposed cleavage and a positive facial expression.
In Figure 182 the man on the right appears unhappy about being excluded and is using the hands-on-hips gesture (aggressive readiness) to show his displeasure.

assets.topic: Boss Level: Read the Photo Sequence, Disapproval to Victory
assets.visual_frame_description: A boss door opens onto a gallery of photo cards: each card is a freeze-frame in which one signal glows and is tagged, a sideways-glancing woman with down-turned mouth corners, a teeth-baring child with hands on hips, a folder-shielded man whose eyes are hidden, a man pointed at the exit, a middle man locked out by a closed formation, and a final card reading 'The man on the left has won the woman's attentions'.
assets.player_mission: Your mission is to defeat the final boss, the live photo-sequence: decode the disapproving sideways-glancing woman of Figure 168 with her down-turned eyebrows, arm-cross and mouth corners; the defiant hands-on-hips child baring her teeth in Figure 170; the negative wall of Figure 171 with its folder barrier, buttoned coat and hidden eyes; the ready-to-leave starter's position and the closed body formation of Figures 175 and 176; the tense maximum-distance circle of Figure 177; the inconsistent tightlipped smile of Figure 178; the woman's clenched-fist rebuttal and the middle man's steeple and figure 4 in Figure 179; and finally the party verdict, that the man on the left has won the woman's attentions and the other man should look elsewhere.
key_concepts: In Figure 168 the woman disapproves of the person at whom she is looking, having turned neither her head nor body toward him but giving him a sideways glance with her head slightly down (disapproval).
In Figure 168 the woman's eyebrows are slightly turned down (anger), she has a full arm-cross gesture (defensive) and the corners of her mouth are turned down.

In Figure 170 the hands-on-hips gesture is used by the child to make herself appear larger and more threatening, with the chin jutting forward to show defiance and the mouth opened wide to expose the teeth, just as animals do before they attack.

The cluster in Figure 171 can be summed up in one word, negative: the folder has been used as a barrier, the arms and legs are folded due to nervousness or defensiveness, the coat is buttoned and the sunglasses hide any eye or pupil signals.
In Figure 171 much of the man's face is hidden by his beard, which gives him a suspicious appearance, and the wearer of the cluster is unlikely to get to first base with another person.

In Figure 175 the man on the right has heard enough and has taken the starter's position (ready to leave), with his foot and body pointed toward the nearest exit and his eyebrows, mouth corners and head slightly down, all demonstrating disapproval.
In Figure 176 the man on the left and the man on the right have taken the closed body formation to show the middle man that he is not accepted into the conversation.

In Figure 176 the man on the left of the sequence responds defensively with crossed legs and aggressively with the upper-arm grip gesture (self-control) and a sideways glance, and he also has a palm-in-pocket (unwilling to participate) while looking at the floor and using the pain-in-neck gesture.

In Figure 177 all three men are sitting back in their chairs to keep the maximum distance from each other, and the man in the middle has issued a non-verbal challenge to the man on the right by pointing his body at him.

In Figure 178 the man in the middle has a tightlipped smile which can make him appear interested in what the other man has to say, but it is not consistent with his other facial and body gestures, including head down (disapproval), eyebrows down (anger) and a sideways glance.

In Figure 179 the woman is sitting back in her chair with her legs crossed away (defensive), a partial arm-barrier (defensive), a clenched fist (hostile), head down and the critical evaluation gesture (hand to face), while the man in the middle uses the raised steeple gesture indicating confidence or superiority in the figure 4 leg position.
In summary of the party sequence, the man on the left has won the woman's attentions and the other man should look elsewhere for a partner.
